title: Chromebook will not turn on
steps: Put the Chromebook on a desk. Look for the charging port on its side; use only the school charger that fits without force.
Ask your teacher to connect it to an approved outlet if needed. Wait 10–15 minutes and look for a light near the charging port.
Open the lid and press the power key or side power button once. Look for a sign-in screen. If there is no light or screen, tell your teacher.
why: A drained battery may need time to charge. Never open the device or use a damaged charger.

alternatives.label: It is on but the screen is dark

title: Chromebook will not charge
steps: Look at the cable and plug without pulling them apart. If you see damage, smell burning or feel unusual heat, stop and tell an adult.
Check that the approved charger is plugged into the Chromebook and an approved outlet. Do not force the connector.
If the screen works, click the clock at bottom right and look at the battery symbol for a charging indicator. If it does not charge, ask your teacher to test a school spare.
why: Using the correct charger and intact cables matters.

alternatives.label: The charger only works at an angle

title: Chromebook touchpad not working
steps: Find the flat rectangle below the keyboard. Wipe your fingers dry; use only a clean dry cloth if your teacher permits.
Slide one finger across the center without pressing down. Watch for the arrow moving on screen.
Tap once on an ordinary button. If neither movement nor tapping works, ask to try a school USB mouse.
why: Touchpads need clean, dry contact.

title: Right-click on a Chromebook
steps: Place the pointer over the item you want to open a menu for.
Tap the touchpad with two fingers at the same time. A small menu should appear beside the pointer.
Choose the needed command or click an empty area to dismiss the menu.
why: A two-finger tap opens the context menu on most Chromebooks.

title: Take a Chromebook screenshot
steps: Find Show windows on the top row: it looks like a rectangle with two lines beside it. Press Ctrl + Show windows for a full screen picture.
Look for a small capture notification. Click its preview if you need to see what was captured.
Open Files using Shift + Alt + M, then My files > Downloads. Find the recent PNG. If you see private information, do not submit it.
why: The Show windows key typically looks like a rectangle with two lines beside it.

alternatives.label: I only need part of the screen

title: Chromebook screen too dark
steps: Find the little sun and large sun keys on the top keyboard row. Press the large sun key a few times.
Look for a brightness bar on screen. If it appears, stop when the screen is readable.
If no bar or picture appears, connect the approved charger and ask your teacher if the screen remains dark.
why: Brightness is an everyday control, not an administrator setting.

title: Chromebook screen is sideways
steps: Tell your teacher that the picture is turned sideways or upside down, not that the Chromebook itself is broken.
Show them the screen without changing its orientation settings. Ask them to restore the approved view.
why: Display settings can affect accessibility and classroom equipment; do not experiment with them.

title: Chromebook is frozen
steps: Wait briefly, then move a finger on the touchpad. Check whether the pointer moves.
Press Alt + Tab once to see if another open app responds. If it does, return to the original app and save any work you can.
If only a webpage is stuck, ask before closing its tab; if nothing responds, tell your teacher before restarting.
why: A forced power-off can lose unsaved work.

title: Chromebook no sound
steps: Find the speaker with sound waves on the top row and press it once or twice. Look for the volume bar.
In the video player, move the pointer over the video and look near the bottom for its speaker icon. If crossed out, click it when audio is allowed.

If using wired headphones, lower the volume and check that the plug is fully seated in the matching port. Try the assigned audio again. If silent, tell your teacher whether speakers or headphones were in use.
why: Device volume and app volume are separate.

title: Chromebook Wi-Fi problem
steps: Click the clock at the bottom right. Look for the Wi-Fi symbol and the name of the connected network, without changing it.
Open another teacher-approved page in a new tab. If both fail, tell your teacher the connection appears unavailable.
If just one page fails, note its exact error message. Do not join another network or bypass a blocked page.
why: The teacher can distinguish a network outage from a device issue.

alternatives.label: Wi-Fi is connected but the page fails
It asks me to sign in

title: Find a Chromebook download
steps: Press Shift + Alt + M to open Files, or press Launcher (the key where Caps Lock usually sits), type Files and click the blue folder app.
In the left column click My files, then Downloads. If Downloads is already visible, click it directly.
Look in the Name column for your filename. Click Date modified to find recent files if needed. If missing, open Chrome and press Ctrl + J to check downloads.
why: Local Downloads and Google Drive are different locations.

alternatives.label: I need to search for a file

title: Switch apps on Chromebook
steps: Hold Alt and tap Tab. A strip of open windows should appear.
Keep holding Alt and tap Tab until the window you want is highlighted, then release Alt.
If you prefer clicking, press Show windows (rectangle with lines on the top row) and click the preview of your app.
why: Your work can be open behind another window.

title: Mouse not moving
steps: Follow the cord from your mouse to the computer. If there is no cord, look underneath for an ON/OFF switch.
With permission, check that your own USB plug or receiver is seated in an accessible port. Move the mouse on a plain mouse pad.
Watch the arrow on screen. If it stays still, ask to try a school spare; if the keyboard also fails, tell the teacher.
why: The connection, surface or mouse power can prevent movement.

title: Switch mouse handedness
steps: Ask your teacher first. Click the Windows logo on the taskbar and type Mouse settings; open the matching Settings result.
Look for Primary mouse button (Windows 11) or Select your primary button (Windows 10). Choose Right for left-handed use or Left for right-handed use.
Test the primary button on an empty area. Close Settings without changing anything else. If blocked, ask staff.
why: This is a specifically allowed example of a basic accessibility adjustment, subject to school rules.

title: Mouse scroll wheel not working
steps: Open a long page in an approved app. Put the pointer over its text, not the toolbar.
Roll the wheel toward you to move down the page. Look for the scrollbar on the right moving.
Drag the scrollbar thumb instead. If that works but the wheel fails in several apps, ask to test a spare mouse.
why: Some panels capture scroll input differently.

title: Keyboard not responding
steps: Click inside a blank part of your own document until a blinking text cursor appears. Type a test word.
If no letters appear, follow the keyboard cord to its accessible USB plug. With permission check that it is seated.
Tap Caps Lock and look for its indicator if present. If nothing responds or the mouse also fails, tell the teacher.
why: An inactive text field may make a working keyboard seem broken.

title: Number keypad not typing numbers
steps: Find Num Lock near the top of the separate number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard.
Tap it once, then click in a blank document and try the number 5 on the pad.
If the pad still moves the cursor instead, use the number row above the letters and ask staff.
why: Num Lock changes the keypad's usual behavior.

title: Letters are all capitalized
steps: Find Caps Lock directly left of A. Tap it once; its indicator may turn off.
Click in a blank document and type a few letters without holding Shift.
If capitals remain, release both Shift keys. If a key is stuck, ask staff rather than pulling it off.
why: Caps Lock and Shift affect letter capitalization.

title: Monitor is black
steps: Look along the monitor's bottom edge or back edge for a small power light and power symbol. If permitted, press the monitor power button once.
Check whether the computer itself has a power light. If the monitor displays No signal, it has power but may lack a picture.
Tell the teacher which lights or messages you see. Do not reach behind heavy equipment or move power cables.
why: A monitor can be off even when the computer is running.

title: Headphones have no sound
steps: Pause the video. Follow the headset cable to its assigned USB or round audio port; check it is seated with permission.
Find any volume wheel or mute switch on the headset cable or earcup. Click the speaker symbol in the Windows taskbar near the clock and check volume.
Play a teacher-approved sound at low volume. If speakers play instead or only one ear works, choose that related guide.
why: Many headsets have their own controls.

title: Microphone does not work
steps: Find the microphone boom or inline mute switch on your headset. Some headsets mute when the boom is raised.
In the approved app, look along the meeting controls for a microphone symbol; a slash usually means muted. Unmute only when directed.
Use the app's mic test if allowed. If access is denied or no level moves, tell the teacher; do not change permissions.
why: Microphone access is controlled by the school and the app.

title: Webcam is not showing video
steps: Look at the camera lens above the screen or on the external webcam. With permission open its physical privacy cover if present.
In the approved app, find the video camera icon in the meeting controls. A slash indicates video is off; enable only when directed.
Check for your preview. If another app is using the camera or access is blocked, choose the matching help topic.
why: Camera privacy restrictions should not be bypassed.

title: USB device not recognized
steps: Check that this is your assigned USB device. Match its plug shape to an approved accessible port without force.
For a flash drive press Windows+E, then click This PC in the left column. Look under Devices and drives for its name.
For a mouse or other peripheral test its normal action. If missing, ask staff; never format, install drivers or use unknown USB devices.
why: A school policy or hardware issue may prevent USB devices from appearing.

alternatives.label: What kind of USB plug is this?

title: Drawing tablet pen not working
steps: Check that the pen belongs to your assigned tablet. Hover over the drawing surface and watch the pointer.
In Photoshop open a practice document, press B, and select a visible unlocked pixel layer in the Layers panel.
Try a small stroke. If hover works but ink does not appear, use the tablet drawing guide. If hover fails, tell staff.
why: A locked layer can look like a tablet problem.

title: Windows app is frozen
steps: If the pointer spins or the title bar says Not Responding, wait about a minute without repeated clicks.
Try clicking the app title bar once. If it responds, save your own project using Ctrl+S.
If it stays frozen, tell the teacher the app and whether the file was saved. Do not force-close or restart shared computers.
why: Closing an unresponsive program can lose work.

title: Take a Windows screenshot
steps: Find the Windows logo key near the bottom left of the keyboard. Hold it and Shift, tap S, then release.
When the screen dims, use the rectangular capture option and drag around only your own work.
Click the capture notification if shown. In Snipping Tool use the disk/save icon to choose your assigned folder, or paste with Ctrl+V into your slide.
why: Capture only your own permitted work, not another student's information.

alternatives.label: Capture only part of the screen

title: Find a minimized Windows app
steps: Look at the taskbar along the bottom for the icon of the app you were using. Click it once.
If several previews appear, choose the one showing your document name.
If you cannot identify it, hold Alt and tap Tab until the desired window is highlighted, then release Alt.
why: Minimizing does not close an app.

title: Printer did not print
steps: If you have permission to print, open your document and press Ctrl+P (or File > Print).
Find the printer name and preview. Compare the name with the one assigned by the teacher; check pages and copies.
If you already clicked Print, do not send again. Tell the teacher the document, printer and time you sent it.
why: Repeated printing wastes paper and can duplicate jobs.

title: Game controller not responding
steps: Check the controller's cable or power light. Only use your assigned controller and accessible connection.
Click inside the approved game's play area. Look for Controls or Help in its pause menu to see whether controllers are supported.
Try a movement in practice mode. If nothing responds, ask staff rather than pairing or installing software.
why: Not every classroom game supports controllers.

alternatives.label: Menus work but game does not

Check that the status says Turned in. Seeing an attached file alone does not mean you submitted it.

Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Check whether the filename has finished loading. If a progress indicator is moving, wait; do not click Turn in again.
If you get an error, read the message. Keep your original file saved and show the error to your teacher. Do not unsubmit or delete files to try to fix it.
why: Some submission errors need teacher action.

title: Find teacher feedback
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Look beside or below Your work for Private comments. Scroll down on a small screen.
Look near the assignment title for the score and rubric, if returned. Click your attachment to see comments inside the document.
Read the feedback before editing. If nothing is visible, ask whether the work has been returned.
why: Returned work may include specific correction instructions.

title: Resubmit corrected work
aliases: how do i turn in corrections
steps: Ask your teacher whether corrections are allowed for this assignment before changing your submission.

At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.

why: Resubmission can affect the recorded submission time.

title: Find a missing assignment
steps: Open Classroom and click the class tile matching your schedule.
Click Classwork at the top. Choose the topic in the left list, or scroll through All topics.
Press Ctrl+F and type a few words from the assignment title. Press Esc to close the search after finding it.
If you cannot locate it, click the Classroom menu at upper left, choose To-do, and check Missing or Assigned. Ask your teacher if it is still absent.
why: Classwork is often organized by topic rather than date.

title: Find a Google Drive file
aliases: where did my drive file go
cant find my google drive file
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Click Search in Drive at the top. Type two or three words from the file name and press Enter.
If no result, click Recent or Shared with me on the left. Check your school account using the profile icon at top right.
Open the matching file and check its title and contents before editing.
why: A shared file may not appear in My Drive.

title: File says access denied
steps: On the access denied page, look at the account shown or the profile icon at top right. Confirm it is your assigned school account.
Return to Classroom, open the correct class and Classwork, then open the original assignment link.
If it still says You need access, ask your teacher to check sharing. Do not use another student’s account.
why: The file owner or school controls access.

title: Rename a file
steps: In Google Docs, Slides or Sheets, click the name at the upper left, type the required name and press Enter.
For a downloaded file, open Files (Chromebook) or File Explorer (Windows), right-click your file and choose Rename.
Enter the new base name. Keep the extension such as .png or .psd unchanged. Check the new name appears.
why: Clear filenames make your work easier to find.

title: Make a copy of a Google file
steps: Open the Google document your teacher permits you to copy.
Click File at upper left, then Make a copy. Enter a new name and choose your school Drive folder in the dialog.
Click Make a copy. Check the new tab title before editing; do not submit a copy if the teacher requires the original assigned document.
why: A copy is separate from the original and may not be automatically attached in Classroom.

title: Find a Windows download
aliases: where did my download go windows
steps: On Windows, press Windows+E to open File Explorer. Click Downloads in the left navigation list.
Look for the filename or sort by Date modified. Double-click your file to check it.
If missing, open Chrome and press Ctrl+J. Find the download and use Show in folder if offered.
why: The browser and the file browser can help locate downloads.

title: Understand file types
aliases: png jpg psd ai pdf zip
steps: Look at the filename in Files or File Explorer. The ending after the last dot is called the extension.
PNG and JPG are pictures; PSD and AI are editable Adobe files; PDF is a document; ZIP contains other files.
If the extension is hidden, right-click the file and check Properties on Windows or file information on Chromebook. Compare to your assignment requirements; renaming does not convert a file.
why: Exporting actually converts a file to a different format.

title: Open a ZIP file
steps: Open Files on Chromebook or File Explorer on Windows and choose Downloads. Find the teacher-provided ZIP file.

Windows: right-click the ZIP, choose Extract All, choose your folder and click Extract. Chromebook: double-click the ZIP in Files, select the needed contents, copy them, then paste into your own approved folder.
Open the extracted folder and check the individual files. Do not run unknown programs from an archive.
why: A ZIP is a container; files often need to be extracted first.

title: Save work in the correct folder
steps: In your editing app, open File at the top left. Use Save for the same project or Save As for a new copy.
In the dialog, select your assigned folder on the left or navigate to it. Enter the filename, keep the editable file type and click Save.
Open Files or File Explorer and navigate to that same folder. Check the file name is there. If a cloud document, check its title and save status instead.
why: A successful save is not the same as a Classroom submission.

title: Google Docs text formatting
steps: Drag over the words until they are blue-highlighted.
Above the page, look for the font name and number boxes or B, I and U buttons. Pick the requested style.
Click back in the page and check that only your selected words changed. Undo with Ctrl+Z if needed.
why: Formatting changes appearance, not the content of your work.

title: Google Docs page break
steps: Click immediately before the first word that belongs on the next page.
At the top choose Insert > Break > Page break, or press Ctrl+Enter.
The following text should move to the next page. If Pages mode is missing, ask your teacher before changing File > Page setup.
why: A page break is more reliable than many empty lines.

title: Insert image in Google Docs
steps: Click in the document where the picture should appear.
At the top choose Insert > Image > Upload from computer, or Drive for an approved Drive image.
In the file picker select your own image and click Open or Insert. Click the picture and drag a corner to resize it.
why: Choose an image you have permission to use.

title: Google Slides presentation mode
steps: Open your presentation and click the slide thumbnail on the left where you want to begin.
Click Slideshow near the upper right, beside Share.
Use the right and left arrow keys to move; press Esc to return to editing. If it opens on the wrong slide, select the correct thumbnail first.
why: Presenting is different from editing the slides.

title: Google Slides crop a picture
steps: Click the picture on the slide once; a blue border should appear.
Click the Crop image button above the slide (two overlapping right angles). Black crop handles appear.
Drag a black edge or corner inward to hide that part, then press Enter. Undo if you cropped too much.
why: Cropping changes the visible area rather than merely stretching the picture.

title: Add a Google Slides text box
steps: Choose Insert > Text box from the top menu.
Drag a rectangle on the slide where your words should go.
Type your own text inside it. Select the text and use the font and size controls above the slide.
why: TechGuide can explain the tool but cannot write your text.

title: Google Sheets formula not working
steps: Click the cell that displays an error. Look at the formula bar beside fx above the column letters.
Read the error message by hovering over or selecting the cell. Check that your formula begins with = and that parentheses and references match your lesson.
Correct your own typing mistake in the formula bar and press Enter. If it still fails, show the teacher the exact error.
why: The syntax matters; TechGuide will not solve assignment calculations.

title: Google Sheets cell text is cut off
steps: Click the cell with the cut-off words.
Choose Format > Wrapping > Wrap from the top menu.
The row should expand to show the words. If still narrow, drag the boundary between its column letter and the next letter to the right.
why: Wrapping can make long text visible without changing the text itself.

title: Google Forms cannot submit
steps: Scroll to the bottom of the form and click Submit only after completing your own answers.
If it stays on the form, look for red text below a question or a required asterisk. Read the exact warning and fix your own entry.
Try Submit again; look for a confirmation page. If the form is closed or access denied, ask your teacher instead of switching accounts.
why: Required fields must be complete before the form accepts a response.

title: Google Meet audio or camera
steps: In the meeting, move your pointer over the window and locate the microphone and camera icons along the bottom.
With permission, click the needed icon once if it has a slash. Check that your approved headset is connected and the camera cover is open if video is required.
Ask your teacher if they can hear or see you. If a crossed-out icon remains or the browser blocks access, ask staff for help.
why: School-managed permissions must be respected.

title: Website will not load
steps: Check the tab address against the link your teacher gave you. Do not try alternate addresses to bypass a block.
If you have no unsaved form answers, click the circular reload arrow beside the address bar once.
Open another approved class site in a new tab. If both fail, tell your teacher; if only one fails, report its exact error.
why: A loading error may be a website, connection or school policy issue.

title: Browser page looks too big or small
steps: Click inside the browser tab that looks wrong.
Press Ctrl+0 to restore normal page zoom only if you do not need your current accessibility zoom.
Use Ctrl+plus or Ctrl+minus to fit the page comfortably. If only document text is tiny, use the document font size or zoom instead.
why: Browser zoom is separate from system display scaling.

title: Reopen an accidentally closed tab
steps: Click the Chrome window where the tab was closed.
Press Ctrl+Shift+T once. A tab should reopen near the others at the top.
Check its title and contents. Unsaved answers might not return; ask your teacher before restarting an assessment.
why: The browser may remember recently closed tabs.

title: Browser full screen stuck
steps: If a video is filling the screen, press Esc first.
If Chrome itself fills the screen without tabs, press F11 on Windows or the full-screen top-row key on a Chromebook (rectangle with corners).
Check that tabs and the address bar return. If your lesson uses a locked test screen, do not try to exit it; ask your teacher.
why: Browser full-screen and video full-screen are different modes.

title: Website is blocked by school
steps: Stop at the block notice and leave the page as it is.
Tell your teacher the name of the assigned resource and the error shown; do not enter account details into a block page.
Wait for school staff to decide whether access is allowed. Do not use proxies, alternate links or another account to get around it.
why: Only authorized staff can review school access restrictions.

title: Suspicious pop-up or message
steps: Do not press buttons inside the pop-up, download files, call a number or enter information.
If it is an ordinary browser tab, close it using the X on the tab at the top, not a button inside the alert.
Tell your teacher what appeared and whether you clicked anything. If you cannot close it safely, leave it alone and ask for help.
why: Fake alerts often try to pressure people into unsafe actions.

title: Forgot school password
aliases: i cant login to google school account
cant sign in to my school google account
steps: Check that the sign-in page is the one your teacher provided and the displayed school username is yours.
Look for a Caps Lock indicator on your keyboard or screen. Try your known password carefully once.
If it fails, stop guessing and ask the teacher or approved school support for a reset. Never share your password with TechGuide.
why: Account recovery is handled through the school's approved process.

title: Photoshop Layers panel is missing
aliases: where are the layers in photoshop
steps: At the very top of Photoshop, click Window, then Layers. Look on the right side for the layer thumbnail list.
If Layers is already checked but hidden, check the small panel icons along the right edge. Click Layers to expand it.
If most Photoshop panels disappeared, click Window > Workspace > Essentials (Default) and then Window > Workspace > Reset Essentials (some versions show Reset > Essentials (Default)).
If everything is still hidden, finish editing any text and press Tab once. Ask your teacher if Layers does not return.
why: Panels can be closed without deleting the document's layers.

title: Photoshop brush will not paint
steps: Press B for Brush. Open Window > Layers and click the image thumbnail of a visible editable layer or create a blank layer with the + at the bottom.
At the top, set Mode to Normal and Opacity and Flow to 100% for a test. Click the front color square at the bottom of the left toolbar and pick a contrasting color.
Make a short test stroke on the blank layer. If it works there, check the original layer's lock, mask and selection boundary; undo the test with Ctrl+Z.
why: Layer state, selections and brush options all affect painting.

alternatives.label: Smart Object cannot be directly edited

title: Remove moving dotted selection lines
steps: Look for moving dashed lines around part of your image. They show the current selection, not a permanent mark.
When you no longer need that selection, click Select at the top and choose Deselect, or press Ctrl+D.
The dashed outline should disappear. If edits are still limited, check whether you are painting a layer mask instead of the image.
why: The dotted boundary marks the selected area; deselecting does not delete the pixels.

title: Photoshop image will not move
steps: Press V to choose Move. Open Window > Layers; click the row containing the object you want to move.
At the top, turn off Auto-Select if clicking the canvas picks a different layer. Check for a lock beside the chosen layer.
Drag a small distance on the canvas. If the layer is locked or the wrong object moves, undo and ask before unlocking a protected layer.
why: The Move tool moves the selected layer or object.

title: Photoshop picture disappeared
steps: Open Window > Layers. Find the missing photo by its thumbnail; click the empty square to its left if no eye is visible.
Check Opacity near the top of Layers. If the photo is behind an opaque layer, temporarily toggle that upper layer's eye to test.
If a mask is attached, Shift-click its thumbnail to temporarily disable it, then Shift-click again to restore it. Do not delete layers to find the photo.
why: Hidden or covered layers may still exist.

title: Photoshop text is hard to see
steps: Open Window > Layers and find the row with a T thumbnail. Turn on its eye if needed.
Press T, select the text layer, and use the font size and color controls in the bar across the top. Choose a color that contrasts with the background.
If text is behind a picture, drag its layer above that picture in Layers. Click the checkmark at the top to finish editing and inspect at Ctrl+0.
why: Text needs contrast and the correct layer order.

title: Add a stroke to Photoshop text
aliases: how to put an outline on text
make text have a colored edge photoshop
steps: Open Window > Layers and click the row with the T thumbnail for your title.
At the bottom of Layers click fx, then Stroke. In the Layer Style dialog choose Position: Outside, Opacity: 100%, and click the Color swatch to choose a contrasting color.
Increase Size a few pixels until the outline is visible in Preview. Click OK. If it looks too thick, expand Effects beneath the text layer and double-click Stroke to adjust it.
why: A stroke outlines the text while keeping the text layer editable.

title: Export a Photoshop PNG or JPG
steps: Save the editable PSD with Ctrl+S first. At the top click File > Export > Export As.
On the right of the export dialog choose PNG or JPG in Format. Check the preview and required dimensions; for an opaque background make sure the canvas already has the required background color.
Click Export, pick the assigned folder, and give the file a clear name. In Windows File Explorer (Windows+E), open that folder and double-click the exported image to verify it.
why: PNG can preserve transparency; JPG does not. Keep the editable PSD separately.

alternatives.label: Find where Photoshop saved a file

title: Save a Photoshop PSD
steps: Click File > Save As. If Photoshop asks where to save, choose On your computer when the assignment requires a local file.
In the save dialog choose the teacher-approved folder, type your project filename and select Photoshop (*.PSD) in the format list.
Click Save and accept the compatibility prompt if shown. Check the document tab for the .psd name; do not replace your editable file with a PNG.
why: A PSD preserves editable Photoshop features better than an exported JPG.

title: Photoshop eraser not working
steps: Press E for Eraser and open Window > Layers. Click the image thumbnail, not the white or black mask thumbnail.
Check the eye and lock on the layer. At the top choose a visible brush size and 100% opacity for a test. Check for a selection limiting the area.
If the layer is a Smart Object or type layer, do not rasterize it just to erase; use a layer mask instead. Undo any unwanted test erasing.
why: Erasing pixels can be destructive; a mask may be safer.

alternatives.label: Smart Object cannot be directly edited

title: Photoshop image looks pixelated
steps: Press Ctrl+1 to see the image at 100%. If the pixels look normal there, the earlier blur may have been from zooming far in.
Click Image > Image Size and read Width and Height in pixels without changing them. Compare with the assignment and source image size.
If the source was enlarged a lot, replace it with an approved higher-resolution image rather than repeatedly resizing it. Ctrl+0 restores fit view.
why: Zoom and source resolution are different; enlarging does not restore lost detail.

title: Photoshop layer mask basics
aliases: layer mask white rectangle black circle
how to use the japan flag in photoshop
steps: Open Window > Layers. Select your picture layer and click the rectangle-with-circle icon at the bottom to add a mask if it has none.
Click the mask thumbnail (usually white) beside the image thumbnail. Press B, then D for default colors; paint black to hide pixels and white to reveal them (X swaps colors).
Use a small test stroke; the image itself should remain intact. Click the image thumbnail again before editing actual pixels.
why: Masks hide pixels without permanently erasing them.

title: Change part of a photo's color
steps: Select the clothing or object with Quick Selection (hold the selection-tool icon on the left to find it). Avoid selecting skin or the background.
At the bottom of Layers click the half-black half-white circle and choose Hue/Saturation. Move the Hue slider in Properties; use Saturation or Lightness gently.
The adjustment should affect only the selected region. Click its mask thumbnail and use black or white Brush strokes to remove or restore affected areas.
why: An adjustment layer allows you to revise the color without permanently changing the original.

title: Illustrator tools or panels missing
aliases: tools on the left illustrator are gone
steps: At the top of Illustrator, click Window > Workspace and choose Essentials (or the default Essentials workspace) if it is not already selected.
Open Window > Workspace again and choose Reset Essentials (or Reset followed by the workspace name, depending on version). This restores the usual layout.
Look for the toolbar on the left. If it is still missing, choose Window > Toolbars > Advanced. If only Layers or Properties is missing, open that panel from Window.
If all panels are hidden, click the artboard outside any text field and press Tab once. Ask your teacher if the tools still do not return.
why: Illustrator workspaces arrange tools and panels. Reset Essentials restores the standard layout without deleting your artwork, but may change a custom panel arrangement.

title: Fill and stroke are mixed up
steps: Press V and click your shape with the black arrow.
At the bottom of the left toolbar, the solid square is Fill and the hollow square is Stroke. Click the one you want in front.
Double-click that square, pick a color and click OK. The inside or outline should change, not both.
why: Fill and stroke are independent object attributes.

title: Illustrator object will not move
steps: Press Esc to leave text editing, then V. Click the edge or filled middle of your shape.
If no blue selection outline appears, open Window > Layers and expand the triangle beside your layer. Look for an eye or padlock beside your object.
Show or unlock only your own artwork, then drag it with V. If the teacher locked it, ask before changing it.
why: The white-arrow Direct Selection tool edits individual points instead of the whole object.

title: Make a shape in Illustrator
steps: Look for the rectangle icon in the left toolbar; press M for Rectangle or L for Ellipse.
Click and drag across the white artboard. Hold Shift as you drag for a square or circle.
Press V, select the shape and use the solid Fill square and hollow Stroke square at the bottom of the toolbar to style it.
why: Vector shapes can be resized without the same pixelation as a raster photo.

title: Illustrator text tool
steps: Press T or click the T icon on the left toolbar.
Click once on the artboard and enter your own text. Highlight the letters with the text cursor.
Open Window > Type > Character for font and size. Press Ctrl+Enter to exit typing, then V to move the whole text object.
why: TechGuide explains the tool, not what to write.

title: Align objects in Illustrator
steps: Press V and Shift-click each shape you want to align; all should have colored selection edges.
Open Window > Align. At the bottom of the panel find Align To; choose Selection to line shapes up with each other.
Hover over the alignment icons to read their names, then click the required edge or center. Undo with Ctrl+Z if the wrong objects move.
why: Aligning to the artboard is different from aligning to other selected objects.

title: Illustrator Shape Builder basics
steps: Use V and Shift-click two overlapping vector shapes until both have selection outlines.
Press Shift+M for Shape Builder. Move over an overlapping region; it should highlight.
Drag across regions to combine them. Release and press V to check the new outline. Ctrl+Z reverses a mistake.
why: Shape Builder works with selected shapes and their overlapping regions.

title: Illustrator artboard is too small
steps: Press Shift+O to activate the Artboard tool and click the board containing your project.
In Properties or the top controls, find W and H. Type the dimensions from the assignment, including units if needed.
Press Esc to leave the tool. The white board should resize while the artwork retains its size.
why: Resizing an artboard is not the same as resizing the artwork.

title: Illustrator export PNG or JPG
steps: Press Ctrl+S to save your editable AI file first. Open File > Export > Export As.
Choose your approved folder, enter a filename, choose PNG or JPEG in the format list and check Use Artboards. Select the required range or All.
Click Export. For PNG, pick White under Background Color when an opaque white background is required; do not pick Transparent for that assignment. Choose the required resolution and click OK.
Open File Explorer with Windows+E, locate the exported file and double-click it. Check the crop, background and readability.
why: An exported image does not replace your editable AI project.

alternatives.label: My PNG needs a solid background

title: Illustrator save editable AI file
steps: Click File > Save As at the top left. Choose On your computer if a cloud-save prompt appears and your teacher requires local files.
Choose the assigned folder, type a meaningful filename and select Adobe Illustrator (*.AI) as the format.
Click Save, accept the required Illustrator options, then check the document tab and folder for the .ai file.
why: The AI file keeps your editable objects.

title: Illustrator artwork appears as outlines
steps: Click View in the top menu. If you see Preview or GPU Preview instead of Outline, you are probably in Outline mode.
Click Preview or GPU Preview; Ctrl+Y also toggles outline and preview.
Your fills should return. If not, check whether the objects actually have a Fill color.
why: Outline mode shows paths rather than the filled appearance of artwork.

title: Illustrator object behind another object
steps: Press V and click the object; if covered, expand its layer in Window > Layers and select it using the far-right selection column.
Open Object > Arrange > Bring to Front to move it above objects in the same layer, or Bring Forward for one step.
Check the result. If another layer covers it, inspect layer order rather than deleting the covering object.
why: Objects higher in the stacking order may cover objects below them.

title: PlayForge game will not load
steps: Return to the PlayForge hub using the original tab. Check that your teacher allows this activity now.
Open the correct activity card once. Look for a loading screen or exact error message.
If it does not open, report the game name and error to your teacher. Do not try alternate URLs or clear browser data.
why: Some apps require a first online load and school policy may restrict access.

title: PlayForge saved progress is missing
steps: Check you are using the same assigned computer and browser profile where you last played.
Open the same activity and look for a saved-progress or profile screen. If you made a backup, ask your teacher about the app's Import option.
If the progress is still missing, it may be stored only on the original device. Do not erase browser data or use another student's profile.
why: Many PlayForge apps save locally and do not automatically sync across devices.

title: Chromebook battery drains quickly
aliases: chromebook battery low all the time
steps: Click the clock at bottom right and read the battery level.
Save work in unused tabs, then close those tabs using their small X. Lower the screen brightness with the smaller sun key.
Check the battery again after working briefly. If it continues dropping fast, report the approximate battery level and time to your teacher.
why: Open pages and bright screens consume energy; persistent rapid drain may need service.

title: Chromebook charger only works at an angle
steps: Stop wiggling the connector. Put the device flat on a desk.
Tell your teacher the charging light or battery indicator changes when the plug moves. Do not try to bend or repair it.
why: A loose port or lead can be damaged further by movement.

title: Chromebook feels unusually hot
steps: Stop using the Chromebook. If it is too hot to touch, move away and tell an adult immediately.
Do not cover it, charge it, or try to cool it with water. Let staff handle it.
why: Heat can indicate blocked airflow or a hardware problem.

title: Liquid spilled on Chromebook
steps: Move away from the wet device and tell an adult immediately.
Do not plug or unplug wet electrical equipment, turn it on, or use a hair dryer. Let staff handle it.
why: Liquid can damage electrical components even when the outside appears dry.

title: Chromebook dropped or cracked
steps: Put the device down if safe. Do not touch broken glass or move damaged hinges.
Tell your teacher what happened and point out the damage from a safe distance. Do not try to repair it.
why: Physical damage can create a safety hazard.

title: Chromebook lid or hinge is stuck
steps: Set the Chromebook flat on a desk. Stop pulling if the hinge resists.
Ask your teacher to check it before opening or closing it further.
why: Forcing a hinge can break the display cable or case.

title: Chromebook wakes to sign-in screen
steps: Look at the sign-in screen for your own school account name or picture.
If it is your account, enter your password privately. If the screen shows someone else, stop and tell your teacher.
Wait for your own desktop to appear. Ask staff if you cannot sign in.
why: Closing the lid or inactivity can lock a managed device.

title: Chromebook going to sleep during work
steps: Tap one key or slide a finger on the touchpad to wake the display.
If you see your sign-in screen, unlock your own account privately.
If it keeps sleeping while you are actively working, tell your teacher what you were doing. Do not change power settings.
why: School-managed sleep rules are not a student setting to change.

title: Safely shut down a Chromebook
steps: Save each open assignment and wait until uploads are finished.
With permission, click the clock in the bottom-right corner, then the power symbol (circle with a line). Choose Shut down if a menu appears.
Wait for the screen and power lights to go off before closing the lid. If the menu is unavailable, ask your teacher.
why: A normal shutdown lets apps finish their work.

title: Safely restart a Chromebook
steps: Save your work, then explain to your teacher why you need to restart.
With permission, click the clock at bottom right and select the power symbol, then Shut down if shown.
Wait for the screen to go off. Press the power button once and sign back into your own account. Try the affected app again.
why: A restart can clear temporary problems but unsaved work may be lost.

title: Chromebook screen too bright
steps: Look along the top keyboard row for the small sun symbol.
Tap it a few times until the display is comfortable. Stop if text becomes hard to read.
If the screen is still uncomfortable, ask your teacher about approved accessibility support.
why: Brightness is an ordinary display control.

title: Chromebook screen flickers
steps: Look away if the flashing bothers you. Stop using the device if it is unsafe.
Tell your teacher whether the flashing happens in one app or across the whole screen. Do not change display settings.
why: Flicker can be a display or software fault.

title: Only one app is blank
steps: Press Alt + Tab to bring another open app forward. Check whether you can see it normally.
Return to the blank app. If you can reach your work, save it first.
Ask before closing and reopening the affected app. If all windows are blank, tell your teacher.
why: This helps separate an app error from a screen problem.

title: Chromebook browser text too large
steps: Click the Chrome webpage, then hold Ctrl and tap minus once. Look for the zoom percentage near the address bar.
Repeat only until the page is readable; Ctrl + 0 returns to the usual page zoom if appropriate for your accommodations.
If the clock and shelf are also huge, ask your teacher to check display magnification instead.
why: Page zoom affects the webpage rather than other apps.

title: Chromebook browser text too small
steps: Click the webpage and hold Ctrl while tapping plus (or the = key) to enlarge it.
Look for the percentage near the address bar and stop when the text is readable.
If you need larger text throughout school work, tell your teacher; do not change system accessibility settings.
why: Page zoom is a reversible reading control.

title: Chromebook entire desktop is enlarged
steps: Look at the clock and app icons at the bottom. Are they enlarged too?
If only the webpage is large, use the browser zoom guide. If everything is large, tell your teacher which parts are enlarged.
Do not turn off magnification or other accessibility features without checking with staff.
why: System magnification is different from webpage zoom and may be an accommodation.

title: Chromebook window is full screen
steps: If a normal video fills the display, press Esc once. Look for the browser tabs to return.
For a regular Chrome window, press the full-screen key on the top row (rectangle with arrows/corners).
If the screen is locked for an assessment, stop and ask your teacher rather than trying to exit.
why: Full-screen view hides some controls.

title: Chromebook maximize a window
steps: Look at the top-right corner of a normal app window for the square between the dash and X.
Click the square once. The window should fill the screen.
To restore its earlier size, click the overlapping squares in the same spot.
why: Maximizing uses the available display area.

title: Chromebook minimize a window
steps: Find the dash at the top-right of the window, left of the square and X.
Click it. The window disappears but stays open.
Click that app's icon on the bottom shelf to bring it back.
why: Minimize hides the window without closing it.

title: Chromebook close an app safely
steps: Check the document's save status and wait for any upload to finish.
Find the X at the top-right of the app window, not the X beside a single Chrome tab unless you only want to close that tab.
Click once. If asked to save, choose the appropriate save option for your work.
why: Closing a window may close unsaved work.

title: Chromebook view all open windows
steps: Find the Show windows key along the top row, marked with a rectangle and lines.
Press it once. Smaller previews of your open windows should appear.
Click the preview you want. Press the same key again if you want to leave the overview.
why: Overview helps locate open work without closing anything.

title: Chromebook split screen two apps
steps: Open both apps and save current work. Click the first window.
Press Alt + [ to place it on the left side. Select the second window and press Alt + ] to place it on the right.
Check that both windows are readable. If an app does not support resizing, maximize it instead.
why: Side-by-side windows make it easier to follow directions while working.

title: Chromebook missing shelf
steps: Move the pointer to the bottom edge and wait briefly for the shelf of app icons.
If a normal video fills the screen, press Esc. For a regular full-screen window, use the top-row full-screen key.
If the shelf still does not appear, ask your teacher rather than changing shelf settings.
why: The shelf can be hidden by full-screen apps or managed preferences.

title: Chromebook open an app from Launcher
steps: Press the Launcher or Search key where Caps Lock usually sits, or click the circle at the bottom-left corner.
Type the approved app name, such as Files. Look at the matching results.
Click its icon. If it is not listed, ask your teacher rather than installing anything.
why: The Launcher searches available apps.

title: Chromebook move a window
steps: If the window fills the screen, click the overlapping squares at the top right to make it smaller.
Put your pointer on an empty part of the top bar, hold the touchpad down, then slide your finger.
Release when the window is where you want it. Do not drag by a browser tab unless you intend to move that tab.
why: Moving a window does not alter its contents.

title: Chromebook resize a window
steps: Restore the window using the square control at the top right if it is maximized.
Move the pointer to the window corner until it becomes a two-way arrow.
Hold down the touchpad and drag the corner. Release when the window is large enough to read.
why: Some apps impose minimum window sizes.

title: Chromebook Caps Lock is on
steps: Click in your own document and type a test letter without Shift.
If the letter is uppercase, hold Alt and tap Launcher/Search (where Caps Lock usually sits). If your keyboard has Caps Lock, tap that instead.
Type another test letter. If still wrong, ask your teacher to check the keyboard layout.
why: Caps Lock affects letters until it is turned off.

title: Chromebook letters typed are wrong
aliases: keyboard typing different letters on chromebook
steps: Click in your own document and type a few letters without holding Shift or Alt.
Check near the clock for a language code such as US. Tell your teacher if the letters do not match the keys.
Do not switch input settings yourself; ask staff to restore the expected layout.
why: A different layout or held modifier can change the characters typed.

title: Chromebook key is physically stuck
steps: Stop pressing the problem key. Look for visible damage or debris without inserting tools.
Tell your teacher which key is stuck. Do not remove keys or use liquid cleaner.
why: Forcing a key can damage the keyboard.

title: Chromebook keyboard completely unresponsive
steps: Move the pointer with the touchpad. If it moves, click in another approved app and try typing.
If only one app fails, save using its menu if possible and ask before reopening it.
If no app accepts typing or the pointer also fails, ask your teacher for help before restarting.
why: Testing another app helps identify whether this is a keyboard fault.

title: Chromebook Backspace and Delete
steps: Click your own text so the blinking cursor appears.
Tap Backspace to remove the character to the left. Hold Alt and tap Backspace to remove the character to the right in a normal text field.
Check the text and use Ctrl + Z if you removed the wrong part.
why: The two actions delete in opposite directions.

title: Chromebook type a capital letter
steps: Click where you want the uppercase letter.
Hold Shift, tap the letter key once, then release both.
Type the next letter without Shift. It should be lowercase unless Caps Lock is on.
why: Shift changes a single keystroke without keeping Caps Lock on.

title: Chromebook copy text
aliases: how do i copy and paste
steps: Click and drag across the text you want until it is highlighted.
Hold Ctrl and tap C. The text stays where it is.
Click the approved destination and press Ctrl + V. Check that the correct text appears there.
why: Copying leaves the original in place.

title: Chromebook paste text
steps: Click the destination until you see a blinking text cursor.
Hold Ctrl and tap V once.
Check what appeared. If it was the wrong content, press Ctrl + Z and copy the intended text again.
why: The clipboard holds the most recent copied item.

title: Chromebook paste without formatting
steps: Copy the text, then click the destination in Google Docs or another compatible editor.
Hold Ctrl and Shift, then tap V. The text should appear without the original font and colors.
If the shortcut does not work, look under Edit for Paste without formatting, if offered.
why: This avoids importing unwanted source formatting.

title: Chromebook cut and move text
steps: Highlight your own text by dragging across it.
Press Ctrl + X; it should disappear. Click the new location and press Ctrl + V right away.
Check that it arrived. If not, undo with Ctrl + Z rather than cutting again.
why: Cut removes the selection from its old location.

title: Chromebook undo a mistake
steps: Click inside the document where the unwanted edit happened.
Press Ctrl + Z once and check the change before pressing again.
If you backed up too far, use Ctrl + Shift + Z in Google Docs or the app's Edit > Redo command.
why: Undo reverses recent edits in many apps.

title: Chromebook redo an edit
steps: Click inside the document where you just used Undo.
Press Ctrl + Shift + Z in Google Docs or choose Edit > Redo in the editor.
Check that only the intended change returned. Shortcuts can vary by app.
why: Redo restores an action you recently undid.

title: Chromebook select all text
steps: Click inside your own document, not on the browser address bar.
Press Ctrl + A. The text in the active editing area should become highlighted.
Click elsewhere or press an arrow key to clear the selection without deleting it.
why: Selection depends on which app or field has focus.

title: Chromebook find a word
steps: With the webpage active, press Ctrl + F. A small search field appears near the top.
Type the word you are looking for. Matching text should be highlighted.
Press Enter to move to the next match, then Esc to close the search box.
why: Find locates existing text without changing it.

title: Chromebook move through form fields
steps: Click the first field of the assigned form.
Press Tab to move to the next field; Shift + Tab moves back.
Watch the outline or blinking cursor before typing. Do not press Enter on a Submit button until you are ready.
why: Keyboard navigation can help when a mouse is inconvenient.

title: Chromebook open keyboard shortcut help
steps: Press Ctrl + Launcher/Search + S (Launcher is usually where Caps Lock sits).
The keyboard shortcut viewer should open. Search for the action you need.
If it does not open, use TechGuide's shortcut library instead. Do not edit shortcut settings.
why: The viewer shows shortcuts supported by the device.

title: Chromebook touchpad scroll
steps: Place two fingertips on the touchpad together without pressing down.
Slide both up or down slowly while watching the page move.
If nothing moves, put the pointer over the page content and try again. You can also drag the visible scrollbar.
why: Scrolling works only where content extends beyond the visible area.

title: Chromebook touchpad click and drag
steps: Move the pointer onto the item you need to move.
Press down on the touchpad with one finger and keep it pressed while sliding across the pad.
Release over the destination. If it lands in the wrong place, use Undo if available.
why: Dragging moves or repositions selected items.

title: Chromebook touchpad pointer jumps
steps: Take your hand off the touchpad and dry your fingers.
Try moving one finger along the center of the pad, avoiding extra fingers or your palm.
If the pointer still jumps, ask your teacher to test an approved mouse. Do not change touchpad settings.
why: Extra contact can cause unexpected pointer movement.

title: Chromebook touchscreen not responding
steps: Check that the Chromebook model actually has a touchscreen.
With clean, dry hands, tap an ordinary button once. If it does not respond, try the touchpad.
If the touchpad works but touch does not, tell your teacher which screen or app failed.
why: Not all Chromebook displays are touch-enabled.

title: Chromebook touchscreen zoom
steps: In a teacher-approved webpage that supports touch, place two fingers on the content.
Spread them apart to zoom in, or pinch them together to zoom out.
If the app does not respond, use its page zoom controls instead. Do not change system magnification.
why: Touch gestures vary by app and model.

title: Chromebook open a new browser tab
steps: In Chrome, click the plus sign beside the last tab at the top, or press Ctrl + T.
A new tab should show an address bar ready for typing.
Enter the assigned web address or choose the teacher's link. Your old tabs remain open.
why: A tab opens another page in the same window.

title: Chromebook close one browser tab
steps: Check the tab title at the top so you know which page will close. Save any work first.
Click the small X on that tab, or press Ctrl + W while it is active.
If you closed the wrong tab, press Ctrl + Shift + T to reopen it, if permitted.
why: Closing a tab is not the same as closing all Chrome windows.

title: Chromebook move between browser tabs
steps: Look at the row of tab titles across the top of Chrome.
Click the title you need. Alternatively press Ctrl + Tab to move right or Ctrl + Shift + Tab to move left.
Check the page title before typing or submitting work.
why: Tabs allow you to switch pages without reopening them.

title: Chromebook reopen last closed tab
steps: If you accidentally closed your own approved class tab, open Chrome.
Hold Ctrl and Shift and tap T. The most recently closed tab should return.
If it was not the correct page, reopen the link from Classroom instead. Unsaved work may not return.
why: Chrome may restore the page but not every unsaved edit.

title: Chromebook refresh a webpage
steps: Save your work and wait for uploads before refreshing.
Click the circular arrow to the left of the address bar, or press Ctrl + R.
Wait for the page to reload. If an error returns, write down the message for your teacher.
why: Reloading requests a fresh copy of the page and can lose unsaved form input.

title: Chromebook go back to previous webpage
steps: Locate the left-pointing arrow at the top-left of Chrome.
Click once to return to the previous page in that tab. Do not do this during an active upload or unsaved form.
If the arrow is gray, there is no previous page in this tab. Reopen the class link instead.
why: Back returns to a prior page in the current tab.

title: Chromebook go forward to webpage
steps: Find the right-pointing arrow next to the Back arrow in Chrome.
Click it once after you have gone Back. It should restore the next page in the tab's history.
If gray, use the original class link instead. Check for unsaved work first.
why: Forward revisits a page you moved back from.

title: Chromebook address bar search
steps: Click the long address field at the top of Chrome or press Ctrl + L.
Type the teacher-provided website address or an approved search term, then press Enter.
Check the page title and address. If a warning appears, stop and show your teacher.
why: The address bar supports both web addresses and searches.

title: Chromebook save a class bookmark
steps: Open the approved class website you want to revisit.
Click the star at the right end of the address bar or press Ctrl + D.
Keep a recognizable name and choose Done. If bookmarks are restricted, ask your teacher.
why: Bookmarks make it easier to return to a page later.

title: Chromebook find existing bookmarks
steps: Open Chrome and click the three dots at the top-right corner.
Hover over or select Bookmarks and lists (or Bookmarks in older versions). Look for the saved page.
Click its title. If you cannot find it, reopen the teacher's original link.
why: Bookmarks store links rather than copies of pages.

title: Chromebook browser shows download list
steps: In Chrome, press Ctrl + J to open the Downloads page.
Look for the filename and its completion or error status.
If completed, use Show in folder if offered, or open Files > My files > Downloads.
why: The downloads list can identify where a file was saved.

title: Chromebook link opens wrong tab
steps: Look at the Chrome tab row for a new tab with the expected page title.
Click that tab; your original page may still be open on the left.
If no new tab appears and a warning is visible, show the teacher rather than changing pop-up permissions.
why: Links may open outside the current tab.

title: Chromebook too many tabs slow browser
steps: Look at the tabs across the top of Chrome and identify ones you no longer need.
Save any work in those tabs, then click their individual X buttons.
Return to the class page and check whether it responds faster. If not, tell your teacher.
why: Each tab can consume memory and processing time.

title: Chromebook text cursor not in typing box
steps: Click inside the answer or text box rather than on its label.
Look for a blinking vertical cursor. Type a test character if appropriate.
If nothing appears, check whether the field says View only or is disabled; ask your teacher if it should be editable.
why: The page must focus an editable field to receive typing.

title: Chromebook page asks to enable pop-ups
steps: Look near the address bar for the pop-up blocked icon or notice.
Show the teacher the exact page and notice. Do not choose Always allow or change site permissions yourself.
Use the teacher-provided alternative if available.
why: A blocked pop-up may be a protection or school policy.

title: Chromebook website certificate warning
steps: If Chrome shows Your connection is not private or a certificate warning, stop.
Do not select Advanced or proceed to the site. Show the address and warning to your teacher.
Return to an approved class page only when told it is safe.
why: Certificate warnings can indicate an unsafe or misconfigured connection.

title: Chromebook open Files app
steps: Press Shift + Alt + M, or press Launcher and type Files.
Click the blue folder app named Files. Look for My files and Google Drive in the left column.
Choose the location where your work belongs. Do not open another student's files.
why: Files shows device storage and available connected school storage.

title: Chromebook create a folder
steps: Open Files using Shift + Alt + M. In the left column, choose the approved parent folder, such as Downloads.
Click the three-dot menu at the top right and choose New folder if available, or right-click an empty area and choose New folder.
Type a clear name and press Enter. Open the new folder to confirm it exists.
why: Folders organize files without changing their contents.

title: Chromebook rename own file
steps: Open Files and locate your own file. Single-click it to select it.
Press Ctrl + Enter, or right-click and choose Rename if shown.
Type the new name without changing the file extension, then press Enter. Verify the file still opens.
why: Changing a file extension does not convert its format.

title: Chromebook copy a file
steps: Open Files and select your own file with one click.
Press Ctrl + C. In the left column open the approved destination folder.
Press Ctrl + V, then check that the copy appears and the original still exists.
why: Copying preserves the original file.

title: Chromebook move a file to folder
steps: Open Files, select your own file, and press Ctrl + X.
Open the correct destination folder and press Ctrl + V.
Confirm the file appears in the new folder. If not, stop before deleting anything and ask for help.
why: Moving changes the location of a file.

title: Chromebook preview a file
steps: Open Files and click the file once to select it.
Press Space to open a preview if supported. Inspect the picture or document without changing it.
Press Esc to close. If there is no preview, ask which approved app opens that file type.
why: A preview is useful for identifying a file before using it.

title: Chromebook search for a local file
steps: Open Files and choose the likely location in the left column, such as Downloads.
Click the search icon near the top and type part of the filename.
Check the location and name of matching results. If the file is in Drive, try searching in Drive itself.
why: Searching within the likely location narrows results.

title: Chromebook sort downloaded files
steps: Open Files > My files > Downloads.
In list view, click the Date modified column heading to sort. Click again if the oldest files appear first.
Look for the most recent file with the expected name and extension. In icon view, use the sort menu instead.
why: Sorting by date helps locate recently saved work.

title: Chromebook select several files
steps: Open the folder containing your own files.
Hold Ctrl and click each file you need, checking the highlighted names. For a continuous range, click the first, hold Shift and click the last.
Verify only the intended files are selected before copying or uploading.
why: Selecting several files makes it easier to upload or organize them together.

title: Chromebook extract a ZIP archive
steps: Open Files > Downloads and double-click the approved .zip file. It may appear as a mounted folder in the left column.
Select the contents you need, press Ctrl + C, then open an ordinary folder under My files and press Ctrl + V.
Open the copied file from the ordinary folder. If the ZIP will not open or asks for a password, ask your teacher.
why: A ZIP is a container; some apps need extracted files.

title: Chromebook make a ZIP of class work
steps: Open Files and select only the files you are supposed to package using Ctrl + click.
Right-click the selection and choose Zip selection if shown.
Find the new .zip file in the same folder. Open it to confirm the required files are inside before submitting.
why: A ZIP bundles multiple files together.

title: Chromebook local file versus Google Drive
steps: Open Files and look at the left column. My files contains local files; Google Drive > My Drive contains your cloud files.
Click the folder where you saved the work. Local Downloads files may not be available on another Chromebook.
If you need the file on another school device, copy it to your approved Drive folder and check it appears there.
why: Local files may not appear on a different Chromebook.

title: Chromebook Drive file is offline
steps: Open Files > Google Drive or the Drive website. Look for an Offline label or unavailable file.
If the file was already made available offline, open it and work only if the teacher permits.
If unavailable, ask your teacher and wait for the school connection. Do not close unsynced work.
why: Offline access is not available for every cloud file.

title: Chromebook file will not open
steps: In Files, check the filename extension, such as .png, .pdf or .zip.
Select it once and press Space to see if a preview is available. If it is a ZIP, use the ZIP guide.
If unsupported, tell your teacher the extension and error. Do not rename the extension or install an app to force it open.
why: Different file types need compatible apps.

title: Chromebook storage is full
steps: If you see a low-storage message, save current work in the approved location first.
Open Files and note whether there are large personal class downloads, without deleting anything.
Ask your teacher which files may be moved or removed. Do not clear system or browser data.
why: Low local space can prevent saving and downloading.

title: Chromebook file has duplicate name
steps: Open Files and inspect the filenames for a number such as (1) or (2).
Click Date modified to find the most recent version; preview it with Space if possible.
Submit the intended version. Keep the others until your teacher confirms they can be deleted.
why: Repeated downloads can create numbered copies.

title: Chromebook upload a local file
steps: In the approved assignment page, find its attachment button (in Classroom, Your work > Add or create > File).
When the file picker opens choose Browse if shown, then My files > Downloads or Google Drive from the left.
Select the correct file and click Open or Upload. Wait until its name appears in the assignment before submitting.
why: Selecting a file is not the same as finishing its upload.

title: Chromebook download has not finished
steps: Open Chrome and press Ctrl + J. Find the download and read its status.
If it shows progress, wait. If it shows Failed, note the error rather than clicking download repeatedly.
Check with your teacher if the file is blocked or the connection has failed.
why: Large files can take time or require a stable connection.

title: Chromebook screenshot only part of screen
steps: Hold Ctrl and Shift, then tap Show windows (the top-row rectangle with lines).
In the toolbar near the bottom, select the camera icon for screenshot and the dashed rectangle for partial screen.
Drag a box around only the needed area, then click Capture. Check the notification or Files > Downloads for the PNG.
why: A partial capture excludes unrelated information.

title: Chromebook screenshot only one window
steps: Press Ctrl + Shift + Show windows to open the capture toolbar.
Choose the camera icon, then the window capture icon (a window outline). Click the window you need.
Look at the capture preview and make sure no private work is included before attaching it.
why: Window capture helps keep other apps out of the image.

title: Chromebook screenshot not found
aliases: i took a screenshot where did it go
where is the screenshot i just took
steps: Look near the bottom-right corner for the capture notification and click its preview if present.
If gone, open Files with Shift + Alt + M, choose My files > Downloads and sort by Date modified.
Look for a recent Screenshot file ending in .png. If screenshots save elsewhere on your device, ask your teacher to locate the configured folder.
why: Captures normally save to a local folder and can also appear in a notification.

title: Chromebook screenshot saved as video
steps: If recording is active, click the red stop recording control near the clock.
Press Ctrl + Shift + Show windows to reopen the capture toolbar. Choose the still camera, not the video camera.
Choose an area and click Capture. Check that the new file is a PNG rather than a WEBM video.
why: Screenshots are still images; recordings are video files.

title: Chromebook screen recording for class
steps: Get teacher permission and close private messages or other students' work.
Press Ctrl + Shift + Show windows, select the video camera in the bottom toolbar, choose the approved area and click Record.
When finished click the red stop control near the clock. Inspect the WEBM file in Downloads before sharing.
why: Screen recordings can expose personal information and should be intentional.

title: Chromebook volume too quiet
steps: Tap the top-row speaker-with-waves key to raise volume slowly.
Move the pointer over the class video and check its separate volume slider or speaker icon, usually near the bottom.
If it remains quiet, ask to test an approved spare headset. Keep audio at a comfortable level.
why: Device and app volume are separate controls.

title: Chromebook volume muted
steps: Look for the crossed-out speaker symbol on the top row. Press the volume-up key once if sound is allowed.
Move the pointer over the video and check for a crossed-out speaker in the player as well.
Play a short portion at low volume. If there is no sound, try the headphones or no-sound guide.
why: Muted audio may be controlled by the device or the app.

title: Chromebook sound comes from speakers instead of headphones
steps: Turn volume down first. Find the headphone port on the side and make sure an approved plug is fully seated without force.
Play a short assigned audio clip. If the speakers still play, click the clock and show your teacher the audio output controls.
Let the teacher select the approved output. Do not change accessibility audio settings.
why: Audio can be routed to a connected device or the built-in speakers.

title: Chromebook headphones sound only on one side
steps: Lower volume and check the approved headset plug is fully seated.
Adjust the headset comfortably and play a brief assigned audio clip.
With permission, compare a school spare headset. Tell staff whether the missing side follows the headphones or stays with the Chromebook.
why: A cable or headset fault can affect one channel.

title: Chromebook headphone plug will not fit
steps: Look at the headphone plug: round audio plugs need a round audio port; USB plugs need a matching USB port.
Compare the shape with the port without pushing. If it does not match, stop.
Ask the teacher for a compatible school headset or adapter.
why: Ports have different shapes and purposes.

title: Chromebook Bluetooth headset not connecting
steps: Check whether the approved headset has power or a battery indicator.
Show the headset and Chromebook to your teacher. Ask staff to check pairing rather than connecting unknown devices.
Use an approved wired headset if the teacher offers one.
why: Wireless accessories may need approved pairing and school policies may restrict it.

title: Chromebook microphone muted in class app
steps: In the assigned Meet or recording app, move the pointer over the window and look for a microphone symbol, often along the bottom.
If it is crossed out, click it only when instructed to speak or record.
Check for the unmuted icon. If disabled or missing, tell your teacher rather than changing permissions.
why: App mute prevents audio capture without changing system settings.

alternatives.label: It does not detect my voice

title: Chromebook microphone not detecting voice
steps: Check that the headset cable is connected and look for a mute switch on the headset or cord.
In the assigned app, look for the microphone icon and unmute only when permitted.
Say a few words in the approved test or recording. If no voice is detected, show the teacher the app and headset.
why: A physical mute switch and app mute can both block sound.

title: Chromebook microphone permission denied
steps: Read the permission message and confirm the page is the one your teacher assigned.
Show the warning to your teacher, including the site name. Do not open browser permissions or approve unfamiliar requests.
Use another approved activity if staff cannot resolve it immediately.
why: Microphone access may be intentionally restricted.

title: Chromebook camera black image
steps: Look above the screen for the small camera lens. If the model has a privacy slider, ask before opening it.
In the assigned app, look for a crossed-out camera icon near the bottom and click only when video is required.
If the preview stays black, tell your teacher whether the camera is physically covered or the app reports an error.
why: A closed shutter or app camera control can hide video.

title: Chromebook camera permission denied
steps: Read the camera permission warning and check the app name.
Show the teacher the warning. Do not change site permissions or grant access to an unapproved site.
Wait for staff guidance or an approved alternative.
why: Camera access is sensitive and may be managed by school IT.

title: Chromebook video plays but stutters
steps: Pause the assigned video briefly using the play/pause button at its bottom.
Save work in unused tabs and close those tabs, then resume playback.
If it still stutters, tell your teacher whether other videos or classmates have the same issue.
why: Streaming relies on available device and network resources.

title: Chromebook Wi-Fi icon shows disconnected
steps: Click the time at the lower right and look at the Wi-Fi icon or network label.
If it says disconnected or no network, show your teacher without selecting a different network.
Keep any unsaved document open and use available offline work while waiting.
why: The icon helps distinguish connection loss from a single website error.

title: Chromebook Wi-Fi connected but website fails
steps: Leave the Wi-Fi settings alone. Open a new Chrome tab with Ctrl + T and try another approved class page.
If it loads, copy or write down the first page's error for your teacher. If neither works, report both.
Do not change DNS, proxy or network settings or bypass restrictions.
why: This checks whether the fault is specific to one website.

title: Chromebook says offline in Google Docs
steps: Keep your Google Docs tab open. Look near the document title for the cloud/save status or an offline banner.
Continue only if the editor accepts your work. Do not refresh or close the tab while changes are unsynced.
When the approved connection returns, wait until the status confirms changes are saved; ask the teacher if unsure.
why: Offline edits may sync later if the app supports it.

title: Chromebook school Wi-Fi asks for sign-in
steps: Stop when the Wi-Fi sign-in prompt appears. Do not type a password into an unfamiliar page.
Show the network name and sign-in prompt to your teacher.
Wait for staff instructions rather than switching networks.
why: Unexpected sign-in pages can be legitimate or unsafe; school staff must verify them.

title: Chromebook read text aloud
steps: If Select-to-speak is already approved and enabled, look for its speaking icon near the clock or in the accessibility menu.
With teacher permission, select the assigned text and use the existing Select-to-speak control to listen.
If the control is missing, ask your teacher. Do not enable or disable system accessibility features yourself.
why: Text-to-speech can support reading without producing assignment answers.

title: Chromebook screen reader is speaking
steps: If the Chromebook begins speaking unexpectedly, tell your teacher what the voice says.
Check with staff whether spoken feedback is an approved accommodation before changing anything.
Keep the feature enabled until staff confirms how to proceed.
why: Screen reading can be an essential access tool.

title: Chromebook captions for a class video
steps: Move the pointer over the assigned video to reveal its bottom control bar.
Click CC or the subtitles button if offered. Select a caption language if needed.
Check that words appear when the video plays. If no captions are available, ask for an accessible version.
why: Captions provide text for spoken audio and may vary in accuracy.

title: Chromebook need larger text for reading
steps: Click the webpage and press Ctrl + plus to enlarge text a little at a time.
Stop when the text is readable. For a document, use its own zoom menu if preferred.
Tell your teacher if you need this regularly or if the whole screen needs adjustment; do not disable existing accommodations.
why: App zoom is reversible; system accessibility should follow approved accommodations.

title: Chromebook on-screen keyboard appears
steps: Tap outside the current text field and look for the on-screen keyboard to close.
If using a convertible Chromebook, ask whether it should be in laptop position; do not force its hinge.
If the keyboard keeps blocking work, tell your teacher. Do not change accessibility keyboard settings.
why: An on-screen keyboard may be a model feature or an accommodation.

title: Chromebook use dictation for own words
steps: Ask whether speaking your own words is permitted for this assignment.
In Google Docs on a supported browser, open Tools > Voice typing if available; click the microphone only after approval.
Speak your own words, stop the microphone and read the transcription. If permission is requested, ask the teacher.
why: Dictation transcribes your speech rather than writing the assignment for you.
