title: Chromebook keyboard focus indicator
steps: Press Tab once and watch for an outline around the next link or button.
Press Shift + Tab to move backward. Press Enter or Space only on a control you recognize.
If the outline interferes with work, ask your teacher; do not change accessibility settings.
why: Focus indicators show where keyboard input will go.

title: Chromebook tablet mode display
steps: Check whether the Chromebook has a convertible hinge. Ask your teacher which position is allowed.
Gently return it to laptop position only if the model supports it; never force the hinge.
Try typing in your own document. If the keyboard remains unavailable, tell staff.
why: Some convertible models disable the keyboard when folded.

title: Chromebook sign in to own school account
steps: Open the normal school sign-in screen and select your own account or enter your school email.
Enter your password privately. Do not tell TechGuide or another student your credentials.
Wait for your desktop. If an error appears, show it to your teacher without revealing the password.
why: Managed school devices require authorized accounts.

title: Chromebook wrong account showing
steps: If you see another student's account name or files, stop without opening anything.
Tell your teacher whose account is showing if appropriate. Let staff return the Chromebook to the proper sign-in screen.
Sign in only with your own school account once instructed.
why: Account separation protects student work and privacy.

title: Chromebook forgotten password
steps: If your password fails, check for a typing mistake or Caps Lock without telling anyone the password.
If you cannot sign in, tell your teacher that you need school account recovery.
Follow the staff-approved process only. TechGuide cannot recover or reset passwords.
why: Account recovery requires authorized staff.

title: Chromebook assignment tab says access denied
steps: Check the account picture near the top-right of the Google page without opening someone else's account.
Return to Classroom and open the exact teacher-provided assignment link again.
If Access denied or Request access remains, show the teacher the message and assignment title; do not request broad access yourself.
why: A site may require an assigned account or teacher access approval.

title: Chromebook looks different from teacher demo
steps: Read the title of the app and compare it with the teacher's demo. Check whether your window is smaller or a different app is open.
Maximize a normal window with the square at top right if needed. Look for the named menu or label, not just its color.
If still different, show the teacher your screen and the expected control. Do not install updates yourself.
why: Device models and app versions can differ.

title: Chromebook unknown app asks to install
steps: If a website or app asks you to install an extension, application or update, stop.
Close the prompt with Cancel or its X if safe. Do not accept it or open a downloaded installer.
Show the teacher the original site or message and use the approved resource instead.
why: Unexpected installers can be unsafe or prohibited.

title: Chromebook print a school document
steps: Ask permission to print. Open the assigned document and press Ctrl + P.
In the print preview, choose the approved printer under Destination and check page range and page count.
Click Print only when approved. If the printer is missing or an error appears, tell your teacher instead of adding printers.
why: Print preview reduces accidental extra pages and wrong-printer jobs.

title: Chromebook save a permitted page as PDF
steps: Open the required document or approved page and press Ctrl + P.
In Destination select Save as PDF if allowed. Check the preview for missing pages.
Click Save, choose an approved folder and name the file. Open it in Files to verify the PDF before submitting.
why: PDF captures a fixed layout and may not preserve editable features.

title: Chromebook safely use school USB storage
steps: Ask permission to use a school USB drive. Match the connector shape to the port and insert gently.
Open Files and look for the drive name in the left column. Copy only approved class files.
Wait for copies to finish, click the eject symbol beside the drive name and remove it only after it disappears.
why: Ejecting allows pending file writes to finish.

title: Wired mouse disconnects repeatedly
steps: Save your project first. Follow the mouse cable and look for visible cuts or a loose plug.
With permission, unplug only your own accessible mouse USB plug, wait briefly, then reconnect it without force.
Move the mouse and watch for pauses. If it disconnects again, report the cable and port to staff.
why: A loose cable or worn connector can cause intermittent input.

title: Wireless mouse has no power
steps: Turn your assigned wireless mouse over and look for a small ON/OFF switch.
Slide it to ON if permitted. A light may blink, but not every mouse has a visible light.
Move it on a mouse pad. If no response, ask staff to check the battery or provide a spare; do not open it.
why: Wireless mice need battery power as well as a working link.

title: Wireless mouse receiver missing
steps: Look for a tiny USB receiver in an accessible port on your assigned computer; it may be almost flush with the port.
Compare any label with your mouse without removing another device. Some mice use Bluetooth instead.
If you cannot find the matching receiver, tell your teacher the mouse model or station number; let staff handle pairing.
why: Some wireless mice need a particular receiver to communicate.

title: Mouse pointer jumps around
steps: Place the mouse on a plain matte mouse pad, not glass or a shiny desk.
Lift it and look for obvious dust or hair around the sensor opening underneath; don't insert anything.
Move in a slow straight line and watch the pointer. If it still jumps, ask staff for a spare.
why: Optical sensors can struggle with reflective or uneven surfaces.

title: Mouse pointer moves very slowly
steps: Clear a wider space on the mouse pad and move the mouse from one side to the other.
Open another approved window and compare how far the pointer moves for the same motion.
If slow everywhere, report it to staff. If only in a game, ask about that game's approved controls.
why: Slow movement may be a device issue or an app that is busy.

title: Mouse pointer moves too fast
steps: Move the mouse a small distance on a matte pad and watch the arrow.
Try the same motion in a normal document, not only a game. If it is fast everywhere, tell staff.
Do not press unfamiliar DPI buttons or alter system sensitivity; ask for a comfortable approved mouse.
why: Some mice have hardware sensitivity controls that differ by model.

title: Mouse clicks twice by itself
steps: Open your own folder using Windows+E; click a file name once without moving the mouse.
A normal single click highlights it; if it opens unexpectedly, repeat in another approved app on a harmless control.
Tell staff whether one click behaves like two in several places. Ask to test a spare.
why: A worn switch can register extra clicks.

title: Mouse left click not responding
steps: Click a blank area of your own document, then a known toolbar button with the usual primary button.
If the other mouse button opens a menu, press Esc to dismiss it. Check whether the mouse is left-handed by asking the teacher.
If the primary button never responds, ask to test another mouse.
why: Identifying the affected button helps isolate the problem.

title: Mouse right-click menu missing
steps: Open File Explorer with Windows+E. Place the arrow over one of your own files and press the secondary mouse button once.
A menu with commands such as Copy or Rename should appear; press Esc without choosing anything.
If it works here but not in another app, that app may use different controls. If it fails everywhere, ask staff.
why: Context menus depend on both the button and the selected object.

title: Accidentally dragging instead of clicking
steps: Release the mouse completely and stop moving it.
Rest your hand lightly, position the arrow, and tap the primary button without sliding the mouse.
If you accidentally moved part of your own project, use Edit > Undo or Ctrl+Z once and check the result.
why: A held button plus movement usually starts a drag.

title: Mouse cursor disappears while typing
steps: Move the mouse away from the text and over the app's toolbar.
If a normal arrow appears, the earlier thin I-shaped cursor was the text cursor. A brush may instead show a circle.
If no pointer appears anywhere, try the mouse movement guide or tell staff.
why: Some apps hide the pointer during typing or change its appearance for tools.

title: Mouse pointer looks like a spinning circle
steps: When the pointer becomes a spinning circle, stop clicking and wait for the current operation.
If the normal arrow returns, save the project with Ctrl+S.
If it continues and the app says Not Responding, use the frozen app guide; ask staff before closing.
why: The busy cursor can indicate an operation is still running.

title: Only one keyboard key fails
steps: Click a blank area in your own document where a blinking cursor appears.
Tap the affected key once, then a nearby key. Record which character appears or whether nothing appears.
If only one fails, show its label to the teacher; do not remove the key.
why: A single failed key can indicate a physical problem.

title: Keyboard repeats letters
steps: Click in a blank practice document and tap the affected letter very briefly, then release.
If several copies appear after release, test another key the same way.
Tell the teacher whether one or many keys repeat. Do not change repeat or accessibility settings.
why: Held or worn keys may produce repeated characters.

title: Keyboard types symbols instead of numbers
steps: Find the two Shift keys (left below Caps Lock and right below Enter). Release both.
In a blank document tap a number above the letters without Shift; it should type a number, not its upper symbol.
If it keeps typing symbols, show staff which keys are affected; leave keyboard layout settings alone.
why: Shift changes what the number row types on many keyboards.

title: Keyboard letters in wrong places
aliases: my keyboard types the wrong letters windows
steps: Click in a blank practice document and tap A, Q and one other letter, comparing the output with the labels.
Release Ctrl, Alt and Shift if held. Check whether the mismatch continues.
Show staff the actual characters and labeled keys. Do not change the keyboard layout or language.
why: A mismatched layout or held key can change characters.

title: Spacebar not typing spaces
steps: Click in a blank document and type two letters with a tap of the long Spacebar between them.
Look for a space between the letters. If other keys work but Spacebar does not, tell staff.
Do not lift the key or attempt repairs; ask for a spare keyboard.
why: The issue may be a single key rather than the whole keyboard.

title: Backspace versus Delete key
steps: In your own practice text, place the blinking cursor between two letters.
Tap Backspace (usually above Enter) to remove the left letter; Ctrl+Z restores it. Tap Delete to remove the right letter.
Use this only on text you own; Delete in File Explorer is a different action that can remove a file.
why: These keys work in different directions when editing text.

title: Enter key does not start a new line
steps: Look for a blinking cursor in your document, not a selected button or browser address bar.
In a text document, tap Enter (right side of the letter keys) to start a new paragraph.
In a chat or form Enter may send; use the app's displayed instructions instead of testing on a real submission.
why: Enter behavior depends on the application.

title: Tab key jumps to another box
steps: Look at the current box. In a form, pressing Tab highlights the next field; Shift+Tab usually goes back.
In a document, click the paragraph you want and use the toolbar's indent button if your teacher asks for an indent.
If you are unsure which control to use, ask staff rather than repeatedly pressing Tab.
why: Tab is also a keyboard navigation control.

title: Arrow keys scroll instead of moving cursor
steps: Click within your own editable text until the blinking insertion cursor appears.
Tap a left or right arrow key and watch the cursor move one character.
In a spreadsheet, arrow keys normally change the selected cell. If they scroll instead, show the teacher without changing navigation settings.
why: Arrow keys may navigate a page or an editable selection.

title: Ctrl shortcut is not working
steps: Click the correct app or select the object the shortcut is meant to affect.
Find Ctrl at the bottom of the keyboard; hold it, tap the second key once, release both.
Check the corresponding menu command if nothing happens. Shortcuts differ by app; report the exact combination if blocked.
why: Shortcuts depend on keyboard focus and the selected item.

title: Escape from an open menu
steps: Find Esc in the top-left corner of the keyboard. Tap once to close an open menu.
If the menu remains, click a blank area outside it, not an unfamiliar command.
Check that the document is still visible and unchanged.
why: Escape often cancels a menu or dialog without applying changes.

title: Sticky or jammed keyboard key
steps: Stop pressing the key. Look at its label and whether it sits lower than nearby keys.
Tell staff which key is stuck and whether typing continues without touching it.
Do not pry, spray or pour liquids on the keyboard; request a spare.
why: Physical cleaning and repair belong to staff.

title: Keyboard cable does not fit
steps: Look at the plug: USB-A is a wide rectangle; USB-C is a small rounded oval.
Compare with an accessible port assigned by your teacher. If it does not fit gently, stop.
Ask staff to identify the correct port. Never bend or force a connector.
why: Forcing a connector can damage its pins or port.

title: Monitor says no signal
steps: Read the message on the monitor. No signal means the monitor is on but not receiving a picture.
Look for the computer's power indicator. If your teacher permits normal startup, press its power button once only if it is off.
If the computer is on but No signal remains, tell the teacher. Leave rear cables and input selection to staff.
why: A powered monitor may not be receiving a video signal.

title: Monitor shows wrong input
steps: Look for a name such as HDMI 1 or DisplayPort in the monitor's message.
Check whether the computer has a power light and whether another assigned display shows your desktop.
Tell staff the input label and station number. Do not cycle through display inputs yourself.
why: The display may be listening to a different video connector.

title: Monitor flickers or flashes
steps: Look away immediately if flashing causes discomfort. Tell the teacher and request another station.
If comfortable and safe, save your document without staring at the flickering screen.
Describe whether it flashes all the time or only in one app. Leave cables and display settings to staff.
why: Flicker may come from several hardware or display issues.

title: Colored lines on monitor
steps: Without touching the display, check whether lines cross the desktop as well as your app.
If safe, switch to another open app with Alt+Tab and see whether the lines remain.
Show the teacher the lines. Do not press the panel or disconnect cables.
why: Lines may indicate a monitor, cable or graphics problem.

title: Monitor image is blurry
steps: Look at the taskbar clock and app menu text. Are those blurry too, or just your artwork?
If just the artwork, use the app's zoom controls to view it at 100% and compare the image with the menu text.
If everything looks blurry, ask staff to check the display. Do not change resolution or scaling.
why: Image quality problems differ from display-wide problems.

title: Monitor picture looks stretched
steps: Compare a familiar square or circle in your artwork with the app icons and text.
If only the artwork looks stretched, undo the last resize if appropriate. If all windows look stretched, show staff.
Do not change display resolution, monitor aspect ratio or scaling.
why: An incorrect display mode or app layout can distort the picture.

title: Monitor color looks unusual
steps: Compare the colors of your artwork with a familiar image and the normal Windows icons.
If all images look unusually tinted, tell staff rather than changing color settings. If only one document is affected, use the app's color help.
Do not disable accessibility filters or alter monitor calibration.
why: Color appearance depends on display and app settings.

title: Monitor shows a cracked screen
steps: Stop using the monitor if there is a crack, broken glass or physical damage.
Move your hands away and tell the teacher immediately. Do not press or clean the damaged area.
Ask to use another workstation; let staff handle any repair.
why: Broken screens may have sharp edges and require replacement.

title: Second monitor missing
steps: Look for the second monitor's power light and any No signal message.
Press Alt+Tab on the working screen to see if your open app is still available.
Tell the teacher what each screen shows. Do not change display modes or reach behind the monitors.
why: Multiple displays depend on approved classroom configuration.

title: Window is on another monitor
steps: Look at both working screens for the window. If it is maximized, click the overlapping squares near its top-right corner.
Hold the mouse button on the window's title bar and drag it across the edge toward your other screen.
Release on the desired screen. If you cannot see the window or the second screen is off, ask staff.
why: Extended desktops can place windows on different displays.

title: Projector not showing computer
steps: Check whether your own desktop monitor shows your correct project.
Read any visible projector message from your seat, such as No signal. Do not handle the projector or its cables.
Tell the teacher what appears on both screens; staff will manage projection.
why: Classroom projection is shared equipment controlled by staff.

title: Sound plays from speakers instead of headphones
steps: Pause the sound immediately if it is playing aloud. Check the headset plug at its assigned accessible port.

In Windows 11, the speaker area near the clock opens Quick Settings; look for the output chooser beside the volume slider if present. With teacher permission select only the assigned headset. In Windows 10, the speaker flyout may offer a device name or arrow.
Test at low volume. If you cannot identify the assigned output, or the option is blocked, ask staff rather than changing more settings.
why: Audio can be routed to a device other than the one you intended.

title: Headphones only play on one side
steps: Pause audio and turn volume down. Check that the earcups are positioned over both ears.
With permission, check the headset's round plug is fully seated or its USB plug is secure, without forcing it.
Test a familiar approved clip at low volume. If the same side is silent, ask to test a school spare.
why: A partial connection or damaged headset can affect one channel.

title: Headphones sound crackly
steps: Pause the sound and lower volume using the speaker icon near the clock.
Look at the plug and cable for visible damage. With permission check the connector is seated without twisting it.
If crackling returns during low-volume playback, stop using the headset and ask staff for a spare.
why: Connection or device problems can produce unwanted noise.

title: Headphones are too quiet
steps: Look on the headset cable or earcup for a volume wheel; turn it slightly up if present.
In the video player, find the speaker icon near the playback bar and increase its slider a little. Check Windows volume near the clock.
Test at a comfortable level. If still too quiet, tell staff instead of raising all controls to maximum.
why: The headset and app may have separate volume controls.

title: Headphones are too loud
steps: Remove the headset if the sound hurts. Pause playback with the video player's pause button.
Click the speaker symbol near the Windows clock and move the volume slider left; also lower the headset wheel if present.
Resume at a low comfortable level. If volume suddenly jumps again, ask staff.
why: Keeping volume comfortable protects hearing.

title: Windows volume muted
steps: Look at the bottom-right of the Windows taskbar near the clock for the speaker icon. Click it.
If the speaker is crossed out, click the mute symbol in the volume panel; move the slider to a low level.
Play an approved clip. If it stays silent, check the player speaker icon and headset connection.
why: The taskbar and the app can mute sound separately.

title: Audio works in one app but not another
steps: Open the silent app and look for its speaker symbol near the playback controls. Check whether it is crossed out.
In Chrome, a muted site may show a crossed-out speaker or an Unmute site option when you right-click its tab. Unmute only an approved site when permitted.
Test a short approved clip. If another app plays but this one remains silent, tell staff which two apps you tested.
why: Separate apps can have separate playback controls.

title: Headset microphone arm is in wrong position
steps: Look for the microphone arm attached to the headset earcup. With permission, gently position it beside your mouth, not directly in front of it.
Check any mute switch on the headset cord or boom; some models mute when raised.
Use the assigned app's mic level test if allowed. If the meter never moves, ask staff.
why: Microphone position and mute can affect speech pickup.

title: Microphone sounds very quiet
steps: Locate the microphone opening at the end of the boom. Keep it close to the side of your mouth without touching it.
In the approved meeting app, look for a microphone level or test near its audio controls. Speak normally only with permission.
If the level stays low, tell the teacher; do not change Windows input gain.
why: Distance and obstruction affect microphone volume.

title: Microphone makes an echo
steps: Mute your microphone in the meeting using the microphone symbol and lower speaker volume.
With permission use your assigned headset so the microphone does not pick up sound from the speakers.
Unmute when directed. If you still hear repeated voices, tell the teacher whether it affects other participants too.
why: Speakers can feed sound back into a nearby microphone.

title: Wrong microphone selected in an app
steps: In Google Meet, look for the three-dot More options menu and open Settings, then Audio, if your teacher permits. Other approved apps may have an audio menu by the microphone icon.
Find the Microphone list and compare names with the headset assigned by staff. Select only the known assigned mic.
Use the app's level indicator if available. If the name is unclear or access is blocked, stop and ask the teacher.
why: App-level device selection can differ from the computer's default.

title: Webcam image is blurry
steps: Look at the external camera or the small lens above the screen. With permission, check its privacy cover is fully open.
Move a little farther from the lens and look at the approved app's video preview. Avoid touching the lens.
If the preview stays blurry, ask staff to clean or inspect the camera.
why: Obstruction, distance or smudges can reduce camera clarity.

title: Webcam image is too dark
steps: Look at the camera preview. If a bright window is behind you, turn toward a permitted light source or move the object being shown.
Check whether the physical camera cover is partly closed, opening it only with permission.
If everything remains dark, tell staff. Do not adjust protected camera settings.
why: Lighting matters for camera exposure.

title: Webcam says in use by another app
steps: Read the camera-in-use message. Look at the taskbar for another approved meeting or recording app you opened.
Save your work there and close that app normally only if permission and your session allow it.
Return to the intended app and try its camera button once. If still busy, ask staff; do not end background processes.
why: Some camera devices cannot be shared by multiple apps at once.

title: Camera or microphone permission denied
steps: Read the blocked camera or microphone message and note the app name.
Leave the permission prompt unchanged and stop trying to access the device.
Show the message to your teacher. Do not alter site permissions, privacy settings or school restrictions.
why: School staff decide which apps can use recording devices.

title: Identify a USB-A connector
steps: Look for a rectangular USB-A plug, often with a USB trident symbol. The matching port is a wide rectangle.
Compare it to the assigned accessible USB port. The plug fits in one orientation; stop if it resists.
Ask staff if uncertain. A port's color does not guarantee its speed or function.
why: USB-A plugs have a specific orientation.

title: Identify a USB-C connector
steps: Look for a small rounded oval plug with a matching oval port. USB-C usually fits either way up.
Check with the teacher that this is the intended port and cable for your assigned device.
If it does not fit gently, stop. Similar-looking USB-C ports may support different features.
why: USB-C describes connector shape, not all supported functions.

title: Identify an HDMI connector
steps: Look for HDMI printed near a display port or on the cable. Its plug is wide with tapered corners.
Compare the shape visually with the port without moving the existing monitor cable.
Ask the teacher to identify or reconnect the cable; do not unplug classroom displays.
why: HDMI commonly carries picture and sound.

title: Identify a DisplayPort connector
steps: Look for DP or DisplayPort markings. A full-size DisplayPort plug typically has one angled corner.
Some plugs have a release latch; do not pull or press it on classroom equipment.
Ask staff which display cable your station uses. Do not force any connector.
why: DisplayPort and HDMI are different connectors.

title: Identify a headphone and microphone jack
steps: Look for a small round jack marked with a headphone, microphone or combined headset symbol.
A headset may have one combined plug or two separate plugs. Match only the teacher-assigned connection.
If you cannot identify the correct jack, ask staff rather than forcing the plug.
why: Audio jacks may be separate or combined.

title: USB connector feels loose
steps: Stop wiggling the plug and leave the device still.
Point out where it feels loose, such as the front USB port or cable end, to the teacher.
Do not bend the connector or keep retrying it; staff can test a spare port or cable.
why: A damaged port can worsen if stressed.

title: USB hub not working
steps: Look for the assigned USB hub, a small box with several USB ports. Check for its power light if it has one.
See whether more than one of your connected devices stopped responding. Save your project if possible.
Tell staff which ports or devices fail. Do not unplug shared devices or power adapters.
why: Several peripherals may depend on one hub.

title: File Explorer cannot see flash drive
steps: Connect only the teacher-approved flash drive to an accessible port if allowed.
Press Windows+E. Choose This PC on the left; look under Devices and drives for the assigned drive name.
If it is absent, tell staff. If a prompt asks to format it, cancel; never format or install anything.
why: A recognized storage device should normally appear under This PC.

title: USB asks to format drive
steps: Look for Cancel or No on the message asking to format the drive. Click it without accepting.
Keep the drive connected until staff advises you; note whether it contains your schoolwork.
Show the exact message to the teacher. Formatting could erase files; do not attempt repairs.
why: Formatting can erase files.

title: USB drive is read-only
steps: If the app reports Read-only or Write protected, keep your original unchanged.
In the app use File > Save As or Save a Copy, if offered, and select your assigned school folder with a new filename.
Confirm the copied file opens. Ask staff about the drive; do not change permissions or switches.
why: Read-only storage may protect existing files or reflect school policy.

title: USB file copy is slow
steps: Look at the file transfer window for its progress bar and remaining time.
Wait while progress is moving. Do not pull the flash drive out or close the copying window.
If the bar remains unchanged for a long time or an error appears, tell staff before disconnecting.
why: Interrupting a write can damage the transferred file.

title: Safely eject a Windows flash drive
steps: Finish copying and close your own files that are open from the flash drive.
Near the Windows clock, click the up arrow for hidden icons if needed. Find Safely Remove Hardware, then select Eject for your assigned drive.
Wait for the safe-to-remove message before unplugging. If the drive is busy or you cannot identify it, ask staff.
why: Ejecting helps protect pending writes.

alternatives.label: It says device is in use

title: USB says device is in use
steps: When Windows says the USB device is in use, leave it connected.
Close your own project files stored on that drive and any Explorer window displaying it. Wait briefly and retry Eject.
If the warning remains, ask staff. Do not force removal or close unknown processes.
why: Open files can prevent safe removal.

title: Flash drive is full
steps: When a save message says the drive is full, cancel the failed save but keep the project open.
Use File > Save As to save a copy in your teacher-assigned school folder, if available.
Check the saved filename and location. Do not delete other files or format a drive; ask staff for storage help.
why: A drive needs free space for new files.

title: Drawing tablet is connected but cursor will not move
steps: Find the assigned tablet drawing surface and its matching pen. Check its accessible cable only with permission.
Hold the pen tip slightly above the surface and move it across the tablet. Watch the mouse pointer on screen.
If the mouse works but the pen pointer never moves, tell staff which pen and tablet you used.
why: Some tablets detect the pen before it touches the surface.

title: Tablet cursor moves but pen cannot draw
steps: In Photoshop, select the Brush tool by pressing B. In Window > Layers, click a visible unlocked pixel layer in your own practice document.
Click the foreground color square near the bottom of the toolbar and choose a color that contrasts with the canvas. Set brush opacity above zero in the top options bar.
Draw a small stroke. If the mouse draws but the tablet pen does not, ask staff; if neither draws, use Photoshop brush help.
why: A working pointer does not guarantee the current tool can paint.

title: Drawing tablet pen pressure not working
steps: Open a practice Photoshop document and select a visible unlocked pixel layer. Press B to select Brush.
Choose a brush known to support pen pressure; in Window > Brush Settings, check the brush's Shape Dynamics options if assigned by the teacher.
Draw one light and one firmer stroke. If the width stays the same with a pressure-enabled brush, ask staff to check the tablet.
why: Pressure response depends on the brush and tablet support.

title: Tablet pen draws before touching
steps: Lift the stylus away from the tablet and stop drawing.
Without removing the nib, look for a stuck or crooked tip. Check whether a line continues when hovering.
Show the teacher; do not pull out the tip or change tablet settings.
why: A stuck tip or device fault can register contact unexpectedly.

title: Tablet pen cursor offset
steps: Open a practice document and move the pen above the tablet without drawing.
Compare where the on-screen pointer appears with where you expect it. Test the middle and an edge.
Tell staff whether the offset is constant or changes near the edge. Leave calibration to staff.
why: Calibration and mapping depend on the installed tablet model.

title: Drawing tablet covers wrong screen
steps: Hover the pen over the tablet and look at both monitors, if present.
Identify which screen the pointer moves on; save your project with Ctrl+S if you can.
Tell staff which display should be used. Do not change display mapping or driver settings.
why: A tablet can be mapped to another display.

title: Stylus tip is damaged
steps: Look at the pen tip without pushing it against the drawing surface. If it is broken or sharp, stop.
Show the teacher the damaged nib and assigned pen.
Request an approved spare or staff replacement. Do not remove the nib yourself.
why: A damaged nib can scratch a drawing surface.

title: Drawing tablet buttons do unexpected things
steps: Stop pressing the unfamiliar tablet button. Note which button and what appeared on screen.
Use the normal on-screen toolbar or keyboard shortcut for your intended action.
Ask the teacher what the tablet button is assigned to; do not remap it.
why: Tablet buttons may be assigned custom shortcuts.

title: Drawing tablet is scratched or dirty
steps: Look at the tablet surface without scratching or pressing on a damaged area.
If it is dirty or scratched, tell staff and ask about an approved cleaning method or spare.
Do not apply liquids, solvents or scraping tools.
why: Proper cleaning depends on the device material.

title: Stylus disappears when switching apps
aliases: tablet not working in photoshop only
steps: Press Alt+Tab to return to the approved app where the stylus works. Hover and watch the pointer.
Switch to the intended app, open a practice file and select a normal drawing tool.
If the pen works only in the first app, tell staff both app names. Do not install or change drivers.
why: Different apps can handle pen input differently.

title: Wired game controller not detected
steps: Follow the assigned controller's cord to its accessible USB port. Check the connection with permission.
Open the approved game's Controls or Help screen and confirm controller support.
Click the play area and test a movement in practice mode. If no input registers, ask staff.
why: Games differ in controller support.

title: Wireless controller does not connect
steps: Find the assigned controller's normal power button and indicator light; use it only as directed.
Check whether the light remains steady or flashes. A flashing light may mean it is not connected.
Show staff the light and station number. Let them handle pairing and receivers.
why: Pairing can affect other classroom devices.

title: Controller buttons work in menus but not game
steps: Open the approved game's pause menu and look for Controls or Help. Check whether the current mode supports controllers.
Return to the game and click its play area once to give it focus.
Test one action in practice mode. If menus respond but gameplay does not, tell staff the game and mode.
why: Menu and gameplay input may differ.

title: Controller joystick moves by itself
steps: Set the controller on a flat desk with both sticks untouched.
Watch the character or cursor in an approved practice mode. If it keeps moving, note the direction.
Show staff the symptom and request a spare; do not calibrate or open it.
why: Unwanted movement may indicate stick drift.

title: Controller button sticks
steps: Stop pressing the sticky or jammed button and note its label, such as A or R1.
Show the teacher how the button sits compared with nearby buttons.
Do not pry or use liquid. Ask for a spare controller.
why: Physical cleaning and repair are staff tasks.

title: Game uses the wrong controller
steps: Pause the game if allowed. Open its player selection or Controls menu if it has one.
Identify which player responds when you press one button on your assigned controller in practice mode.
Tell staff the player number if wrong. Do not disconnect other students' controllers.
why: Some games assign devices by connection order.

title: Controller works but game shows keyboard prompts
steps: Open the approved game's Help or Controls screen from its pause or main menu.
Look for controller button labels or a controller diagram. Some games show keyboard prompts even while accepting controller input.
Test a harmless movement in practice mode. Ask staff if the action is not listed.
why: Some games display keyboard prompts even when controllers work.

title: Controller battery is low
steps: Look for the low-battery icon or flashing indicator on your assigned controller.
Pause the game and save if possible; tell staff the indicator you see.
Use only an approved charger or spare supplied by staff. Do not swap unknown batteries.
why: Low battery can cause unexpected disconnections.

title: Wrong printer selected
steps: Open your document and press Ctrl+P or use File > Print. Do not submit again.
Look for Printer or Destination near the top of the print panel. Compare the selected name with the teacher's assigned printer.
Select the assigned printer only if already listed and permitted. Check preview and copies before printing once.
why: School computers may list several shared printers.

title: Printer is missing from the list
steps: Open the approved document and press Ctrl+P. Click the Printer or Destination dropdown.
Look for the exact name supplied by your teacher, including room or printer number.
If missing, close the print dialog and tell staff. Do not use Add printer or install software.
why: Printer availability is managed by school staff.

title: Printer says offline
steps: Read the Offline message in the print dialog and note the printer name.
Cancel an unsent print job. If you already submitted it, do not send it again.
Tell your teacher the printer name and document. Leave cables, network and printer settings to staff.
why: Offline status may reflect a connection or device problem.

title: Print job is stuck
steps: If you already printed but nothing came out, stop sending additional copies.
Note your own document name, assigned printer and approximate time. A stuck job may still print later.
Ask staff to inspect the queue and cancel only your job if necessary.
why: Repeated submissions can waste paper once the queue resumes.

title: Accidentally sent too many copies
steps: Stop sending more copies. Note the document name, printer and number of copies requested.
Tell the teacher immediately so staff can stop the extra jobs.
Do not cancel anyone else's print job or turn off the printer.
why: Shared queues can contain work from many students.

title: Print preview shows cut off edges
steps: Open File > Print or press Ctrl+P and look at the preview page edges.
For this print job only, check Paper size and Layout or Orientation. If the app offers Fit to page, select it when permitted.
Confirm the entire artwork appears inside the preview before printing once. If it still cuts off, ask staff.
why: The artwork may be larger than the printable area.

title: Print is sideways
steps: Open the document's print panel with Ctrl+P and find Layout or Orientation.
Choose Portrait for a tall page or Landscape for a wide page according to the teacher's directions.
Check the preview orientation and that no edges are clipped before printing.
why: Print orientation affects how the page is placed on paper.

title: Only need to print one page
steps: Open the print preview with Ctrl+P and use the preview arrows to find the page you need.
Find Pages or Page range and select Custom if offered. Enter that page number only.
Verify the preview or page count shows one page and Copies is 1 before printing.
why: A page range avoids unnecessary printing.

title: Printed page is black and white
steps: Check your artwork on screen first. Open Print preview using Ctrl+P.
If the assigned printer offers Color or Black and white in its print panel, choose Color only when permitted.
Check preview where available. If the option is missing, ask staff instead of using a different printer.
why: Some school printers are monochrome or have managed color limits.

title: Printed page has streaks
steps: Keep the streaked page and compare it with the on-screen project.
Check whether the streak appears in the file itself or only on the print. Do not print another test without permission.
Show staff the sheet and printer name. Let staff inspect ink, toner or hardware.
why: Streaks may indicate a printer supply or mechanical issue.

title: Printer says paper jam
steps: Stop printing when the printer shows Paper jam or a jam symbol.
Tell the teacher which printer and any displayed tray or location code.
Do not reach inside, open hot compartments or pull jammed paper; wait for staff.
why: Printers can contain hot or moving components.

title: Printer says out of paper
steps: Read the Out of paper or Load paper message and printer name.
Stop sending repeat jobs; the printer may resume when paper is supplied.
Tell the teacher the tray or paper size shown. Let staff refill it or direct you.
why: The printer may need a particular paper type or size.

title: Scanner cannot find device
steps: Open the teacher-assigned scanning app from Start or its known shortcut.
Look for Scanner or Source in its main window and compare the name with the assigned scanner.
If it is not listed, ask staff. Do not install software or change scanner network settings.
why: Scanners may be shared or require school-managed software.

title: Scanned document is upside down
steps: Look at the page preview in the approved scanning app before saving.
If there is a rotate arrow, click it until the text is upright. If there is no rotate option, ask how to place the paper correctly.
Save the corrected scan in your assigned folder and reopen it to check readability.
why: Previewing helps catch orientation errors before saving.

title: Scanned file is missing
steps: Look in the scanning app for Save to, Destination or the folder displayed after saving.
Press Windows+E and open that specific approved folder. Look for the filename or recent date.
If missing, tell the teacher the last displayed path and file type. Do not repeatedly scan sensitive documents.
why: Scanning creates a file in the selected destination.

title: Switch between open Windows apps
steps: Hold Alt near the bottom of the keyboard and tap Tab without releasing Alt.
A row of open-window previews appears. Tap Tab until your document's window is highlighted.
Release Alt to open it. Check the title bar to make sure it is your own file.
why: Alt + Tab switches among open windows.

title: Show all open Windows windows
steps: Hold the Windows logo key and tap Tab to open Task View.
Look for a thumbnail of your intended app. Click that thumbnail once.
Press Esc to leave Task View without choosing; do not create or change virtual desktops.
why: Task View displays open windows.

title: Maximize a small window
steps: Find the three buttons at the top-right of the app window: dash, square and X.
Click the middle square once to maximize. If it shows overlapping squares, the window is already maximized.
To restore the smaller window, click the middle button again. Avoid X, which closes the app.
why: Maximizing increases the app's available workspace.

title: Put two windows side by side
steps: Open both approved apps. Click the first one's title bar to activate it.
Hold Windows and tap Left Arrow, then select the second app from the offered thumbnails if shown.
Both windows should appear side by side. Click the middle window button to maximize again if needed.
why: Snap arranges windows without changing system settings.

title: Window is off the edge of the screen
steps: Click the intended app's icon on the bottom taskbar, choosing its preview if there are several.
Hold Windows and tap Up Arrow to maximize the selected window.
If it does not appear, tell staff whether you use multiple monitors. Do not change display settings.
why: Maximizing can restore a window to the visible work area.

title: Desktop icons disappeared behind windows
steps: Hold the Windows logo key and tap D to show the desktop.
Look for the intended shortcut or file icon. Do not move or delete other desktop items.
Press Windows+D again to restore the open windows and check your project is still there.
why: Showing the desktop hides windows temporarily, not their files.

title: Windows app will not open
steps: Click Start (Windows logo on the taskbar) and type the exact name of the assigned app.
Click the installed app result once and wait for its window or launch screen. Do not select web download results.
If an error appears, show the teacher the text. Do not reinstall or update software.
why: An app may take time to start or need staff repair.

title: Program opens multiple copies
steps: Hold Alt and tap Tab to see each open window; locate the one with your active project name.
Save that project with Ctrl+S. Click X only on an extra window you opened and do not need.
If a save prompt appears, read its document name; choose Cancel if unsure.
why: Repeated launch clicks may create extra windows.

title: App asks to save when closing
steps: Read the project name in the Save changes prompt; check it is your own file.
Choose Save to keep your changes. If a Save As window opens, choose your assigned folder and filename. Choose Cancel if unsure.
Reopen the file if needed to confirm it saved. Avoid Don't Save unless directed and certain.
why: Save prompts protect unsaved work.

title: App asks to update
steps: Read the update prompt without clicking Install or Update.
If the app still responds, save your current project with Ctrl+S. Close or dismiss the update message only if a normal Later or Cancel option exists.
Tell the teacher what the update message says. Do not enter admin credentials.
why: School IT manages application updates.

title: Windows sign-in screen is locked
steps: Look at the Windows sign-in screen and check whether it is your assigned workstation.
Use only your own school-approved account or teacher-directed sign-in method. Do not share or type passwords into TechGuide.
If another user's name remains or your login is rejected, ask staff; do not try other accounts.
why: Shared computers require authorized accounts.

title: Computer says restart required
steps: Read the Restart required message without selecting Restart now.
If your project is open, use Ctrl+S or File > Save to save it in the assigned location.
Tell staff the message and whether you saved. Let them decide when to restart the shared computer.
why: A restart can close work and interrupt classroom activity.

title: Windows computer has no power
steps: Look at the assigned computer and monitor for power lights.
If normal startup is permitted and the computer is off, press its ordinary power button once. Wait for a sign-in screen.
If neither light nor screen appears, tell staff. Do not inspect outlets, power strips or rear cables.
why: The monitor and computer have separate power states.

title: Computer is running very slowly
steps: Save your own project using Ctrl+S if the app responds.
Look at the taskbar and close only your own unused apps with their X buttons, checking save prompts. Close only unused browser tabs.
If it stays slow, tell the teacher which app is affected; do not use cleanup tools or Task Manager.
why: Several open apps can compete for resources.

title: App window is blank white
steps: Wait briefly for the app to finish loading; avoid repeated clicks.
Click its title bar once. If menus respond, save your own document and switch to another app with Alt+Tab.
If the whole window stays blank or says Not Responding, ask staff before closing it.
why: An app may be busy or have a display problem.

title: Windows asks for administrator permission
steps: If a prompt asks to allow changes to the device or enter administrator credentials, stop.
Click No or Cancel if offered. Do not enter a password or approve the request.
Tell your teacher the action you were trying when the message appeared.
why: Protected actions require authorized staff.

title: Windows reports low disk space
steps: If a Low disk space message appears, leave system files alone.
If possible, use File > Save As to save your own work in a teacher-approved location with space.
Show the warning to staff. Do not clear system files, caches or other students' work.
why: Staff can manage shared storage safely.

title: File Explorer open assigned folder
steps: Hold Windows and tap E to open File Explorer. Look at the left navigation column.
Choose the teacher-assigned location, such as Documents or an approved shared folder, and double-click the named class folder.
Check the path in the address bar along the top. If the folder is missing or denied, ask staff.
why: File Explorer is for accessing authorized files and folders.

title: Find Downloads folder on Windows
steps: Press Windows+E to open File Explorer. Click Downloads in the left navigation column if shown.
If Downloads is not pinned, click the address bar and use the school-approved Downloads location, or open Chrome Downloads with Ctrl+J and use Show in folder for your own file.
Look for your filename or sort by Date modified. If the school redirects downloads, ask staff.
why: Browser downloads often go to a designated folder.

alternatives.label: Find file in a class folder

title: Rename your own Windows file
steps: Open your assigned folder in File Explorer and single-click only your own file.
Press F2 or right-click and select Rename. Type the new name; keep the file extension unchanged if it is visible.
Press Enter and check the name. If a warning about changing file type appears, cancel and retry.
why: Renaming a file does not convert it to another format.

title: Create a folder for class work
steps: Press Windows+E and navigate to the teacher-assigned storage folder. Check the path at the top.
Press Ctrl+Shift+N to create a folder, or choose New then Folder from the toolbar if available.
Type the required folder name and press Enter. Double-click it to begin saving your own work.
why: Folders help keep project files together.

title: Copy your own file to another folder
steps: In File Explorer single-click your own file in its current folder and press Ctrl+C.
Navigate to the assigned destination using the left pane or approved folder path. Press Ctrl+V.
Look for the copied filename and open it to confirm it works. Keep the original intact.
why: Copying creates another file without moving the original.

title: File is already open and cannot be moved
steps: Read the message naming the file that is in use. Leave it where it is.
Switch to the app where your file is open, save it with Ctrl+S, then close that document normally.
Return to File Explorer and retry the approved move once. If still blocked, ask staff.
why: Open files can be locked to prevent conflicting changes.

title: File opens in wrong program
steps: Close the wrong app normally if it is showing your file. Open the assigned app from Start or the taskbar.
In that app choose File > Open, navigate to the folder containing your own file and select it.
Check the title bar shows your file. If unsupported, tell staff the file extension; do not change default apps.
why: Opening files from within an app avoids changing system defaults.

title: Windows file says access denied
steps: Read Access denied and note the folder or file path in the window.
Check that it matches the location assigned by the teacher. If not, return to your approved folder without exploring other users' directories.
Ask staff if the assigned location is denied. Do not change permissions or try someone else's account.
why: Access restrictions protect other people and school resources.

title: Screenshot copied but not saved
steps: If you just captured the image, look for the Snipping Tool notification near the clock and click it if shown.
Use the Save icon and select your assigned folder, or paste with Ctrl+V into your approved slide if the image is still on the clipboard.
Check the saved image opens or appears on the slide. If the clipboard changed, take another permitted screenshot.
why: A screenshot can be copied without becoming a file.

title: Capture just part of the Windows screen
steps: Hold Windows and Shift, tap S and release. The screen should dim and a small capture toolbar should appear.
Choose the rectangular snip option, then drag from one corner of your own work to the opposite corner; release.
Use the notification to save or Ctrl+V to paste into your assigned document. Avoid including names, passwords or other students' work.
why: A selected region is useful for process screenshots.

title: Cancel a screenshot in Windows
steps: If the screen is dim and the capture toolbar is visible, press Esc in the top-left of the keyboard before selecting anything.
The dim overlay should disappear and your original app should be visible.
If not, wait briefly and tell staff. Do not force-close the computer.
why: Esc normally cancels an unfinished capture.

title: Paste a screenshot into an assignment
steps: Take a permitted screenshot of your own work with Windows+Shift+S and select the area.
Open the correct slide or document and click where you want the picture, then press Ctrl+V.
Check the image appeared; resize using a corner handle if required. If nothing pastes, use the screenshot save guide.
why: The clipboard can transfer images between supported apps.

title: Windows taskbar is hidden
steps: Move the pointer to the bottom edge of the screen and pause. If the taskbar is set to hide, it may slide up.
If your app is in full-screen browser mode, press F11 once if permitted to return to the normal window.
Use Alt+Tab to switch to your intended app if needed. If the taskbar remains unavailable, ask staff; do not change settings.
why: The taskbar may be temporarily hidden or covered by an app.

title: Find an approved installed app
steps: Click the Windows logo on the taskbar or tap the Windows key.
Type the exact name of the teacher-approved app, such as Illustrator. Look for the result labeled App rather than a web result.
Click the installed app once. If not listed, ask staff rather than downloading it.
why: Start search can locate installed applications.

title: Classroom class is missing
steps: Open Classroom. Click the three-line menu at upper left and choose Classes or Home.
Look for the class tile that matches your schedule. Click your profile picture at the top right to check the account is your assigned school account.
If the tile is missing, ask the teacher to check enrollment. Do not join random classes or use another student’s account.
why: Only enrolled classes appear for your account.

title: Find assignments by topic
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
Click Classwork at the top. Select a topic from the topic list on the left, or scroll through the topic headings.
Click the assignment title under the correct heading, then open its full instructions. If it is not there, choose All topics.
why: Classwork is organized separately from Stream posts.

title: Classroom Stream versus Classwork
steps: Open the class tile in Classroom. Look at the tabs across the top.
Stream shows announcements and recent posts. Click Classwork beside it to find assignments organized by topic.
Select an assignment title and open the full directions; submitting happens there, not in a Stream comment.
why: The two tabs have different purposes.

title: Find due dates in Classroom
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Look near the assignment title for the due date and time. If no due date appears, ask your teacher rather than assuming there is none.
why: Not every item has a due date.

title: Find your Classroom to-do list
steps: Open Classroom. Click the three-line menu at upper left.
Choose To-do. Use the class filter near the top to choose your class.
Select Assigned, Missing or Done to see that list. Click an item to open its details.
why: The overview helps you find work, but teachers can update statuses.

title: Find all your work for one class
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
Click Classwork, then View your work near the top of the page.
Use the status filters to see assigned, returned or missing work. Select a title to inspect its instructions and due date.
why: The class-specific view helps separate assignments from different classes.

title: Classroom material has no Turn in button
aliases: no turn in button on material
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
A Material is a resource, not a submission. If the page has no Your work card or completion button, return to Classwork.
Look for the separate assignment named in the material. Ask your teacher if there is no matching assignment.
why: Materials may be reference documents rather than assignments.

title: Find a linked tutorial in Classroom
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Below the directions, look for a link or a card showing a video, PDF or document title. Click the resource named by your teacher.
If it opens a new tab, keep Classroom open. If it asks for access, show your teacher the message.
why: Resource attachments are separate from your submitted work.

title: Classroom instructions are cut off
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Scroll down the main directions area. Click any Show more text if displayed.
Open the attached directions or rubric card below the text if your teacher included one. Return to the assignment tab when finished.
why: The full assignment may contain more directions than the overview.

title: Classroom assignment is locked or unavailable
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Read the message at the top of the assignment or in the Your work card. If it says access denied, closed, or unavailable, stop.
Show your teacher the assignment title and exact message. Only the teacher can resolve class permissions or availability.
why: The teacher controls assignment availability.

title: Classroom calendar for assignments
steps: Open Classroom. Click the three-line menu at upper left and choose Calendar if available.
Use the week arrows to find the date. Choose the class from the filter if shown.
Click an assignment entry to see its title and open Classroom for full instructions. Ask your teacher if Calendar is unavailable.
why: Calendar entries are a reminder, not a substitute for assignment directions.

title: Classroom class code does not work
steps: On the Classroom home page, use the + near the top right and choose Join class if your teacher told you to join.
Enter the code directly from your teacher, checking similar letters and numbers. Choose Join.
If it fails, show your teacher the error. Do not guess codes or join unrelated classes.
why: Class codes may expire or be disabled.

title: Open your assigned copy of a document
aliases: teacher made copy for each student
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Click the attached document that includes your name. Do not open the example in the directions instead.
Check that you can type in your own copy. If it says View only, ask your teacher to check access.
why: A teacher may provide a separate editable copy for every student.

title: Classroom document says view only
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Open your named attachment, not the example link. Look near the top right of the document for View only or the editing mode.
If your work is Turned in, editing may be locked. Ask the teacher whether you may unsubmit. If still locked, ask for access.
why: The original resource or submitted copy may not be editable.

title: Classroom Mark as done versus Turn in
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
If the assignment requires a file, attach it with Add or create. Some tasks instead ask you to finish work elsewhere.
Use Turn in or Mark as done as shown, only once the required work is complete. Confirm if prompted and check the status.
why: Assignments without attached student work may use a different completion label.

title: Classroom upload stuck in progress
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Look for a moving progress indicator or a filename that has not finished appearing. Leave this tab open while it uploads.
Keep the source file saved. If the progress stops or an error appears, show your teacher the message instead of uploading multiple copies.
why: An unfinished upload may not become part of the submission.

title: Classroom submit a downloaded image
aliases: how do i turn in my png
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Click Add or create, then File. In the picker, select Downloads or the folder used during export.
Select the PNG or JPG your teacher requested, then Open or Upload. Wait for its filename and check the image preview.
After all attachments appear in Your work, click Turn in below them. Confirm in the pop-up if asked.
Check that the status says Turned in. Seeing an attached file alone does not mean you submitted it.
why: Exporting an image does not automatically attach it to Classroom.

alternatives.label: I cannot find my Windows download

title: Classroom attach a Google Drive document
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Click Add or create, then Google Drive. Use Recent or search by the document name in the picker.
Select your finished document and click Add or Insert. Check the file appears in Your work.
After all attachments appear in Your work, click Turn in below them. Confirm in the pop-up if asked.
Check that the status says Turned in. Seeing an attached file alone does not mean you submitted it.
why: The Drive picker links the chosen file to the assignment.

title: Classroom submit more than one file
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
In Your work, click + Add or create. Choose File for a file on this computer, or Google Drive for a file already saved online.
Select the first required file, then repeat Add or create for the next. For example, attach the AI or PSD project and the exported PNG if required.
Check every filename against the assignment directions. Open the image preview to verify it.
After all attachments appear in Your work, click Turn in below them. Confirm in the pop-up if asked.
Check that the status says Turned in. Seeing an attached file alone does not mean you submitted it.
why: A project may require both editable work and an exported image.

title: Classroom wrong file attached before submitting
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Check the attachment name or open its preview. If it is the wrong file and not yet submitted, click the X or Remove control next to that attachment, if shown.
Use Add or create to attach the correct file. This removes the attachment, not your saved original. Ask your teacher if the control is absent.
why: Removing an attachment is not the same as deleting its original file.

title: Classroom accidentally submitted too early
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
If the status says Turned in, do not remove the submission without permission.
Ask your teacher whether you may unsubmit. If allowed, click Unsubmit, confirm, finish your work and turn it in again. Check the status afterward.
why: Unsubmitting changes the submission status and may affect deadlines.

title: Classroom submission status is still assigned
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
If the card says Assigned, the attachment alone has not submitted the work. Check that all required files are listed.
Click Turn in or Mark as done when finished and confirm. If it still says Assigned, show your teacher the screen.
why: Uploading a file alone may not complete submission.

alternatives.label: I only see Mark as done

title: Classroom late or missing label
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Read the due date near the title and the status in Your work.
A Missing label means Classroom considers the work overdue and not submitted; Late means it was submitted after the deadline. Check the actual status and attachments.
If your teacher gave a different deadline or the status looks wrong, show them the page. Do not submit duplicates.
why: A missing or late label does not always mean a file was lost.

title: Classroom returned work is editable again
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Look for a returned score and Private comments near Your work. Read them first.
Ask whether corrections are allowed. If yes, open your attached file and edit your copy, or attach the revised export.
After all attachments appear in Your work, click Turn in below them. Confirm in the pop-up if asked.
Check that the status says Turned in. Seeing an attached file alone does not mean you submitted it.
why: Returned work may allow editing without granting permission for unlimited corrections.

title: Classroom cannot open attachment preview
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Click the attachment title below the directions or in Your work, depending on which file you need.
If the preview is blank, wait briefly. A normal Open with option may be available for an approved app.
If it still fails, show your teacher the filename and error. Do not install a viewer.
why: Some file types or permissions prevent previewing.

title: Classroom submission includes old version
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
On the assignment details page, look to the right of the directions for the card titled Your work. On a narrow screen, scroll below the directions.
Open the attached file preview and compare it with the new file in Downloads or Drive. Check the title and contents, not just the filename.
If already submitted, ask permission to change it. If not, remove the incorrect attachment using its X and add the correct copy.
After all attachments appear in Your work, click Turn in below them. Confirm in the pop-up if asked.
Check that the status says Turned in. Seeing an attached file alone does not mean you submitted it.
why: A downloaded file and a live Drive document update differently.

title: Classroom upload file too large
steps: Keep the original project saved. On Windows, open File Explorer, right-click the file and choose Properties to see Size. On Chromebook, open Files, select the file and use its information/details option if available.
Read the upload error and assignment requirements. Show the size and error to your teacher.
Only if approved, export a smaller copy from the original application. Do not overwrite the source or change the filename extension to shrink it.
why: Reducing size can affect image quality or remove editable features.

title: Find private comments in Classroom
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Look on the right, below Your work, for Private comments. On a narrow screen, scroll below the assignment directions.
Read the teacher’s message. If there is a reply field, use it only for school-related questions or your own correction explanation.
why: Private assignment comments are distinct from class-wide posts.

title: Find comments inside a Google document
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Open your named document from Your work. Look for highlighted text and comment boxes along the right edge.
Click a highlighted passage or the comments icon near the top right to read the conversation. Do not resolve comments unless your teacher asks.
why: In-document comments may not appear in the main Classroom comment area.

title: Find a Classroom rubric
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Below the directions or beside the assignment details, look for a Rubric card with criteria and points. Click it to expand.
Read each criterion and its scoring descriptions. If there is no rubric card, check the attached instructions or ask your teacher.
why: A rubric may be attached only to certain assignments.

title: Classroom grade does not appear
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Look near the title and Your work for a returned score. You can also go back to Classwork and click View your work.
If it is still Turned in or no score is displayed, ask when grades will be returned. There may be no grade yet.
why: Teachers decide when grades are returned.

title: Classroom grade is different from expected
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Check the assignment title and score, including the maximum points. Open the rubric if shown and read Private comments.
Tell your teacher which score or criterion you have a question about. Do not change or resubmit the work without permission.
why: Only the teacher can correct grading records.

title: Classroom reply to teacher feedback
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Find Private comments below Your work (scroll down on a small screen). Click the text field if shown.
Write your own explanation of what you changed, then use the send arrow or Post button. Confirm the comment appears.
If the field is absent, ask your teacher how they want corrections documented.
why: TechGuide can show where to reply, not write your response.

title: Classroom comment box is missing
steps: In Chrome, open your school Google Classroom page. Click the tile with your class name.
At the top of the class, select Classwork (next to Stream).
Click the assignment title, then View instructions or View assignment if shown. You should see the full directions.
Look below Your work for Private comments. A class comment in Stream is different and may be visible to classmates.
If there is no private field, do not post personal information publicly. Ask the teacher for the approved way to respond.
why: Teachers and school policies may restrict comments.

title: Classroom announcement disappears
steps: Open the class tile and click Stream at the top.
Scroll through the announcements. If it is not there, click Classwork and look under the relevant topic for related materials.
If it is still missing, ask the teacher whether the post was moved or removed.
why: Stream posts can be updated by the teacher.

title: Classroom notification opens wrong class
steps: Close the incorrect notification tab if you are not editing work in it. Open Classroom from your school bookmark.
Click the correct class tile, then Classwork and the assignment title. Open its full directions.
If that item is missing, show the teacher the notification and title.
why: Old notification links may not reflect updated assignments.

title: Classroom cannot see classmate work
steps: Go to Classwork in your class. Look under the topic where the teacher posted examples or materials.
Open only the example link your teacher shared. Another student’s private submission or feedback is not a class resource.
Ask the teacher for the location of the approved example if you cannot find it.
why: Student submissions and grades are private.

title: Find recently opened Google Drive files
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Select Recent on the left. Look near the top for files you opened most recently.
Check the title and owner before opening your own or teacher-shared file. If absent, use Search in Drive.
why: Recent is a view of files, not their actual storage folder.

title: Find files shared by a teacher
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Click Shared with me on the left. Look for the file title and the person who shared it.
Use Search in Drive to search for the title if needed. If unavailable, ask the teacher to confirm the share.
why: Shared files may not appear in My Drive.

title: Search Drive by file type
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Click Search in Drive and type the filename or part of it. Press Enter.
Click the Type filter chip near the top of the results and choose the file type (for example PDFs or Images). Check the filtered results.
why: Filtering helps narrow a long search list.

title: Search Drive by modified date
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Click the Modified filter chip near the search area. Choose a date range matching when you worked on the file.
Add a filename word in Search in Drive if too many results appear. Check the title and modified date.
why: Modified dates can be different from creation dates.

title: Create a class folder in Google Drive
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
