Click My Drive on the left and open your teacher-approved location. Click + New at upper left, then New folder.
Type your class or project name and click Create. Double-click the new folder to confirm it opens.
why: Folders organize files without changing their format.

title: Move your own Google Drive file into a folder
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Find your own file, right-click it and choose Organize > Move, or the Move option if shown.
In the folder picker, open your own class folder and click Move. Open the destination to check the file appears. Do not move shared originals.
why: Moving a file changes its location and can affect access in shared folders.

title: Star an important Drive file
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Right-click your own or approved shared file. Open Organize and choose Add to starred.
Click Starred in the left navigation. Confirm the file appears; this does not move the original.
why: A star is a personal shortcut and does not move the original.

title: Remove a personal Drive star
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Click Starred on the left. Right-click the intended file and choose Organize > Remove from starred.
Check it disappears from Starred. This is not deletion; the file stays in its original location.
why: Unstarring is not deleting the file.

title: Find where a Drive file is stored
aliases: which folder is my doc in
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Find the file in search results. In list view, check the Location column if available; click the location to open the folder.
Alternatively right-click the file and look for File information > Details or Show file location, if available. If the folder is shared, ask before moving anything.
why: A search result can come from different folders.

title: Drive grid versus list view
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Open My Drive or a folder. Look for the list/grid toggle near the upper right of the file area.
Select list view to see names in rows or grid view to see thumbnails. This changes the view, not the files.
why: List view makes names easier to compare.

title: Sort your Drive files by name
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Open your own folder. In list view, click the Name heading or use the sort control near the top.
Check that names are in alphabetical order. Click the sort direction if you need the reverse order.
why: Sorting changes the view, not the files themselves.

title: Drive shortcut versus actual file
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Look at the file icon: a small arrow can indicate a shortcut rather than a separate copy.
Double-click it to open the original file. If it is unavailable, ask the owner to check access. Do not assume removing a shortcut removes the original.
why: A shortcut points to another item rather than copying its contents.

title: Find a file in Drive Trash
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Click Trash on the left. Find the exact file you accidentally removed by name.
If it is your own file, right-click and select Restore if offered. Return to its original folder to check it is back. Never empty Trash or restore other people’s files without permission.
why: Restoration may return a file to its former location; do not empty Trash.

title: Drive duplicate files with similar names
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Search for part of the shared filename. Use list view to compare the owner and modified date.
Open your own likely versions in separate tabs and compare the work. Ask which version to submit if uncertain; do not delete the other versions.
why: Copies are independent files and may contain different edits.

title: Drive file has an untitled name
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Type Untitled in Search in Drive. Use Type and Modified filters to narrow the results.
Open your own likely file and check the contents. Click its title at upper left, enter the required name and press Enter.
why: A meaningful name helps prevent accidental submissions.

title: Drive folder appears empty
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Check the folder name at the top and the school profile icon at upper right.
Use Search in Drive to look for one expected filename. If search finds it, check its location.
If the folder was shared and still looks empty, ask the owner to check access. Do not change sharing.
why: An empty view may be a different folder or restricted access.

title: Upload a local file to Google Drive
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Open your assigned folder. Click + New at upper left and choose File upload.
In the computer file picker, choose Downloads or the folder where you saved your file. Select it and click Open.
Wait for the upload-complete notice, then check the file appears in the Drive folder and opens.
why: Uploading creates a Drive copy; your local original remains separate.

title: Download an approved Google Drive file
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Find your own or teacher-approved file. Right-click it and select Download if allowed.
In Chrome press Ctrl+J to see the completed download. On Chromebook open Files > Downloads; on Windows open File Explorer > Downloads.
Check the filename and open the file in the approved app. If Download is absent, ask the teacher.
why: Drive downloads may be disabled by the owner or school.

title: Drive download contains several files in a ZIP
steps: Press Ctrl+J in Chrome and check the downloaded archive name. Open Downloads in Files or File Explorer.
On Windows right-click the ZIP and choose Extract All, then Extract. On Chromebook double-click the ZIP and copy its needed contents to your own folder.
Open the extracted files, not the ZIP itself. Check for the individual files you expected.
why: A ZIP packages several files together without changing their contents.

title: Drive upload failed or interrupted
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Look at the upload notice in the lower corner of Drive. If it is still progressing, wait. If it failed, read the exact error.
Keep the original file in Downloads or your project folder. If no error remains and the connection works, retry once only.
If it fails again, ask the teacher and show the message. Do not upload repeated copies.
why: An interrupted transfer may not create a usable copy.

title: Drive says you are offline
steps: Keep the affected document tab open. Do not close it if you have unsaved edits.
Click the Chromebook clock at bottom right or look at the Windows network icon near the clock. Check whether it shows a connection without changing network settings.
Tell your teacher if offline. Once connected, wait for the document to show it is saved before closing.
why: Offline access depends on school policy and whether a file was prepared for offline use.

title: Google Docs changes have not saved to Drive
steps: Keep the Google document open. Look near the title at upper left for the cloud/save status icon or saving message.
Wait until it reports saved to Drive. If it reports offline or an error, keep the tab open and tell your teacher.
Do not refresh, close or sign out while edits may be unsaved.
why: Unsynced changes may be lost if the page closes unexpectedly.

title: Drive file shared link opens wrong account
steps: On the Drive or access page, check the profile icon in the upper-right corner. Compare the displayed account with your assigned school account.
If the assigned account is already available and your teacher permits switching, select it. Otherwise ask the teacher.
Open the original teacher-provided link again. Never use someone else’s credentials.
why: Access is tied to the account the owner shared with.

title: Request access to a teacher file
steps: Open the teacher’s original Classroom link using your assigned school account.
If the page says You need access, look for Request access. Use it only if your teacher directs you to; otherwise show them the page.
Wait for approval and reopen the original link. Do not change permissions or use other accounts.
why: Only the file owner or authorized staff can grant access.

title: Understand viewer, commenter and editor access
steps: Open the assigned Google document. Look near the top right for View only or the Editing/Viewing/Suggesting control if available.
Viewer can read; commenter can comment when permitted; editor can change content. A locked mode may mean the teacher has not given editing access.
Ask your teacher if you need an editable copy. Do not change sharing yourself.
why: Access levels protect shared work from unintended changes.

title: Drive says storage quota exceeded
steps: Keep the editing app open and preserve your original work. Read the storage-full message in Drive or in your upload notice.
Tell the teacher or IT which file you need to save and the exact warning. Ask for an approved storage location.
Do not delete files, empty Trash or create a new account to get around the limit.
why: School storage limits are managed by staff.

title: Google file not owned by you
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Find the file in list view and check its Owner column, or right-click and open File information > Details.
If the owner is someone else, use the file only as assigned. Ask for your own copy if editing is required.
why: Shared ownership and editing access are different things.

title: Find file size in Google Drive
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Find the file. Switch to list view using the layout toggle at the upper right. Look for File size or right-click and choose File information > Details.
Compare the displayed size with your teacher’s limit. Google-native documents may not show a normal downloaded file size.
why: Native Google documents may not show a conventional file size.

title: Drive PDF preview appears blank
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Double-click the teacher-approved PDF. Wait for the page thumbnails or preview to load.
If it stays blank and downloads are allowed, use the download icon in the preview and open the PDF from Downloads using the approved browser.
If it still fails, tell your teacher the file name and error. Do not install a viewer.
why: Blank previews can result from a damaged file or a rendering problem.

title: Drive file is a shortcut with access denied
steps: In Chrome, open drive.google.com using your school account. The navigation list is on the left.
Check for a shortcut arrow on the icon. Open the shortcut using your assigned account.
If the original target asks for access, return to the teacher’s original link and report the message. A shortcut does not grant access to the original.
why: A shortcut does not give permission to open its target.

title: Editable project versus exported image
steps: Open File Explorer or Files and find your project. A Photoshop project usually ends in .psd; an Illustrator project usually ends in .ai.
Keep that editable source saved. In Photoshop use File > Export > Export As; in Illustrator use File > Export > Export As. Choose the required PNG or JPG and a folder.
Open the exported image to check it. Submit both only if your directions require both.
why: An image export is not a substitute for editable source work.

title: PNG versus JPG
steps: Read the file type requested in the assignment. PNG can retain transparent areas; JPG does not support transparency and compresses photos.
In the Adobe export dialog, choose the requested format. For a required solid background, choose an opaque background before exporting.
Open the output and verify the background, image quality and extension.
why: JPEG compression can reduce detail and does not support transparent backgrounds.

title: PDF versus Google document
steps: Read the assignment to see whether it requires an editable Google Doc or a PDF.
In your Google Doc, click File at upper left, then Download > PDF Document (.pdf) if a PDF is required.
Open Downloads using Ctrl+J in Chrome and preview the PDF. Keep the editable document in Drive.
why: A PDF preserves layout but is not the same as the editable source.

title: SVG versus PNG
steps: Check whether the teacher requested SVG (vector) or PNG (pixel image). Open the editable artwork in Illustrator.
Click File > Export > Export As, then choose the requested format. Use artboards if the assignment requires only the artboard.
Save in the assigned folder and open the output to check it. Keep the AI source.
why: SVG can store scalable vectors; PNG stores pixels.

title: File extension seems wrong
steps: Find the file in Files or File Explorer and check its type or Properties. A name ending in .png does not guarantee it is a PNG.
Open the original in your approved editing app. Use File > Save As for an editable format or File > Export for an image format.
Choose the actual requested format in the dialog. Check the new file opens; never just change the extension.
why: Renaming an extension does not convert the file.

title: File opens in wrong application
steps: Find the file and check its extension (for example PSD, AI or PDF).
Open the correct approved application from the Start menu or school launcher. In that application, choose File > Open and select the file.
If the app cannot open it, ask your teacher. Do not change the computer’s default apps or install software.
why: Opening from the intended program avoids modifying system settings.

title: Downloaded file name ends with (1)
steps: Open Downloads in Files or File Explorer. Find the two similarly named files (one may end in (1)).
Compare their modified dates and open them to see which contains your finished work.
Rename the correct copy with the assignment name if allowed. Keep both until you know which is right.
why: Browsers often add a number to avoid overwriting a file.

title: A file is too large for the assignment
steps: Find your saved file. On Windows right-click it and choose Properties to see its Size; on Chromebook check the file information if available.
Show the size and assignment limit to your teacher. Keep the editable original.
If the teacher approves a smaller image, use the Adobe Export As dialog to choose smaller dimensions or an approved format. Preview it for readability.
why: Compression or resizing can remove details, so keep the original.

title: Cannot find a saved Adobe project on Chromebook
aliases: adobe file from windows not on chromebook
steps: On the Windows computer where you made the Adobe project, open File Explorer (Windows+E). Find the folder you used when saving.
If the file is only on that computer, ask your teacher which approved Drive folder or storage location to use. Upload your own saved file through Drive > + New > File upload if permitted.
On Chromebook open that same Drive folder and check the filename. Adobe desktop project files may not open for editing on a Chromebook.
why: Local files do not automatically appear on another computer.

title: Cloud copy versus computer copy
aliases: why file different on another computer
steps: Open Drive in Chrome to check files stored online. Open Files or File Explorer > Downloads or Documents to check local files.
Compare filenames, modified times and contents. A download is a separate copy; edits do not necessarily sync back.
Use the school-approved location and verify that the intended version is there before switching computers.
why: A local copy may not sync when a cloud file changes.

title: Check an exported image before turning it in
steps: Open the folder you selected during export in Files or File Explorer. Find the PNG or JPG by name.
Double-click it to preview. Check edges, orientation, text readability, background and whether the entire artwork appears.
If something is wrong, return to your editable project and export again with the correct options. Do not overwrite the source.
why: An export may look different from an editable project.

title: Keep source and export together
steps: In your approved project folder, save the editable project through File > Save As if needed.
Use File > Export > Export As to create the requested image in that same folder. Use matching base names, such as Project.ai and Project.png.
Open the folder and check both files appear and the exported image looks right.
why: A consistent folder makes it easier to find the correct version later.

title: Avoid accidentally overwriting your project
steps: If a Save dialog asks whether to replace an existing file, pause and read the filename and folder.
If uncertain, click Cancel. Use File > Save As to create a new clearly named version in your approved folder.
Open both versions to check which is final. Keep the editable original and submit the version your teacher requests.
why: Replacing a file can remove an earlier version.

title: Google Docs rename a document
steps: Click the document name next to the blue Docs icon in the upper left.
Replace the name with your assigned filename and press Enter.
Look at the title again and wait for the saving indicator to finish.
why: The document title helps you locate it in Drive.

title: Google Docs undo accidental typing
steps: Click in the document where you made the mistake.
Press Ctrl+Z once or click the curved left arrow in the top toolbar.
Check what returned. Repeat only if needed; for much older changes ask before restoring version history.
why: Undo reverses recent editing actions.

title: Google Docs redo a change
steps: Click inside the document after undoing a change.
Click the curved right arrow beside Undo near the upper left, or press Ctrl+Y.
Check that the intended change returned. If the arrow is gray, there is nothing to redo.
why: Redo reapplies an action you just reversed.

title: Google Docs select all text
steps: Click inside the editable document body, not the browser address bar.
Press Ctrl+A once. The document text should become highlighted.
Apply the intended formatting only if you really need it on all text. Click in the page to cancel the selection.
why: Selecting broad content can affect the entire document.

title: Google Docs paste without formatting
steps: Highlight your own source text and press Ctrl+C.
Click where it belongs in Docs and press Ctrl+Shift+V.
The pasted words should use the surrounding style. If you see unwanted formatting, undo and try again.
why: Plain-text paste avoids bringing in the original font and color.

title: Google Docs text is tiny
steps: If only some words are small, drag over those words.
Find the numeric font-size box beside the font name in the toolbar; type the assigned size and press Enter.
If everything including the page appears small, use the Docs zoom percentage instead. Keep required accessibility zoom.
why: Font size changes the document; zoom changes your view.

title: Google Docs change text color
steps: Drag over the words you want to recolor.
In the top toolbar click the A with a colored line underneath (Text color). Choose a swatch.
Click elsewhere and check contrast against the page. Undo if you changed the wrong words.
why: Text color is different from the background highlight.

title: Google Docs remove text highlight
steps: Drag over the highlighted words.
Find the marker-shaped Highlight color button near Text color in the toolbar and select None.
If the color remains, click in the table cell or paragraph; it may be cell or paragraph shading instead.
why: Highlight is a separate format from font color.

title: Google Docs bold, italic and underline
steps: Select the words by dragging over them.
Click B for bold, I for italic or U for underline in the toolbar above the page.
Click elsewhere to see the change. Click the same button again on the selected words to remove that style.
why: Formatting applies to the selected words or future typing at the cursor.

title: Google Docs remove unwanted formatting
steps: Select only the text with unwanted styling.
Choose Format > Clear formatting at the top.
The selected text should return to basic styling. Reapply the teacher's required size, heading style or color.
why: Clearing formatting changes styles, not the text itself.

title: Google Docs center a heading
steps: Click anywhere within the heading paragraph.
Choose Format > Align & indent > Center, or press Ctrl+Shift+E.
The whole paragraph should move to the middle of the page. Undo if the wrong paragraph moved.
why: Paragraph alignment is not controlled by extra spaces.

title: Google Docs line spacing
steps: Drag across the paragraphs you want to change.
Choose Format > Line & paragraph spacing at the top and select Single, 1.15, 1.5 or Double as assigned.
Compare the gaps between the lines. This changes the selected paragraphs rather than the entire file automatically.
why: Line spacing controls vertical distance between lines.

title: Google Docs extra space between paragraphs
steps: Click in the gap and look for an empty line; press Backspace only on an accidental blank paragraph.
If the gap remains, click in the paragraph and open Format > Line & paragraph spacing.
Choose Remove space before/after paragraph if offered and appropriate, then check the gap again.
why: Blank lines and paragraph spacing create gaps differently.

title: Google Docs indent a paragraph
steps: Click inside the paragraph to indent.
Choose Format > Align & indent > Indentation options. For a first-line indent, choose First line under Special indent.
Enter the amount assigned by your teacher and click Apply. Check that only the intended lines moved.
why: Indentation formats paragraphs more consistently than repeated spaces.

title: Google Docs make a bulleted list
steps: Click where your list begins or select your existing list lines.
In the toolbar find the dots-with-lines Bulleted list button (possibly under More). Click it.
Enter each item yourself and press Enter for the next bullet. Press Enter twice at the end to stop.
why: List formatting keeps the bullets aligned.

title: Google Docs make a numbered list
steps: Click where the numbered list begins or select your own list lines.
Click the toolbar icon with 1, 2, 3 and lines (Numbered list).
Type one item per line; press Enter for the next number. Press Enter on an empty item to end the list.
why: Automatic numbering follows the list structure.

title: Google Docs numbering restarts incorrectly
steps: Right-click the number beside the item where numbering went wrong.
Choose Continue previous numbering or Restart numbering, as needed. Enter the starting number if asked.
Look at the numbers above and below the item. Undo if the wrong list changed.
why: Separate list sections may use independent numbering.

title: Google Docs heading styles
steps: Click inside your written heading.
In the toolbar open the box often labeled Normal text and choose the heading level your teacher requested.
The paragraph should change style. If the outline is visible, look for your heading there too.
why: Heading styles identify structure for navigation and accessibility.

title: Google Docs find a word
steps: Click inside the document and press Ctrl+F.
Type the word in the small Find box near the top right.
Use its up/down arrows to jump between highlighted matches. Click X or press Esc to close Find.
why: Find does not alter document text.

title: Google Docs replace a repeated typo
steps: Choose Edit > Find and replace from the top menu.
Enter the old spelling in Find and your corrected spelling in Replace with.
Use Next and Replace for each intended match rather than Replace all unless every occurrence really should change.
why: Replacing all without reviewing may change unintended words.

title: Google Docs spelling underlines
steps: Right-click a word with a red spelling underline.
Read the suggested spellings in the menu and compare them with what you intended.
Choose a matching correction or leave your word unchanged if it is correct. Do not accept every suggestion blindly.
why: Spelling checks are suggestions, not proof that a word is wrong.

title: Google Docs word count
steps: To count only one passage, drag over that passage; otherwise leave text unselected.
Choose Tools > Word count from the top menu.
Read Words in the dialog. Click OK to close it and continue writing your own work.
why: Word count can apply to the document or selected text.

title: Google Docs insert a link
steps: Drag over the words that should become a link.
Press Ctrl+K or choose Insert > Link. Paste the approved address into the link field.
Click Apply. Click the linked text to preview the address before opening it.
why: A hyperlink can have a readable label separate from its address.

title: Google Docs insert a table
steps: Click where the table should appear.
Choose Insert > Table. Move your pointer across the grid to choose columns and rows, then click.
A table appears at the cursor. Click individual cells to enter your own information.
why: A table organizes data into rows and columns.

title: Google Docs add a table row
steps: Right-click a cell in the row next to where you need another row.
Choose Insert row above or Insert row below.
Look for an empty new row. Click its cells to enter your own data.
why: A table row is different from a text line.

title: Google Docs table column too narrow
steps: Move the pointer onto the vertical border between the two table columns.
When the resize pointer appears, drag the line slightly to make the narrow column wider.
Check the surrounding columns still fit. Undo if the table goes off the page.
why: Wider columns reduce wrapping but use more page width.

title: Google Docs merge table cells
steps: Drag across the adjacent cells you want to join.
Right-click the selected cells and choose Merge cells.
Check the combined cell and its text. Use Ctrl+Z if the result is not what you expected.
why: Merging changes the table layout.

title: Google Docs image moves text around
steps: Click the picture and look just below it for layout icons.
Choose In line if it should behave like text, or Wrap text if the teacher wants words around it.
Watch where the paragraph moves. If it still overlaps, resize the picture using a corner.
why: Image positioning affects text flow.

title: Google Docs resize an image without stretching
steps: Click the image until a blue selection box appears.
Drag one of the blue corner handles, not the middle of a side.
Release when the image fits. Check faces or circles still have normal proportions; undo if stretched.
why: Corner resizing generally preserves proportions in Docs.

title: Google Docs image crop
steps: Click the picture once and look above the page for Crop image (overlapping right angles).
Click Crop image; drag the dark handles to hide only the unwanted area.
Press Enter to finish. Undo if important content disappears.
why: Cropping hides the unwanted edges instead of stretching the image.

title: Google Docs add alt text to image
steps: Right-click your image and choose Alt text, or open Image options and find Alt text.
Enter a short description of what the image communicates in your own words.
Close the panel and reopen it to confirm your description was saved.
why: Alt text helps people who cannot see the image.

title: Google Docs page margins
steps: Open File > Page setup and select Pages if your teacher requires printed pages.
Enter the assigned top, bottom, left and right margins in the boxes.
Click OK and check the text stays within the page. Ask before changing a shared template.
why: Margins control printable space, not system settings.

title: Google Docs landscape page
steps: Choose File > Page setup in your own document.
In Pages mode choose Landscape under Orientation, then OK.
The page should be wider than tall. If the teacher provided a fixed template, ask before changing it.
why: Orientation changes the document page, not your monitor.

title: Google Docs page numbers missing
steps: Open Insert and look for Page numbers under Page elements or the Page numbers submenu.
Choose the example showing the assigned header or footer position.
Scroll to the next page to verify the number changes. If the option is unavailable, check whether the document uses Pageless mode with your teacher.
why: Page numbers are usually placed in headers or footers.

title: Google Docs header or footer
steps: Double-click near the top or bottom margin of a page in Pages mode.
Type your own assigned header or footer content in the area that opens.
Click in the main text to exit. Check another page to see whether the text repeats.
why: Headers and footers occupy separate areas from body text.

title: Google Docs no page boundaries
steps: Choose File > Page setup and look at the Pages and Pageless tabs.
If your teacher expects individual sheets, choose Pages and click OK; ask first if this is a shared file.
The document should show page boundaries. If not, check View > Show print layout.
why: Pageless layout does not use conventional page breaks.

title: Google Docs blank page at end
steps: Press Ctrl+End inside your own document to move to its end.
Check for extra blank paragraphs after your final text. Delete only those empty lines using Backspace.
If a page break remains, use View > Show non-printing characters to locate it and remove only the unwanted break. Undo if text disappears.
why: Extra paragraphs and breaks can create empty pages.

title: Google Docs print preview
steps: Choose File > Print or press Ctrl+P in the document.
Wait for the print preview. Check the pages, paper size and printer name before doing anything else.
If printing is not approved or the preview is wrong, click Cancel instead of Print.
why: Preview helps avoid wasted paper.

title: Google Docs download as PDF
steps: Open your finished document and check the title.
Choose File > Download > PDF Document (.pdf).
Open Chrome Downloads with Ctrl+J and find the latest PDF. Open it to check every page before attaching.
why: The PDF is a separate exported copy.

title: Google Docs view version history
steps: Open File > Version history > See version history.
A panel on the right lists earlier dates; click one to inspect its contents without restoring it.
Use the back arrow to return to the current version. Ask your teacher before restoring, especially in shared documents.
why: Restoration can replace newer work; viewing history is safer.

title: Google Docs suggestion mode is on
steps: Look at the upper right of the Docs toolbar for the mode menu, often labeled Suggesting or shown with a pencil.
If your teacher permits direct edits, choose Editing.
New typing should appear normally. If Editing is unavailable, request access from the teacher rather than bypassing permissions.
why: Suggesting tracks proposals instead of directly changing content.

title: Google Docs menu or toolbar missing
steps: If the browser tabs are missing, exit browser full screen with F11 on Windows or the Chromebook full-screen key.
If only Docs menus are missing, press Ctrl+Shift+F to toggle compact controls or click the Show menus arrow at the upper right.
The File and Edit menus should return. If you only have view permission, ask your teacher rather than trying to unlock the file.
why: A compact view or limited access can hide editing controls.

title: Google Slides add a new slide
steps: Click the thumbnail on the left that should come before the new slide.
Click the + button at the upper left or press Ctrl+M.
A new numbered thumbnail appears after the selected slide. Choose the Layout menu above the canvas if you need a different layout.
why: Each slide is a separate page in a presentation.

title: Google Slides duplicate a slide
steps: Right-click the thumbnail of your own slide on the left.
Choose Duplicate slide from the menu.
A copy appears immediately below. Edit the copy, not the original, if both must remain.
why: Duplicating preserves the existing arrangement and objects.

title: Google Slides reorder slides
steps: Find the slide thumbnail in the left column.
Drag it between the two thumbnails where it belongs; watch for an insertion line.
Release and check the order using the slide numbers on the left.
why: Reordering thumbnails changes presentation sequence.

title: Google Slides delete an accidental blank slide
steps: Click the unwanted blank slide thumbnail on the left and check it contains no required work.
Right-click the thumbnail and choose Delete.
Check the remaining slides and use Ctrl+Z immediately if you removed the wrong one.
why: Deleting a slide removes all objects on that slide.

title: Google Slides slide layout
steps: Select the slide thumbnail on the left.
Click Layout above the slide or choose Slide > Apply layout.
Pick the layout matching your assignment. Check whether existing text still fits in its boxes.
why: Layouts supply placeholders for titles and content.

title: Google Slides change theme
steps: Open Slide > Change theme, or click Theme above the slide when no object is selected.
Look through the theme choices in the side panel and select the assigned one.
Check several slides for readability. Ask before changing a shared class presentation.
why: Themes may change colors, fonts and placeholders throughout the deck.

title: Google Slides slide background
steps: Click the slide thumbnail whose background needs changing.
Click Background above the slide or choose Slide > Change background.
Select the assigned color or image and click Done. Avoid Apply to theme unless every slide should change.
why: A background differs from a shape placed over a slide.

title: Google Slides page size
steps: Choose File > Page setup in your own presentation.
Open the size dropdown and select the assigned ratio, or Custom for teacher-provided dimensions.
Click Apply and inspect the edges of several slides. A different aspect ratio can change the layout.
why: Page setup changes the dimensions of the entire presentation.

title: Google Slides thumbnail pane missing
steps: Look at the far left edge of the Slides editor for the filmstrip of thumbnails.
Open View and enable Show filmstrip if available, or exit a special view such as Grid view.
Check that numbered thumbnails appear beside the main slide. If the browser is full-screen, Esc or F11 may restore browser controls instead.
why: The slide pane helps navigate and reorder slides.

title: Google Slides speaker notes
steps: Select the slide you want notes for.
Choose View > Show speaker notes if the notes area is hidden.
Click the notes area below the slide and type your own reminders. Drag its top divider upward if needed.
why: Speaker notes are separate from projected slide content.

title: Google Slides skip a slide
steps: Right-click the selected slide thumbnail in the left filmstrip.
Choose Skip slide. A crossed-out eye may appear on that thumbnail.
Present the slideshow to verify it is skipped. Repeat the same menu action to include it again.
why: A skipped slide remains in the file but is omitted from presentation playback.

title: Google Slides text box is cut off
steps: Click the border of the text box, not the words inside.
Drag a blue side or corner handle outward until all text fits, while keeping the box inside the slide.
If it still overflows, select your own text and reduce font size only as allowed. Check the slide in Slideshow mode.
why: Text boxes may extend outside a slide or clip content.

title: Google Slides move a text box
steps: Click the text box border until blue handles appear.
Move the pointer onto the border between handles, then drag the box to its new position.
Release and check that it stays inside the slide. Arrow keys can nudge a selected box.
why: Selecting a box border moves the object instead of editing the text.

title: Google Slides text appears behind a picture
steps: Click the text box border or use Tab to move through objects if it is hidden.
Choose Arrange > Order > Bring to front.
Confirm the words now appear over the picture. Undo if the wrong object moved.
why: Object stacking controls what appears in front.

title: Google Slides insert an image
steps: Select the slide that needs your picture.
Choose Insert > Image and select Upload from computer or Drive for a teacher-approved file.
Pick your file, then drag its corner handles to fit it inside the slide.
why: Inserting a file places a copy as an object on the slide.

title: Google Slides image looks stretched
steps: Select the stretched image and press Ctrl+Z if you just stretched it.
If necessary, use the original approved image again through Insert > Image.
Resize by dragging a corner rather than a side; compare faces and circles with the original.
why: Changing only width or height can distort a picture.

title: Google Slides mask an image into a shape
steps: Select the image on your slide.
Click the small arrow beside Crop image in the toolbar. Choose a shape from the mask menu.
The image should appear within that outline. Double-click it to reposition the crop if needed.
why: A mask changes the visible outline of an image without requiring a new file.

title: Google Slides rotate an object
steps: Select the shape or picture with one click.
Find the round rotation handle above its blue border; drag it to rotate.
For precise rotation, use Arrange > Rotate and choose the assigned option. Confirm the object stays on the slide.
why: Rotation changes object orientation rather than slide orientation.

title: Google Slides insert a shape
steps: Choose Insert > Shape and select a category and shape.
Drag on the slide to draw your shape.
Select the new shape and use the blue handles or toolbar fill control to adjust it yourself.
why: Shapes are editable objects, not imported images.

title: Google Slides shape fill color
steps: Click the shape once so blue handles appear.
Find the Fill color paint-bucket icon above the slide and choose a color.
The inside of the shape should change. If only the outline changes, you used Border color instead.
why: Fill controls the interior of a shape.

title: Google Slides shape border color
steps: Select the shape.
Click Border color (pencil icon) in the top toolbar; choose a swatch. Use Border weight nearby to adjust thickness if needed.
Check the outside edge changes rather than the interior.
why: A border is separate from the shape's fill.

title: Google Slides insert a line or arrow
steps: Choose Insert > Line and select Line or Arrow.
Click and drag from the starting point to the ending point on the slide.
Release, then use Line color or Line weight above the slide to make it visible.
why: Lines connect or emphasize information without being text boxes.

title: Google Slides align several objects
steps: Hold Shift while clicking the objects you want aligned.
Choose Arrange > Align and pick Left, Center, Right, Top, Middle or Bottom as required.
Check that the selected edges or centers line up. Undo if the wrong objects moved.
why: Aligning uses a consistent edge or center rather than eyeballing positions.

title: Google Slides space objects evenly
steps: Select at least three objects by holding Shift and clicking each one.
Choose Arrange > Distribute > Horizontally or Vertically.
Check that the gaps appear even along the intended direction.
why: Distribution spaces selected objects evenly.

title: Google Slides group objects together
steps: Hold Shift and click each object to include in the group.
Choose Arrange > Group (Ctrl+Alt+G).
Click away and select one member; the bounding box should now surround the group. Drag carefully to test.
why: Grouping lets related objects move as a unit.

title: Google Slides cannot edit a grouped object
steps: Double-click within the group to select an individual object if possible.
If that does not work, select the group and choose Arrange > Ungroup.
Click the individual object and edit it. Regroup only the intended objects when finished.
why: An object inside a group may be harder to select independently.

title: Google Slides copy an object to another slide
aliases: slides copy picture to another slide
steps: Select the object on its original slide and press Ctrl+C.
Click the destination slide thumbnail on the left and press Ctrl+V.
Look for the pasted object and move it into position. The original should remain unchanged.
why: Copying an object does not duplicate the entire slide.

title: Google Slides insert a table
steps: Select the slide where the table belongs.
Choose Insert > Table and hover over the grid to choose columns and rows.
Click to insert it, drag its boundary to position it, and enter your own data in its cells.
why: Tables on slides need enough space for projected text.

title: Google Slides link text or object
steps: Select an object by clicking its border, or highlight the words you want linked.
Press Ctrl+K and enter the approved URL or choose a slide in the presentation.
Click Apply. Test the link during presentation when appropriate, without opening unknown sites.
why: Links can point outside the presentation or to another slide.

title: Google Slides add a transition
steps: Click the thumbnail of the slide that needs the transition.
Choose Slide > Transition. In the Motion panel choose a transition under Slide transition.
Preview with Play if offered. Do not select Apply to all slides unless required.
why: Transitions occur between slides, not on individual objects.

title: Google Slides animate an object
steps: Click the object you want to animate.
Choose Insert > Animation (or View > Motion) to open the Motion panel, then add an object animation.
Pick the assigned effect and trigger. Click Play to preview the timing.
why: Animations affect individual objects within a slide.

title: Google Slides animation starts too early
steps: Open View > Motion and find the animation for the affected object in the right panel.
Change its start setting to On click, After previous or With previous as required.
Click Play and watch the order. Reorder the animations if needed using their drag handles.
why: Timing determines when an object animation plays.

title: Google Slides exit slideshow
steps: While the slideshow is active, press Esc once.
If a separate presentation tab remains, return to the original edit tab using its title at the top.
Check that the slide thumbnails and editing tools are visible before changing work.
why: Presentation mode hides editing controls.

title: Google Slides presentation starts on wrong slide
steps: Exit the slideshow with Esc.
Click the numbered thumbnail of the slide you actually want to start on.
Click Slideshow again and check the opening slide. To begin at the first slide, click slide 1 first.
why: Some presentation controls start from the currently selected slide.

title: Google Slides video will not play
steps: In the slideshow, click the approved video and check whether a play triangle or an access error appears.
If there is an error, return to editing with Esc and tell your teacher the source and message. Do not change sharing permissions yourself.
If the video plays but has no sound, check the speaker icon in the player and the device volume.
why: Playback may depend on network access and video permissions.

title: Google Slides audio unavailable
steps: Select the slide containing audio and start Slideshow to test its speaker icon.
Click the speaker or play control if playback is not automatic; check the device volume and approved headphones.
If the audio says access denied or does not appear, ask your teacher to verify the source file's permissions.
why: Embedded audio may depend on a separate Drive file.

title: Google Slides download one slide as PNG
steps: Click the exact slide thumbnail you need to export.
Choose File > Download > PNG image (.png, current slide).
Open Chrome Downloads with Ctrl+J and preview the latest PNG. Check that it shows the intended slide.
why: Image export generally applies to the current slide.

title: Google Slides download as PDF
steps: Check the presentation title and required slides.
Choose File > Download > PDF Document (.pdf).
Find the recent PDF in Downloads and open it to check all pages before submitting.
why: A PDF does not preserve interactive slide animations.

title: Google Slides download PowerPoint copy
steps: Open your presentation and check its title.
Choose File > Download > Microsoft PowerPoint (.pptx). Keep the editable Google file.
Find the downloaded PPTX with Ctrl+J. If your teacher needs a specific format, submit that copy and check compatibility if possible.
why: Conversion can change fonts or effects on some slides.

title: Google Slides image blurry when presented
steps: Press Esc to leave presentation mode and select the blurry image.
Compare it with the original approved file. If it was small and enlarged, use a higher-resolution original if available.
Resize from a corner, run Slideshow again, and check readability at normal viewing size.
why: Stretching a small image cannot create missing detail.

title: Google Slides printing too many pages
steps: Choose File > Print settings and preview if available, or File > Print.
Check the selected page/slide range and number of copies. Use handout layout only if requested.
Cancel if the preview shows extra pages or printing is not authorized; ask before printing again.
why: A handout layout can place several slides on one page.

title: Google Sheets select one cell
steps: Find the column letters along the top and row numbers along the left.
Click their intersection for the cell you need; a blue border surrounds it.
Read its address in the name box to the left of the formula bar, such as B3.
why: A cell is one intersection of a column and row.

title: Google Sheets select a range
steps: Click the first cell of your intended rectangle.
Hold Shift and click the opposite corner, or drag across the rectangle.
The selected cells should be shaded and outlined. Check the range in the name box before formatting.
why: A range contains multiple cells, such as A1:A5.

title: Google Sheets edit a cell without replacing it
steps: Double-click the cell you want to edit, or select it and click the formula bar beside fx.
Place the cursor inside the existing text or formula and edit only the needed characters.
Press Enter and check the result. Press Esc instead if you want to cancel an unfinished edit.
why: Typing immediately into a selected cell may replace its contents.

title: Google Sheets insert a row
steps: Right-click the row number on the far left beside where the new row belongs.
Choose Insert 1 row above or Insert 1 row below.
A blank row appears and the old rows move. Check that related information is still together.
why: Inserting rows shifts existing cells rather than overwriting them.

title: Google Sheets insert a column
steps: Right-click the column letter at the top beside where the new column belongs.
Choose Insert 1 column left or Insert 1 column right.
Check that an empty column appeared at the intended location before entering data.
why: A column groups data vertically.

title: Google Sheets column too narrow
steps: Move the pointer to the line between column letters, such as A and B.
When a horizontal resize arrow appears, drag the boundary to the right; double-click to fit contents if appropriate.
Check the text is visible. For long sentences, Format > Wrapping > Wrap may be better.
why: Changing column width affects every cell in that column.

title: Google Sheets change row height
steps: Move the pointer between two row numbers on the far left.
Drag the boundary downward when the resize cursor appears.
Check that the row has enough height without hiding nearby information.
why: Row height determines the vertical space for a row.

title: Google Sheets wrap long text
steps: Click the cell or drag across the cells containing long text.
Choose Format > Wrapping > Wrap from the top menu.
Rows should grow to show the words. If only a portion is visible, also check the row height.
why: Wrapping displays long content on multiple lines inside a cell.

title: Google Sheets align text inside cells
steps: Select the cells to align.
Click the Horizontal align or Vertical align icon in the toolbar (lines arranged against an edge).
Choose the assigned position and check the content moves inside the cells, not to another cell.
why: Cell formatting changes appearance without changing values.

title: Google Sheets apply cell fill color
steps: Select the cells to color.
Click the Fill color paint bucket in the top toolbar and choose the required color.
Check that cell backgrounds, not letters, changed. Keep the text readable.
why: Fill changes the cell background, not the actual value.

title: Google Sheets add borders to cells
steps: Select the cells requiring borders.
Click the Borders square-grid icon in the top toolbar.
Choose outer, inner or all borders as requested. Look for visible lines around the selected cells.
why: Cell borders differ from default gridlines.

title: Google Sheets numbers display as dates
steps: Select the affected cells and look at their contents in the formula bar.
For future numeric entries, choose Format > Number > Number or Plain text for identifiers, as appropriate.
If Sheets already converted your original data into dates, undo or re-enter from the original source after choosing the right format. Ask if you are unsure.
why: Automatic formatting may interpret some input as a date.

title: Google Sheets leading zero disappears
steps: Select the cells intended to store identifiers such as 007.
Choose Format > Number > Plain text before entering them.
Re-enter the original identifier yourself and check the leading zero remains. Do not use this format for values meant for calculations.
why: Numeric formatting can omit zeros at the beginning of identifiers.

title: Google Sheets percentage formatting
steps: Select the cells containing fractions meant to display as percentages.
Choose Format > Number > Percent or click the % toolbar button.
Check the result against your original data: 0.25 displays as 25%. If 25 becomes 2500%, ask how your data should be entered.
why: Percent formatting displays 0.25 as 25%; it does not independently calculate a ratio.

title: Google Sheets decimal places
steps: Select the numeric cells.
In the toolbar near the % icon, hover over the decimal buttons to find Increase decimal places or Decrease decimal places.
Click until the assigned precision appears. This changes display, not necessarily the underlying value.
why: Display rounding does not normally change the underlying value.

title: Google Sheets currency formatting
steps: Select the numeric cells.
Choose Format > Number > Currency or the currency toolbar icon for the default currency.
Check the currency symbol and decimal places match the assignment. Do not convert currencies unless the lesson asks you to.
why: Currency format changes presentation rather than the amount.

title: Google Sheets freeze header row
steps: In your own sheet, choose View > Freeze from the top menu.
Choose 1 row for a header in row 1, or the assigned number of rows.
Scroll down and check the header stays visible. Use View > Freeze > No rows to undo your own change.
why: Frozen rows stay on-screen while scrolling.

title: Google Sheets find a sheet tab
steps: Look along the bottom edge of the spreadsheet for tabs named after its worksheets.
Use the tab strip arrows or the All sheets list near the bottom left to find the assigned name.
Click that tab and check the correct data appears. Do not try to access a hidden or protected sheet without permission.
why: One spreadsheet file can contain multiple worksheets.

title: Google Sheets rename a sheet tab
steps: Double-click the name of your own sheet tab along the bottom.
Type the requested name and press Enter.
Look at the tab text to verify the new name. Avoid renaming tabs in shared templates without permission.
why: A sheet tab name is separate from the spreadsheet filename.

title: Google Sheets add another sheet
steps: Click the + button at the bottom left beside the sheet tabs.
A new tab appears; double-click its name to give it the assigned title.
Check that you are on the new blank sheet before entering your own data.
why: A new sheet adds another grid to the same file.

title: Google Sheets formula starts with equals
steps: Click the empty result cell where your teacher expects a calculation.
Type = first, then enter your own assigned formula using cell references from the lesson.
Press Enter and check that a result rather than the literal formula appears. Ask your teacher if you need help choosing the operation.
why: The equals sign tells Sheets to interpret an expression as a formula.

title: Google Sheets formula is showing as text
steps: Click the formula cell and look at the formula bar for a leading apostrophe or missing equals sign.
If the cell is intended for a formula, choose Format > Number > Automatic and remove an unintended leading apostrophe.
Re-enter your own formula, press Enter and check that the result appears. If all formulas are visible, check View > Show > Formulas in your own sheet.
why: A text-formatted cell may treat a formula as literal text.

title: Google Sheets formula parse error
steps: Hover over the cell with the error and read its message.
Click the formula bar above the column letters and compare parentheses, separators and cell references with your lesson.
Correct your own typo and press Enter. If the error remains, show the exact message to your teacher rather than guessing.
why: A parse error indicates that the expression cannot be interpreted.

title: Google Sheets REF error
steps: Click the cell showing #REF! and read its error note.
Look in the formula bar for #REF! or a reference to cells that were removed.
If you just deleted a needed cell or column, undo once. Otherwise ask the teacher which reference belongs there; do not invent replacement data.
why: A formula may refer to cells that no longer exist.

title: Google Sheets DIV zero error
steps: Select the cell showing #DIV/0! and inspect the formula next to fx.
Find the divisor referenced after the division sign or used by the calculation. Check whether that input is blank or zero.
Correct an actual data-entry error only. If zero is valid or data is missing, ask the teacher how to handle it.
why: Division by zero is undefined; do not change real data just to hide an error.

title: Google Sheets VALUE error
steps: Hover over the #VALUE! cell to read the explanation.
Click the formula and follow its referenced cells; look for words, spaces or other text where a number was expected.
Correct only a real input mistake using the original data. Ask about valid text values rather than deleting them.
why: Some formulas require particular kinds of data.

title: Google Sheets NAME error
steps: Click the #NAME? cell and examine the formula bar.
Compare the function name or named range with the example in your lesson; look for misspelled names or missing quotes.
Fix your own typo and press Enter. Ask the teacher if the correct function is unknown.
why: An unrecognized name may indicate a misspelled function or reference.

title: Google Sheets circular dependency warning
steps: Select the cell showing the circular dependency error.
Read the formula bar and see whether the result cell is included among the cells it calculates from.
Ask the teacher which input range should exclude the result. Do not enable iterative calculation or change spreadsheet settings.
why: A circular dependency can make a result depend on itself.

title: Google Sheets copy a formula down
steps: Click the cell containing your own completed formula.
Drag the small blue square at its bottom-right corner down the intended rows.
Click one copied result and read its formula bar to verify row references changed as expected. Undo if it filled too far.
why: Relative references usually shift when a formula is filled.

title: Google Sheets absolute cell reference
steps: Click your practice formula and look at the references in the formula bar.
When the lesson calls for a reference to remain fixed, a dollar sign before a column or row keeps that part fixed, for example $B$2.
Copy your own practice formula and inspect the copied formula to see which reference stayed fixed.
why: Fixed references help preserve a constant cell location during copying.

title: Google Sheets formula range includes wrong cells
steps: Click the result cell and double-click its formula or click the formula bar.
Compare the colored outlines around referenced cells with the actual data range assigned by your teacher.
Correct the range in your own formula, press Enter and verify the displayed result against the lesson.
why: A formula can be valid but refer to the wrong cells.

title: Google Sheets sort a table without mixing rows
steps: In your own table, drag across every column that belongs to the records, including headings if present.
Choose Data > Sort range > Advanced range sorting options. Mark Data has header row if appropriate; choose the intended column and order.
Click Sort and check that each row's related information stayed together. Undo immediately if it did not; ask before sorting shared data.
why: Sorting just one column can separate related information.

title: Google Sheets filter hides rows
steps: Look for filter icons in the header and gaps in row numbers.
On your own sheet, click the filter icon in the affected column and inspect selected values or conditions.
Restore the intended filter or choose Data > Remove filter if appropriate. On a shared sheet, ask the teacher before changing the view.
why: Filtered rows are hidden from the view, not necessarily deleted.

title: Google Sheets create a chart
steps: Select your own data including the column labels.
Choose Insert > Chart. In the Chart editor on the right, use Setup > Chart type to choose the assigned chart.
Check that labels and values match your table. Drag the chart away from cells you still need to edit.
why: Charts visualize selected data; a wrong range can produce misleading results.

title: Google Sheets chart has wrong labels
steps: Double-click the chart to open the editor on the right.
Under Setup, inspect Data range, X-axis and Series; check whether the first row is being used as headings.
Compare with the assigned table and correct the source selection. Do not change the original data just to fix labels.
why: Chart labels depend on the range and setup choices.

title: Google Sheets change chart title
steps: Double-click your chart and select Customize in the Chart editor.
Expand Chart & axis titles and choose Chart title in the dropdown.
Type your own descriptive title in Title text and check it appears above the chart.
why: A clear chart title identifies what the data represents.

title: Google Sheets print one selected range
steps: Drag across the exact cells to print.
Choose File > Print, then choose Selected cells in the Print dropdown at upper right.
Inspect the preview; proceed only if your teacher authorizes printing. Otherwise cancel.
why: Printing only the chosen range avoids unnecessary pages.

title: Google Sheets download CSV
steps: Click the worksheet tab you need along the bottom.
Choose File > Download > Comma-separated values (.csv, current sheet).
Locate the new file in Chrome Downloads (Ctrl+J). Keep the original spreadsheet; CSV does not preserve sheets, formatting or formulas as editable formulas.
why: CSV stores plain table data from a sheet, not its charts or formatting.

title: Google Sheets download Excel copy
steps: Open the assigned spreadsheet and verify its title.
Choose File > Download > Microsoft Excel (.xlsx).
Find the new file in Downloads. Keep the original Google Sheet and check the exported file with an approved app if required.
why: Export conversion may affect certain formulas or formatting.

title: Google Forms required question missing
steps: Scroll through the current form section and look for a red asterisk beside an unanswered question.
Enter your own response in each required field; read any red error text below it.
Click Next or Submit at the bottom. If it still stops, show the teacher the message next to the field.
why: A required question must have a valid response before submission.

title: Google Forms answer has invalid format
steps: Find the question with red text below the response box.
Read the stated rule; it may require a specific number format or school-approved email format.
Correct your own entry to match that rule. If your correct answer is rejected, contact the teacher; do not invent data.
why: Forms can enforce response formatting rules.

title: Google Forms cannot go to next section
steps: At the bottom of the current section, click Next once.
If the screen stays put, scroll up and find the question highlighted in red or missing a required response.
Complete your own response and click Next. If there is no visible error, ask the teacher to inspect the form.
why: Multi-section forms may require valid answers before advancing.

title: Google Forms checkbox versus radio button
steps: Look beside the answer choices: circles usually indicate one choice; squares allow multiple choices.
Read the question's directions before selecting your own answer or answers.
Check marks appear in selected squares; only one circle can be filled per single-choice group.
why: Different question controls have different selection behavior.

title: Google Forms file upload question
steps: Find the file-upload question and read its accepted types and size limit.
Click Add file, then choose your approved file using the picker or upload tab. Click Upload or Select as shown.
Wait until the filename appears under the question before submitting. If the file is rejected, show your teacher the reason rather than changing its extension.
why: File upload availability depends on form and school account permissions.

title: Google Forms says school account required
steps: Look near the top of the form for the signed-in account or an access message.
If the wrong account is shown, ask your teacher to help open the form under your assigned school profile.
If your school account is correct but access is denied, ask the form owner to grant access. Do not try another student's account.
why: School forms may restrict access to an organization.

title: Google Forms not accepting responses
steps: Read the message on the form page that says responses are no longer accepted.
Compare the link with the latest assignment link in Classroom.
Tell the teacher which form is closed. Only the form owner can reopen it.
why: Only the form owner decides whether responses are accepted.

title: Google Forms already responded
steps: Read the notice saying you already responded.
Look for an Edit your response link if the teacher permits corrections.
If no link appears, ask the teacher to confirm the submission. Do not submit through another account.
why: Some forms accept only one response per person.

title: Google Forms unsure whether submission worked
steps: After pressing Submit, look for a new confirmation page with the form title and a recorded-response message.
If you are still seeing questions, look for a red error or a required field instead.
If neither a confirmation nor a clear error appears, ask the teacher to verify before sending another response.
why: A confirmation usually indicates a response was received.

title: Google Forms edit submitted response
steps: Open the Edit your response link from the confirmation page or authorized email, if provided.
Change only your own intended answer and click Submit at the bottom again.
Look for a confirmation. If no edit link was provided, request permission from your teacher.
why: Response editing depends on the form owner's settings.

title: Google Forms quiz score not shown
steps: On the confirmation page, look for View score if the teacher enabled immediate results.
Click it only if offered. Read any displayed feedback.
If no score appears, wait for the teacher to release results; do not try to access hidden answers.
why: Quiz results may be released later by the teacher.

title: Google Forms form resets after closing
steps: Reopen the form through the original Classroom assignment link using your assigned school profile.
Check whether earlier responses or a saved-draft indicator appear. Do not clear the browser or change accounts.
If the draft is missing, tell your teacher before re-entering answers, especially during a quiz.
why: Draft saving may depend on form settings and account access.

title: Google Meet microphone muted
steps: Move the pointer over the Meet window to reveal the controls at the bottom.
With permission, click the microphone icon once if it has a slash. Keep it muted when your teacher requests it.
Watch for the slash to disappear and ask whether you can be heard. If it stays muted or blocked, ask staff.
why: A muted microphone does not send your audio.

title: Google Meet camera covered
steps: Look above the laptop screen for the camera lens and any physical privacy shutter.
If the teacher requests video, open the shutter gently and click the camera button at the bottom of Meet if crossed out.
Look for your video tile. If it remains black or access is blocked, ask your teacher; do not alter security settings.
why: A camera cover physically blocks the image.

title: Google Meet captions
steps: Move the pointer over the Meet window and locate the CC button in the bottom controls.
Click it to show captions; in some layouts look under the three-dot More options menu for Captions.
Check that words appear during speech. Leave required accessibility features enabled.
why: Live captions may contain errors and are not a perfect transcript.

title: Google Meet cannot join meeting
steps: Click the meeting link from your teacher's Classroom post.
Check the preview screen and use Join now or Ask to join as shown, following your teacher's microphone and camera rules.
If you see a waiting or access-denied message, tell the teacher; do not create a replacement meeting or use another account.
why: Meeting access is controlled by the host and school policy.

title: Google Meet echo
steps: Click the microphone icon at the bottom of Meet to mute yourself when not speaking.
Use approved headphones at a comfortable volume if permitted.
Ask the teacher whether the echo stops. If it continues, staff can identify which device is causing it; do not adjust someone else's equipment.
why: Microphones can pick up sound from nearby speakers.

title: Google Meet share a school assignment
steps: Open only the approved assignment tab or window and close or hide private material.
When the teacher asks you to present, click Present now in the bottom Meet toolbar and select A tab or A window. Select the exact assignment and click Share.
Check the shared preview, then click Stop presenting when finished. Avoid sharing your entire screen.
why: Sharing a whole screen can expose unrelated tabs or notices.

title: Google Drawings add a shape
steps: Open your own Google Drawing and locate the Shape icon in the toolbar above the canvas.
Open it, select a category and shape, then drag on the canvas.
A shape with blue handles appears. Resize using those handles and choose a fill color from the toolbar.
why: Drawing shapes remain editable objects.

title: Google Drawings object hidden behind another
steps: Click the partly visible object or use Tab to cycle among drawing objects.
Choose Arrange > Order > Bring forward or Bring to front as needed.
Check that your intended object appears above the other one. Undo if the wrong object moved.
why: Objects can overlap in front-to-back order.

title: Google Drawings export image
steps: Open your completed Google Drawing and inspect the canvas.
Choose File > Download > PNG image (.png), or the format specified by your teacher.
Open Chrome Downloads with Ctrl+J and preview the exported file. Keep the editable Drawing in Drive.
why: Downloading creates a separate copy in the chosen format.

title: Google Drawings insert a text box
steps: Choose Insert > Text box or click the T-in-a-box toolbar icon.
Drag a rectangle on your drawing and type your own text.
Select the text and use font-size and color controls; resize the box until the words are readable.
why: A text box can be positioned independently of shapes.

title: Options bar missing
steps: Click Window at the top and make sure Options has a checkmark.
Select a tool such as Brush (B). Look directly beneath File/Edit menus for its settings, including brush size and opacity.
If the whole interface is hidden, press Tab outside text editing to restore it.
why: The Options bar shows controls for the active tool.

title: Toolbar missing
steps: At the very top of Photoshop, click Window > Workspace. If Essentials is not selected, choose Essentials (sometimes called Essentials (Default)).
Open Window > Workspace again and choose Reset Essentials. Some versions show Reset > Essentials (Default). This restores the usual tool and panel layout.
Look down the left side for the tall toolbar with the Move, Brush and other tools. If it is still hidden, choose Window > Tools.
If the entire interface is hidden, finish typing in any text box and press Tab once. If the toolbar is still missing, ask your teacher.
why: Reset Essentials restores the normal Photoshop panel layout without deleting artwork. It can change custom panel arrangements.

title: All panels disappeared
aliases: photoshop everything on the sides disappeared
steps: Finish typing or any active text edit, then press Tab once. Tab can hide or show the toolbar and other panels.
If the panels remain missing, click Window > Workspace > Essentials (Default), then Window > Workspace > Reset Essentials (or Reset > Essentials (Default) in some versions).
Check that the toolbar returns on the left and Layers and Properties appear on the right. To restore only one missing panel, open Window and click that panel name.
If the screen still looks wrong, show the problem to your teacher without changing any computer settings.
why: Adobe workspaces control where Photoshop tools and panels appear. Resetting a workspace does not delete the open project.

title: Find a hidden tool
steps: Look at the left toolbar; many icons have a small triangle at their lower-right corner.
Click and hold a related icon, such as the Lasso, to show a flyout list of tools.
Click the desired tool name. If it is absent, look under the three-dot toolbar button or ask your teacher rather than modifying the toolbar.
why: Several tools share the same toolbar slot.

title: Switch between open images
steps: Look above the artwork for tabs with filenames, next to the Options bar.
Click the tab containing your project name. If tabs are hidden, press F to return to standard screen mode.
Check the name before editing; a star by a tab usually indicates unsaved changes.
why: Each open document has its own layers and history.

title: Return to normal screen mode
steps: Click the top checkmark to finish text or a transform if one is active.
Press F (outside typing) until you see the normal menu bar and document tabs.
If a dialog covers the artwork, finish or cancel that dialog first instead of repeatedly pressing F.
why: Photoshop cycles through screen modes.

title: Zoom to fit entire image
steps: Click View > Fit on Screen or press Ctrl+0.
The entire canvas should fit between the toolbar and panels.
If the artwork is still cut off, check whether the canvas itself is cropped rather than just zoomed.
why: Fitting the view changes magnification, not image size.

title: View actual pixels
steps: Click View > 100% or press Ctrl+1.
Inspect a detail at actual pixel size; scroll or hold Space and drag to inspect another area.
Press Ctrl+0 to fit the whole picture again.
why: At 100%, zoom is useful for checking image quality.

title: Move around zoomed canvas
steps: With no text box active, hold Space; the cursor becomes a hand.
While holding Space, drag the canvas to see a different area. Release Space to return to your tool.
Press Ctrl+0 if you lose track of the image. This changes your view, not the image position.
why: Panning moves the view, not your artwork.

title: Navigator panel
steps: Click Window > Navigator.
In the small preview panel, drag the colored rectangle to a different part of the picture.
Use the slider below the preview to change magnification, then check the main canvas.
why: The Navigator shows the location of your current view.

title: History panel
steps: Click Window > History.
Find the most recent operation at the bottom of the list. Click an earlier state only if you intend to undo later edits.
Check the canvas before making any new edit, because editing after going back can discard later history.
why: History tracks recent changes in this open document.

title: Undo recent edit
steps: Click Edit > Undo or press Ctrl+Z once.
Look at the exact part of the image that changed. Repeat only if you need to undo more.
If you went too far, use Edit > Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z).
why: Undo reverses recent editing actions.

title: Redo an undone edit
steps: Click Edit > Redo or press Ctrl+Shift+Z.
Inspect whether the intended edit returned. Repeat only as necessary.
If Redo is unavailable, the history may have changed after a new edit; ask before attempting recovery.
why: Redo restores an action you just undid when available.

title: Rulers not visible
steps: Click View > Rulers or press Ctrl+R.
Look for numbered strips along the top and left edges of the document.
If you need a guide, drag from a ruler onto the canvas; do not remove guides required for the assignment.
why: Rulers display document measurements.

title: Show or hide guides
steps: Click View > Show > Guides; a checkmark indicates they are visible.
Look for thin guide lines across the document. They do not appear in a normal exported image.
Toggle the same menu item if necessary; do not clear the teacher-required guides.
why: Guides are alignment references, not printed artwork.

title: Show grid in Photoshop
steps: Click View > Show > Grid.
Look for a regular grid across the canvas. It is a view aid, not pixels in the image.
Use the same menu to hide it only if the project does not require a grid screenshot.
why: The grid assists precise placement without becoming artwork.

title: Photoshop canvas rotated
steps: Hold the Hand tool on the left toolbar and choose Rotate View Tool.
Click Reset View in the Options bar at the top.
The canvas should return upright without rotating the actual image. If the exported image is sideways, ask about image rotation instead.
why: Rotate View changes the viewing angle rather than the image pixels.

title: Photoshop cursor is a crosshair
steps: With the Brush selected, press Caps Lock once outside text editing.
Move the cursor over the image; it should show a brush-size outline instead of a precise crosshair.
If it stays a crosshair, increase brush size with ] and test again; ask before changing preferences.
why: Caps Lock can toggle precise cursors.

title: Photoshop frozen
steps: Stop clicking and wait for the current operation to finish. Look for a progress bar or busy cursor.
If Photoshop responds, press Ctrl+S and wait for saving to complete.
If it remains frozen, tell the teacher which file and operation were open. Do not force-close or restart without approval.
why: Repeated input can queue more work and unsaved edits may be lost.

title: Photoshop scratch disk full
steps: Read the scratch disk warning and stop repeating the operation.
If the document responds, press Ctrl+S to save the PSD in its approved folder.
Tell your teacher the exact warning. Do not delete system files, clear disk contents or change scratch disk preferences.
why: Scratch disk problems need authorized storage support.

title: Create a new blank layer
steps: Open Window > Layers. Click the + or new-layer icon at the bottom of the panel.
A new transparent thumbnail (checkerboard) appears above the selected layer. Double-click its name and name it.
Make sure the new row is highlighted before painting.
why: Separate layers keep edits independent.

title: Name a layer
steps: In Window > Layers, double-click the words beside the thumbnail, not the thumbnail itself.
Type a descriptive name and press Enter.
Verify the row shows the new name and the artwork has not changed.
why: Clear names help you locate artwork later.

title: Duplicate a layer
steps: In Window > Layers click the row you want to copy.
Press Ctrl+J with no active selection if you want the entire layer copied.
Look for a new row above the original. Rename it and toggle its eye to check that the original remains.
why: A copy lets you experiment without changing the original.

title: Move layer above another
steps: In Window > Layers locate the two named rows.
Drag the row by its name, not its thumbnail, until a horizontal insertion line appears above the other row. Release.
Look at the canvas: higher opaque layers cover lower ones. Undo if it lands inside a group unintentionally.
why: Layer stacking controls which pixels cover others.

title: Hide a layer temporarily
steps: Open Window > Layers and locate the row for the image.
Click its eye icon at the far left; that layer should disappear from the canvas.
Click the same empty square again to restore the layer. This is not deletion.
why: Visibility changes do not erase layer contents.

title: Layer is locked
steps: Open Window > Layers and look for the padlock at the right of the selected row.
If the lock is on your ordinary editable layer, use the appropriate lock control near the top of Layers only if allowed. For original Background, duplicate with Ctrl+J instead.
Work on the copy and keep the original. Ask if the layer is intentionally protected.
why: Locks protect layer content or position.

title: Layer opacity too low
steps: Select the image row in Window > Layers.
Find Opacity near the upper-right of that panel; click its value and enter the intended percentage.
At 100% the layer is fully opaque where it has pixels. If still faint, check its mask and blend mode.
why: Layer opacity controls the visibility of the whole layer.

title: Layer fill versus opacity
steps: Select a layer that has an fx effect in Window > Layers.
Find Opacity and Fill near the top of Layers. Opacity fades both content and styles; Fill can fade content while leaving many styles visible.
Test on a duplicate layer, then undo the test and retain your required appearance.
why: Fill can reduce layer pixels while leaving many styles visible; Opacity affects the whole layer.

title: Group several layers
steps: In Layers, Ctrl-click separate rows or Shift-click a range to select the intended layers.
Press Ctrl+G. A folder row should appear containing them.
Double-click the folder name to rename it; click its arrow to verify the contents.
why: Groups organize related objects without merging them.

title: Find layers inside a group
