steps: Open Window > Layers and find the folder row for the group.
Click the small disclosure arrow at its left to expand the group.
Click a specific layer inside the folder, not the folder itself, to edit that layer.
why: Collapsed groups hide rows, not the artwork itself.

title: Select multiple layers
steps: Click the first intended layer row in Layers.
Hold Ctrl and click other separate rows; hold Shift and click the last row for a continuous range.
Check that only the intended rows are highlighted. Click one row to return to single-layer editing.
why: Multiple selected layers may move together.

title: Align several layers
steps: Select the intended layers in Layers using Ctrl-click.
Press V and look across the Options bar for alignment icons; hover to read labels such as Align horizontal centers.
Click the intended alignment once and inspect the result. If it moves the wrong items, undo and check the selected rows.
why: Alignment uses the selected layers as references.

title: Auto-select moves wrong layer
steps: Select the intended layer directly in Window > Layers.
Press V; at the left of the Options bar uncheck Auto-Select if enabled.
Drag a short distance; the selected layer should move instead of the object under the pointer. Undo if needed.
why: Auto-Select can choose the top object under your pointer.

title: Delete an unwanted layer safely
steps: Click the eye of the suspected unwanted layer in Layers to confirm what disappears.
If uncertain, keep it hidden rather than deleting it. If certain, select its row and click the trash icon at bottom right of Layers.
Verify the correct content disappeared; Ctrl+Z immediately if you deleted the wrong layer.
why: Confirming visibility helps avoid deleting the wrong work.

title: Layer thumbnail versus mask thumbnail
steps: Open Window > Layers and locate a row with two thumbnails: image on the left, mask on the right.
Click each thumbnail and watch the thin border around the active one. The mask is usually black and white.
Select the image for color edits; select the mask for hiding and revealing. Test on a spare layer if unsure.
why: The image and mask are separate editable targets.

title: Convert a layer to Smart Object
steps: Select the intended layer in Window > Layers.
Right-click its name and choose Convert to Smart Object.
A small Smart Object badge appears on the thumbnail. This preserves source content for transforms but changes how direct painting works.
why: Smart Objects can preserve source data during many transformations.

title: Smart Object cannot be directly edited
steps: Look for the small Smart Object badge on the selected layer thumbnail.
For painting, create a blank layer above it with the + icon, or add a layer mask to hide areas.
Do not rasterize the original without teacher approval. If editing the embedded content is intended, double-click the Smart Object thumbnail.
why: A Smart Object protects its source pixels from direct edits.

title: Edit embedded Smart Object contents
steps: In Layers double-click the Smart Object image thumbnail, not its name.
An embedded document opens in a separate tab. Edit only the intended content and press Ctrl+S there.
Return to the main document tab and check the updated object. Save the main PSD too.
why: Saving embedded source changes updates the parent composition.

title: Clipping mask not working
steps: In Layers place the layer to be clipped directly above the layer that defines its visible shape.
Select the upper row and click Layer > Create Clipping Mask (Alt+Ctrl+G).
Look for an indented row with a downward arrow. If nothing appears, check the base layer has visible pixels and is not hidden.
why: The upper layer is limited to the visible shape of the base layer.

title: Release a clipping mask
steps: Click the indented clipped layer in Layers.
Choose Layer > Release Clipping Mask, or Alt+Ctrl+G.
The indentation disappears and the layer can show beyond the base shape. Undo if the clipping was required.
why: Releasing a clipping mask reveals previously clipped pixels.

title: Merge layers versus keep editable
steps: Open Layers and identify the rows you want to organize.
Use Ctrl+G to group them rather than merge them if you need to edit each independently.
Keep the layered PSD. A PNG/JPG export makes a separate flattened image without destroying the PSD.
why: Merging reduces separate editing options.

title: Select Subject
steps: Select the image layer in Window > Layers.
Click Select > Subject from the top menu and wait for the dashed outline to appear.
Inspect the outline; use Quick Selection to add or subtract missed areas before making a mask.
why: Automatic selection can miss fine details and needs review.

title: Object Selection tool
steps: Hold the selection-tool group on the left toolbar; choose Object Selection Tool (W group).
Select the image layer and choose Rectangle or Lasso mode at the top if available. Drag around the object.
Wait for the dashed outline. If it selects the wrong object, use Quick Selection or Select > Subject instead.
why: Object Selection targets an individual object within an image.

title: Quick Selection tool
steps: Hold the W-group icon on the toolbar and choose Quick Selection Tool.
Choose the image layer, then drag short strokes over the object. Use + or − selection icons in the top bar to add or subtract.
Check the dashed boundary and decrease brush size near edges using [.
why: Quick Selection expands using nearby color and edge information.

title: Magic Wand tool
steps: Hold the W-group tool icon and choose Magic Wand Tool.
Select the image layer, then click a color region. Look at Tolerance and Contiguous in the top bar.
The dashed lines show selected pixels. Undo and adjust Tolerance if too much or too little is selected.
why: The Magic Wand selects pixels with related colors.

title: Magic Wand selects too much
steps: With Magic Wand selected, press Ctrl+Z to undo the excessive selection.
In the top Options bar lower Tolerance (for example from 32 to 15) and check Contiguous if you want only touching pixels.
Click the region again and inspect its dashed outline; adjust gradually.
why: Lower tolerance limits the range of similar colors.

title: Magic Wand selects disconnected areas
steps: Select Magic Wand from the W-group flyout on the left.
At the top check Contiguous so matching colors must touch the clicked region.
Click the intended area again. If the boundary is still wrong, lower Tolerance or use Quick Selection.
why: Contiguous limits selection to connected regions.

title: Rectangular Marquee
steps: Hold the dashed rectangle icon on the left and choose Rectangular Marquee Tool (M).
Drag diagonally from one corner of the intended region to the opposite corner.
Look for a rectangular dashed outline. Ctrl+D removes it when finished.
why: Marquee tools create geometric selections.

title: Elliptical Marquee
steps: Hold the Marquee icon on the left and choose Elliptical Marquee Tool.
Drag across the area; hold Shift while dragging if you need a circle.
Inspect the oval dashed outline before applying any edit.
why: The Elliptical Marquee selects rounded areas.

title: Lasso tool
steps: Select Lasso Tool (L) from the left toolbar.
Hold the mouse button and trace around a region, returning near the start before releasing.
A dashed outline appears. Undo or use add/subtract controls if the outline is inaccurate.
why: The Lasso lets you define an irregular selection by hand.

title: Polygonal Lasso
steps: Hold the Lasso tool and choose Polygonal Lasso Tool.
Click at each corner of a straight-edged object, then click the starting point to close the outline.
Check the dashed polygon; press Esc to cancel an unfinished outline if needed.
why: Straight segments are useful for angular subjects.

title: Magnetic Lasso
steps: Hold the Lasso tool and choose Magnetic Lasso Tool.
Click near an object's contrasting edge, move along it slowly and click to place extra points when necessary.
Close at the starting point and inspect the selection. Use regular Lasso if the edge has weak contrast.
why: Magnetic Lasso follows strong edges but may miss weak contrast.

title: Add to a selection
steps: Choose the same selection tool you used originally.
In its top Options bar click Add to selection (overlapping squares with a plus-style icon), or hold Shift while starting another selection.
Draw over the missing region and check that the dashed boundary expands rather than replaces the original.
why: Adding preserves the original area while including more pixels.

title: Subtract from a selection
steps: Choose the selection tool and select Subtract from selection in the top bar (or hold Alt while starting the next selection).
Draw over the unwanted part of the current selection.
Inspect the dashed boundary to verify that the extra area has been removed.
why: Subtracting excludes pixels without starting over.

title: Invert a selection
steps: With an active dashed selection, click Select > Inverse (Ctrl+Shift+I).
Check that the formerly unselected region is now selected; the canvas edge may also show dashed lines.
Invert again if you need the original region. Do not delete pixels merely to test the selection.
why: Inverse selects everything that was outside the original selection.

title: Feather a selection
steps: With a selection active click Select > Modify > Feather.
Enter a small radius in pixels and click OK. A larger radius produces a softer transition.
Apply a mask on a copy and inspect the edge; undo if important detail disappears.
why: Feathering softens the transition at a selection boundary.

title: Expand a selection
steps: With a selection active click Select > Modify > Expand.
Enter a small pixel amount and click OK.
Zoom in on the outline; it should extend outward. Undo if it includes unwanted nearby pixels.
why: Expanding grows the selection outward.

title: Contract a selection
steps: With a selection active click Select > Modify > Contract.
Enter a small number of pixels and confirm.
Zoom in to check the outline moved inward. Undo if narrow details disappear.
why: Contracting moves the selection boundary inward.

title: Save a selection for later
steps: With the intended dashed selection active click Select > Save Selection.
Give the new channel a recognizable name and click OK.
To restore it later, click Select > Load Selection and choose that named channel.
why: Stored selections can be reused in the same document.

title: Select and Mask workspace
steps: Select the image layer and make a rough selection with Quick Selection or Select > Subject.
Click Select > Select and Mask, or the Select and Mask button at the top when a selection tool is active.
Use View Mode and edge tools to inspect the cutout. Expand Output Settings and choose Layer Mask when ready, then OK.
why: This workspace refines the edges of a selection or mask.

alternatives.label: Output Select and Mask to a layer mask

title: Select and Mask preview background
steps: Inside Select and Mask, find View Mode near the top of the right Properties panel.
Open the View list and choose On Black, On White or Onion Skin to inspect edges.
Change the preview opacity if available. This changes the preview, not the exported background.
why: Different preview backgrounds reveal different edge problems.

title: Refine hair or fur edges
aliases: hair looks bad after cutting out
steps: Make a rough subject selection and open Select > Select and Mask.
Choose Refine Edge Brush from the left toolbar inside the workspace. Paint short strokes across wispy hair or fur edges, not the whole person.
Switch between On Black and On White previews; output to Layer Mask once the edge looks natural.
why: Fine edge detail often needs separate refinement.

title: Smooth jagged selection
steps: Open Select > Select and Mask with your rough selection active.
Find Global Refinements in the right Properties panel and increase Smooth slightly.
Inspect curved edges at higher zoom; too much Smooth loses corners and hair. Reduce it if details vanish.
why: Smoothing reduces irregular bumps in a selection boundary.

title: Shift Edge to reduce fringe
steps: In Select and Mask choose On Black or On White preview to make the unwanted fringe easy to see.
Under Global Refinements on the right move Shift Edge slightly negative to bring the boundary inward.
Inspect hair and narrow details before outputting a Layer Mask. Undo or reduce the adjustment if too much is removed.
why: Moving the edge inward can reduce unwanted background fringe.

title: Output Select and Mask to a layer mask
steps: Inside Select and Mask scroll the right Properties panel to Output Settings.
Expand it and set Output To to Layer Mask (or New Layer with Layer Mask if you need a separate copy).
Click OK. In Layers look for a black-and-white thumbnail beside the picture; the original pixels should be preserved.
why: A mask preserves hidden source pixels for later correction.

title: Quick Mask red overlay
steps: If a red overlay suddenly covers part of the image, look for Quick Mask mode at the bottom of the toolbar.
Press Q once outside text editing to return to standard selection mode.
The overlay should become a dashed selection. If red remains, check whether you are viewing a layer mask overlay instead.
why: Quick Mask often displays selected or masked areas as an overlay.

title: Selection outline hidden
steps: If edits seem limited but the dashed outline is missing, click View > Show > Selection Edges if available.
Ctrl+H toggles Extras, including selection edges. Check whether the outline returns.
Use Select > Deselect (Ctrl+D) only if you no longer need the selection.
why: A hidden outline does not necessarily mean the selection is gone.

title: Black white gray mask meanings
steps: Select a layer with a mask in Window > Layers, then click its mask thumbnail.
Black hides the layer, white reveals it and gray gives partial visibility. Press B and D for a small test on a duplicate.
Press X to switch black and white. Undo the test or paint white to restore an area.
why: A grayscale mask controls visibility without changing source pixels.

title: Restore a masked-out area
steps: Open Layers and click the black-and-white mask thumbnail beside the image.
Press B, then D and use X if necessary so the front toolbar swatch is white. Set Brush Opacity to 100% for a test.
Paint over a missing area to reveal it. If nothing returns, confirm the mask thumbnail has the active border.
why: White on a layer mask reveals underlying layer content.

title: Hide extra background with a mask
steps: Select the picture row in Layers and click the mask thumbnail; add one using the rectangle-with-circle icon if needed.
Press B, choose black foreground color (D then X if needed), and paint over extra background.
Zoom in around edges with Ctrl+plus. Switch to white to restore accidental removals; keep the original pixels.
why: Black on the mask hides extra pixels without deleting them.

title: Invert a layer mask
steps: Click the mask thumbnail in Layers, not the image thumbnail.
Press Ctrl+I to invert the black and white mask values.
Check that hidden and visible regions swap. If you inverted the image colors instead, undo and select the mask thumbnail.
why: Inverting a mask swaps its black and white values.

title: Temporarily disable a layer mask
steps: Find the mask thumbnail in Layers.
Hold Shift and click that thumbnail. A red X appears and the unmasked image becomes visible.
Shift-click again to remove the red X and restore the mask before exporting.
why: Disabling the mask is a reversible comparison.

title: View only the layer mask
steps: Hold Alt and click the mask thumbnail in Layers.
The canvas displays the black, white and gray mask instead of the photo.
Alt-click the mask again to return to the normal composition.
why: The mask-only view makes visibility mistakes easier to find.

title: Mask edge too sharp
steps: Click the mask thumbnail and open Window > Properties.
Increase Feather slightly in the mask Properties panel while watching the edge.
If the cutout becomes blurry or transparent at edges, reduce Feather; keep details visible.
why: Mask feathering softens the transition without erasing pixels.

title: Mask too transparent
steps: Click the mask thumbnail and open Window > Properties.
Check Density; set it to 100% if you want black mask areas fully hidden.
Also check layer Opacity in Layers. If the brush created gray areas, paint black or white at 100% on the mask as appropriate.
why: Density controls the strength of a mask.

title: Move image without moving mask
steps: Find the chain symbol between image and mask thumbnails in Layers.
Click the chain to unlink, then select the image thumbnail and press V to move the image alone.
Test a small move, then click between thumbnails to relink if you want them to move together again.
why: Unlinking allows independent movement of the image and its mask.

title: Remove mask without deleting pixels
steps: Right-click the mask thumbnail in Layers.
Choose Delete Layer Mask only if you truly want to remove it without applying it to pixels. If prompted, choose Delete rather than Apply.
The original image should reappear. A safer reversible option is Shift-clicking to disable it temporarily.
why: Deleting a mask can restore hidden content; applying it removes masked pixels.

title: Place a photo into a project
steps: Open the destination PSD, then click File > Place Embedded.
Choose your approved image in the file dialog and click Place.
Drag the transform handles to position it, then press Enter or click the top checkmark. Find its new Smart Object row in Layers.
why: Placed images commonly remain editable Smart Objects.

title: Combine photos into one composition
steps: Open your panorama or background PSD. Click File > Place Embedded and choose the first approved subject image.
Use Select > Subject or Quick Selection, then add a layer mask with the rectangle-with-circle icon in Layers.
Press V to position the cutout and repeat for other photos. Keep each as a separate named layer above the background.
why: Separate layers make compositing revisions easier.

alternatives.label: Place a photo into a project

title: Resize a placed object proportionally
steps: Select the placed picture row in Layers and press Ctrl+T.
Drag a corner handle; watch width and height stay proportional (check the link icon in the top bar if needed). Do not drag a side to stretch it.
Click the top checkmark or Enter to finish. Undo if the subject looks unnaturally stretched.
why: Maintaining proportions prevents unintended stretching.

title: Rotate a single object
steps: Select the intended layer and press Ctrl+T.
Move the pointer just outside a corner until a curved rotation cursor appears. Drag to rotate.
Press Enter when the angle looks right. This should turn only the selected layer, not the entire canvas.
why: Free Transform applies to selected layers, not the whole image.

title: Flip one layer horizontally
steps: Select the intended image layer in Layers.
Click Edit > Transform > Flip Horizontal.
Inspect that the subject faces the opposite direction while other layers stay unchanged. Undo if the wrong layer flipped.
why: This mirrors the selected layer rather than the entire canvas.

title: Flip one layer vertically
steps: Select the intended layer in Layers.
Click Edit > Transform > Flip Vertical.
Check that only that layer is upside down. Undo if you wanted a horizontal mirror instead.
why: Vertical flipping reverses the layer top to bottom.

title: Distort a layer for perspective
steps: Select a copy or Smart Object of the intended layer.
Click Edit > Transform > Distort; drag individual corner handles to match the perspective.
Press Enter to confirm and inspect the edges. Undo if the picture becomes unnaturally stretched.
why: Distort adjusts corners independently for perspective matching.

title: Warp a placed object
steps: Select the intended layer and choose Edit > Transform > Warp.
Drag the visible grid or control points gradually to bend the content.
Press Enter to confirm. Use a duplicate or Smart Object and undo if the bend becomes excessive.
why: Warp bends a layer without moving every point equally.

title: Object partly outside canvas
steps: Press Ctrl+0 to see the entire canvas and select the object row in Layers.
Press V to move it inward or Ctrl+T to scale it with corner handles.
Confirm the whole object fits inside the canvas; areas beyond its boundary will not appear in the normal export.
why: Pixels beyond the canvas are not visible in the final export.

title: Blend a layer with its background
steps: Select the subject layer and inspect its edges at Ctrl+1.
Click its mask thumbnail and refine visible halos with a soft black or white brush. Use a clipped adjustment layer for matching color and brightness.
At Ctrl+0 compare the subject with the background; keep edges and lighting consistent instead of lowering opacity indiscriminately.
why: Blend modes change how upper and lower colors interact.

title: Add a soft contact shadow
steps: In Layers select the background or row just below the subject and click + to create a shadow layer.
Press B and choose a soft round dark brush from the top brush picker; paint a small shadow directly under the feet or contact point.
Lower the shadow layer's Opacity near the top of Layers until it looks natural. Keep the shadow beneath the subject.
why: Contact shadows help show where an object meets a surface.

title: Match direction of light
steps: At Ctrl+0 look for shadows already visible in the background. Identify which direction they extend.
Create a separate shadow layer below the subject, press B and paint a soft shadow extending consistently with those background shadows.
Lower layer Opacity and compare the whole composition. If the source lighting conflicts strongly, choose a better source image.
why: Consistent light direction helps a composite look believable.

title: Match subject brightness to background
steps: Select your subject row in Layers, click the half-black half-white adjustment icon and choose Brightness/Contrast.
Right-click the adjustment row and choose Create Clipping Mask so the change affects only the subject.
Move Brightness and Contrast in Properties while comparing with the background. Toggle its eye to compare before and after.
why: A clipped adjustment changes the subject independently.

title: Match sharpness of subject and background
steps: At Ctrl+1 compare the subject's edges and detail with the nearby background.
If the subject is much sharper, select a copy or Smart Object and choose Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur with a small radius.
Check at Ctrl+0 and undo if overly soft. A blurry low-resolution source may need replacement instead.
why: Matching focus helps elements feel like they belong in the same scene.

title: Add a Hue/Saturation adjustment
steps: In Layers click the half-black half-white circle at the bottom and choose Hue/Saturation.
Open Window > Properties if the sliders are not visible. Move Hue to change color and Saturation to control intensity.
Toggle the adjustment layer eye to compare; clip it or edit its mask if only one object should change.
why: Adjustment layers remain editable.

title: Hue change affects entire image
steps: Find the Hue/Saturation adjustment row in Layers above your image.
Right-click it and choose Create Clipping Mask if only the layer below should change; an indentation appears.
For only part of that layer, click the adjustment mask and paint black over areas that should keep their original colors.
why: Masks and clipping control the area affected by an adjustment.

title: Colorize a selected area
steps: Select the object or part using Quick Selection (W group).
Click the adjustment icon at bottom of Layers and choose Hue/Saturation. In Properties enable Colorize if appropriate.
Adjust Hue, Saturation and Lightness; refine the automatically created selection mask to avoid recoloring nearby areas.
why: The selected area becomes the adjustment mask.

title: Brightness and Contrast
steps: Click the half-black half-white circle at bottom of Layers and choose Brightness/Contrast.
In Window > Properties move Brightness or Contrast slightly while watching the image.
Toggle the adjustment eye to compare. Clip to the layer below if you only intend to change one picture.
why: Adjustments can improve visibility without replacing the source pixels.

title: Levels adjustment
steps: Click the adjustment icon at bottom of Layers and select Levels.
In Properties find the histogram and its black, gray and white input sliders. Move the middle gray slider slightly to adjust midtones.
Watch shadows and highlights; avoid pushing the end sliders so far that detail disappears. Toggle the eye to compare.
why: Levels adjusts the range and midpoint of image tones.

title: Curves adjustment
steps: Click the adjustment icon at bottom of Layers and choose Curves.
In Properties click near the center of the diagonal line and move the point slightly upward to brighten or downward to darken midtones.
Compare with the eye toggle; avoid extreme bends that eliminate detail.
why: Curves provides precise control of brightness across tonal ranges.

title: Photo looks too saturated
steps: Open Layers and click the adjustment icon to add Hue/Saturation.
In Properties reduce the Saturation slider slowly while checking the picture.
If only one object is too bright, clip the adjustment to that layer or mask other areas.
why: Excess saturation can hide natural color differences.

title: Use Vibrance
steps: Click the adjustment icon at bottom of Layers and choose Vibrance.
In Properties adjust Vibrance gently; it generally affects less saturated colors more strongly than Saturation.
Toggle the layer eye to compare and keep skin or other important colors natural.
why: Vibrance generally changes less-saturated colors more strongly.

title: Make a reversible black and white image
steps: Click the half-black half-white adjustment icon at bottom of Layers and choose Black & White.
The image becomes grayscale while the original color layer stays intact.
Toggle the adjustment eye off to restore color. Save as PSD to keep it editable.
why: An adjustment retains the original color data.

title: Unexpected black and white image
steps: Open Layers and look for a visible Black & White or Hue/Saturation adjustment above your photo.
Toggle its eye temporarily to see whether color returns. Also check whether you are viewing only a mask (Alt-click its thumbnail again).
If the document itself is grayscale, check Image > Mode without changing it and ask your teacher before conversion.
why: Several different conditions can cause a grayscale appearance.

title: Color Balance adjustment
steps: Click the adjustment icon at bottom of Layers and select Color Balance.
In Properties choose Midtones, Shadows or Highlights and move a color slider slightly.
Compare by toggling the adjustment eye; clip to a subject layer if the background should not change.
why: Color Balance shifts the relationship between color channels.

title: Clip adjustment to one layer
steps: Place the adjustment directly above the layer you intend to affect.
Right-click the adjustment row in Layers and choose Create Clipping Mask.
Look for an indented arrow pointing toward the layer below; the other layers should remain unchanged.
why: A clipped adjustment is restricted to its base layer.

title: Edit existing adjustment later
steps: Open Window > Layers and locate the adjustment row with its adjustment icon and mask.
Double-click the adjustment icon (not the mask) to open its controls in Properties.
Change a slider and toggle the eye to compare. Save your PSD to retain editability.
why: Adjustment layer settings can be revised after creation.

title: Fill with a solid color layer
steps: Click the half-black half-white circle at the bottom of Layers and choose Solid Color.
Pick the required color in the dialog and click OK.
Drag the fill layer below your artwork if it is a background, then confirm the artwork remains visible.
why: A fill layer stays editable after the color is chosen.

title: Gradient fill layer
steps: Click Layer > New Fill Layer > Gradient and confirm the new layer dialog.
In Gradient Fill choose a preset or click the gradient preview to edit colors, then choose style and angle.
Click OK, position the layer in Layers and inspect the composition.
why: Gradient fill layers retain editable gradient settings.

title: Brush size too large or small
steps: Press B, then [ to shrink the brush or ] to enlarge it.
Look for the circular brush outline on the canvas, or click the brush preview near the left of the top Options bar to enter Size.
Test on a new blank layer and undo the test when finished.
why: Brush diameter determines the area covered per stroke.

title: Brush edge too hard
steps: Press B and click the brush preview dropdown near the top-left of the Options bar.
Find Hardness; lower it for a softer edge or raise it for a crisp outline.
Make a short test stroke on a blank layer and compare, then undo the test.
why: Hardness controls the transition around the brush edge.

title: Brush strokes are faint
steps: Press B and look at Opacity and Flow in the top Options bar; set both to 100% for a test.
Check the selected layer's Opacity near the top of Layers and whether the mask thumbnail is active.
Create a new blank layer, choose a contrasting color and test a stroke. Undo it and adjust the original layer only as intended.
why: Both brush and layer controls affect visible paint strength.

title: Brush paints the wrong color
steps: Look at the front overlapping color square near the bottom of the left toolbar.
Click it, choose the intended color and click OK. Press B and test on a spare layer.
If only black and white are available, check whether the mask thumbnail is active; click the image thumbnail for color painting.
why: Masks accept grayscale rather than ordinary color painting.

title: Swap foreground and background colors
steps: Look at the two overlapping color squares near the bottom of the toolbar.
Press X outside text editing to swap the front (foreground) and back (background) colors.
Check which square is in front before making a brush stroke.
why: Swapping is useful when alternating black and white mask strokes.

title: Reset foreground and background colors
steps: Press D outside text editing to reset the foreground and background swatches.
Look near the bottom of the toolbar for the black and white squares; press X if you need them reversed.
On a mask, verify which is foreground before painting to hide or reveal.
why: Default colors are useful for mask editing and basic brush tests.

title: Eyedropper picks color
steps: Press I or select Eyedropper from the left toolbar.
Click a visible color in the artwork; the front color square near the bottom of the toolbar should change.
Press B to use the sampled color. If the sampled color is wrong, inspect the Sample settings in the top bar.
why: The Eyedropper samples color from the image.

title: Paint only inside selection
steps: Make a selection with an appropriate tool and check its moving dashed boundary.
Open Layers and click + to create a blank layer. Press B and paint inside the selected area.
The stroke should stop at the boundary. Press Ctrl+D after finishing and inspect the result.
why: Active selections restrict many painting operations.

title: Paint Bucket fills too much
steps: Press Ctrl+Z to undo the unwanted fill. Hold the Gradient tool group on the left and choose Paint Bucket.
At the top lower Tolerance and enable Contiguous to restrict matching connected pixels.
Click again on a copy or blank layer with appropriate sampling. If it still spreads too far, make a selection first.
why: The Paint Bucket fills related pixels according to its options.

title: Create a rectangle shape
steps: Hold the shape-tool group near the bottom of the left toolbar and choose Rectangle Tool (U group).
At the top set mode to Shape, choose Fill and Stroke colors, then drag across the canvas.
Look for a new shape layer in Layers; use V to reposition it.
why: Shape layers retain editable vector properties.

title: Shape has no fill
steps: Select the shape layer in Layers and choose its shape tool (U group).
Click Fill in the top Options bar or Properties. Choose a solid color rather than the None swatch (diagonal slash).
The shape interior should become visible. Check layer opacity if it remains faint.
why: Fill controls the interior; Stroke controls the boundary.

title: Change shape outline
steps: Select the shape row in Layers and activate its shape tool.
At the top click Stroke, select a color and set the stroke width in pixels.
Inspect the outline at Ctrl+0; if it is invisible, make sure Stroke is not None and width is above zero.
why: A shape stroke is independently editable from its fill.

title: Rounded rectangle corners
steps: Select your rectangle shape layer and open Window > Properties.
Find corner radius controls under shape properties; enter a small radius or drag a corner widget if shown.
Check the corners become rounded; use a smaller radius if the shape changes too much.
why: Corner settings preserve editable shape geometry.

title: Spot Healing Brush
steps: In Layers click + to create a blank retouch layer above the photo.
Hold the healing-tool group (J) and choose Spot Healing Brush. Enable Sample All Layers at the top and choose a brush slightly bigger than the spot.
Click a small dust mark and toggle the retouch layer eye to compare. Use small strokes; undo errors.
why: Spot Healing blends a small region with neighboring image detail.

title: Healing Brush with sample
steps: Create a blank retouch layer above the photo with + in Layers.
Hold the J-tool group and choose Healing Brush. Set Sample to Current & Below or All Layers at the top; Alt-click a clean nearby area.
Release Alt and paint a short stroke over the small mark. Resample if the texture looks wrong.
why: Healing combines sampled texture with surrounding tones.

title: Clone Stamp tool
steps: Create a new blank layer above the photo and press S for Clone Stamp.
In the top bar set Sample to Current & Below or All Layers. Hold Alt and click a clean source point, then release Alt.
Paint a short stroke over the target. Resample nearby points frequently and toggle the new layer's eye to inspect.
why: Clone Stamp copies source pixels directly.

title: Clone Stamp does nothing
steps: Press S and select a visible editable blank layer above the photo.
At the top set Sample to Current & Below or All Layers; check Opacity is above zero. Alt-click a visible source on the photo.
Release Alt and paint a short test stroke. If none appears, check selection edges, layer visibility and whether a mask is selected.
why: Cloning needs both a source and an editable destination.

title: Remove small dust spots safely
steps: Open Layers and create a blank layer above the original image.
Choose Spot Healing Brush from the J group, enable Sample All Layers and use a brush slightly larger than the dust spot.
Click each spot individually and compare by toggling the retouch layer eye. Keep the original beneath it.
why: Small localized edits preserve more original texture.

title: Retouch repeats obvious pattern
steps: Press Ctrl+1 to inspect the retouch area. Toggle the retouch layer eye to identify repeating copied texture.
Undo recent bad strokes or mask the retouch layer; choose Clone Stamp or Healing Brush and Alt-click a different nearby source.
Use short varied strokes and compare at Ctrl+0 for a natural result.
why: Reusing the same source can create obvious repetitions.

title: Blur a small region
steps: Duplicate the photo row with Ctrl+J (no selection active). Hold the droplet tool group and choose Blur Tool.
At the top set low Strength and a small soft brush. Paint lightly on the duplicate where blur is needed.
Toggle the duplicate eye to see the difference and undo if the edge is too soft.
why: Selective blurring reduces detail in a localized area.

title: Sharpen a small region
steps: Duplicate the image layer with Ctrl+J. Hold the Blur tool group and select Sharpen Tool.
Set a low Strength at the top and use small strokes on the intended region.
Inspect at Ctrl+1 for bright halos or noise; undo if they appear.
why: Sharpening increases local contrast but cannot restore missing detail.

title: Non-destructive Gaussian Blur
steps: Select a copy or Smart Object layer in Layers.
Click Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur, and move the Radius slider slightly with Preview enabled.
Click OK only when the effect looks right. On a Smart Object it appears as an editable Smart Filter.
why: A Smart Filter can be changed later when applied to a Smart Object.

title: Add your own text
steps: Press T or choose Horizontal Type Tool from the left toolbar.
Click once where your title should start. Type your own words and use the top font, size and color controls.
Click the checkmark at the top to finish. A T thumbnail should appear in Layers.
why: Editable type lives on a separate text layer.

title: Edit an existing text layer
steps: Find the T-thumbnail layer in Layers and select it.
Press T and click directly inside the existing letters, then select and edit your own text.
Click the top checkmark to commit. If a new text layer appears instead, undo and click inside the original text.
why: Editing existing type avoids creating an accidental new text layer.

title: Change text font
steps: Select the T layer in Layers and press T; highlight only the characters if changing part of the text.
Click the font-name box in the top Options bar, or Window > Character, and choose an installed font.
Click the top checkmark and inspect readability at fit view. Do not install fonts on school computers.
why: Font changes affect the shape of characters.

title: Change text size
steps: Select the T layer and press T; highlight the characters if only some need changing.
Click the font Size value in the top Options bar or Window > Character. Enter the intended point size.
Click the top checkmark and inspect whether the title fits the canvas.
why: Font size changes type without requiring rasterization.

title: Change text color
steps: Select the T layer and press T. Highlight specific characters if necessary.
Click the text color swatch in the top Options bar and choose a contrasting color, then OK.
Click the top checkmark and inspect the title against the actual background.
why: Color contrast helps readers see your text against the image.

title: Text is hidden behind another layer
aliases: my text is behind the photo
steps: Open Layers and find the T-thumbnail row. Turn on its eye if needed.
Drag the text row above the image covering it; watch for the horizontal insertion line before releasing.
If still missing, check Opacity and mask visibility. Undo if the text was intentionally behind another object.
why: Layer order can cover otherwise valid text.

title: Text box cuts off words
steps: Select the T layer and press T, then click inside its paragraph text.
Look for the text box border and handles. Drag the bottom or side handle to make more room without scaling the letters.
Click the checkmark and verify all your words are visible; if needed reduce font size slightly.
why: Paragraph type wraps within its text frame.

title: Change paragraph alignment
steps: Select the T layer and open Window > Paragraph.
With Type active, click the left, center or right alignment icon (horizontal lines) in Paragraph or the top bar.
Check the position of the words and adjust the text box if needed, then commit with the checkmark.
why: Alignment positions text relative to its text origin or frame.

title: Change spacing between letters
steps: Select the text with T and open Window > Character.
Find Tracking (VA with a horizontal arrow) to adjust spacing across selected letters. For one pair, put the cursor between them and use Kerning.
Adjust in small amounts and inspect the title at normal zoom, then click the top checkmark.
why: Tracking adjusts spacing across selected characters.

title: Change space between lines
steps: Select the multiline text with T and open Window > Character.
Find Leading (stacked A letters with vertical arrow); increase the point value if lines overlap, or choose Auto.
Inspect the space between lines and click the top checkmark.
why: Leading controls baseline-to-baseline line spacing.

title: Text layer will not accept brush
steps: Find the T thumbnail of the text layer in Layers. Type layers cannot be painted directly without conversion.
Click + at the bottom of Layers to create a blank layer above it; press B to paint there.
Keep the original text editable with T. If you need to hide part of it, use a layer mask rather than rasterizing it.
why: Type layers are not ordinary painted pixel layers.

title: Add a drop shadow to text
steps: Select the T-thumbnail row in Window > Layers.
Click fx at the bottom and choose Drop Shadow. In the dialog adjust Opacity, Distance and Size while Preview is checked.
Click OK when the title is readable. Expand Effects and double-click Drop Shadow to adjust later.
why: A layer style adds an editable effect behind the type.

title: Edit an existing text stroke
steps: Open Layers and expand the small arrow beside the text layer's fx symbol.
Double-click the Stroke entry under Effects. In Layer Style change Size, Position or Color.
Click OK and inspect the title at Ctrl+0; preserve a visible outline if required.
why: Stroke is an editable style, not part of the typed words.

title: Layer style is not visible
steps: Open Layers and expand the arrow next to the layer's fx symbol.
Look for eyes beside Effects and the named effect; turn them on if hidden. Double-click the effect to inspect its settings.
Make sure size and opacity are not zero and layer visibility is on. Click OK and compare.
why: Styles can exist but be hidden or too subtle to notice.

title: Create a document at required size
steps: Click File > New. In the right preset details enter Width, Height and their units exactly as the assignment specifies.
Check orientation, resolution if required and Background Contents (for example White). Click Create.
Look at the new document tab and save as PSD before building the project.
why: Document dimensions set the available image area.

title: Image Size versus Canvas Size
steps: Open your PSD and save a separate copy before changing dimensions.
Click Image > Image Size if you need to scale the picture pixels; choose Image > Canvas Size if you need more or less space around existing pixels.
Read units and preview carefully; canvas reduction can crop edges. Cancel if unsure.
why: Image Size and Canvas Size affect different aspects of the document.

title: Crop a photo without deleting pixels
steps: Press C for Crop and drag the corner handles around the area you want to keep.
In the top Options bar uncheck Delete Cropped Pixels if available so the hidden area is preserved.
Click the top checkmark. Save as PSD; reopen Crop if you need to adjust the boundary later.
why: Preserving cropped pixels can allow later reframing.

title: PNG exports with transparent background
aliases: png background needs to be white
steps: Look at the canvas for gray-and-white checkerboard, which means transparency. Open Window > Layers.

Click the half-black half-white circle at the bottom, choose Solid Color and pick the required background (often white). Drag the fill below the artwork and any visible opaque background layers as appropriate.
Confirm no checkerboard remains where the assignment requires color, save PSD and export PNG. Open the export to check it.
why: A checkerboard represents transparent pixels; an opaque background removes them.

alternatives.label: Fill with a solid color layer

title: Export transparent PNG
steps: Open Layers and hide any background layer you do not want by clicking its eye. Confirm checkerboard around the object.
Click File > Export > Export As; set Format to PNG and enable Transparency if shown.
Click Export and choose the assigned folder. Reopen the PNG in Photoshop to verify transparent areas appear as checkerboard.
why: PNG supports transparency; JPG does not.

title: JPG has no transparency
steps: JPG cannot store transparent pixels. If transparent background is required, choose PNG instead.
If JPG is required, add a Solid Color fill layer below the artwork using the adjustment icon at bottom of Layers.
Click File > Export > Export As and choose JPG. Open the file to verify the background color.
why: JPEG does not store an alpha transparency channel.

title: Exported image is too small
steps: Open the original PSD and click File > Export > Export As.
In the right panel check Image Size width, height and Scale against the assignment; normally use 100% unless another size is required.
Export with a distinct filename. In File Explorer right-click the export > Properties > Details to check its dimensions.
why: Export can resize output independently of the editable document.

title: Exported image missing layers
steps: Open the original PSD and press Ctrl+0. In Layers check the eye of each required image or text layer.
Check the visible composition and canvas edges before clicking File > Export > Export As.
Export the correct format again and open the new file to confirm all required visible layers appeared.
why: Exports include the visible composition, not hidden layers.

title: Find where Photoshop saved a file
steps: Click File > Save As to see the proposed location and name; cancel without overwriting anything. For exports remember the folder selected in the Export dialog.
Press Windows+E and use the left navigation to open Downloads, Documents or the class folder you selected.
Sort by Date modified and verify filename/extension. If you saved to cloud documents, use Photoshop Home > Your files instead.
why: Editable and exported files may be saved in different folders.

title: Save a second version safely
steps: Press Ctrl+S to preserve the current PSD, then click File > Save As.
Choose the approved folder and enter a different filename such as project-v2.psd. Keep Photoshop format.
Click Save and verify the new name in the document tab; the earlier version should remain in its original folder.
why: Versioned PSDs protect earlier work.

title: Submit PSD and exported image
steps: Press Ctrl+S to save the editable PSD, then File > Export > Export As to create the required PNG or JPG in your class folder.
In Google Classroom open your class > Classwork > assignment title > View assignment if shown. Find Your work, click Add or create > File and select the required files from their saved folder.
Check that both filenames appear under Your work. Click Turn in and confirm; if a file is too large or Turn in is absent, ask your teacher.
why: The editable project and final image are different deliverables.

alternatives.label: Export a Photoshop PNG or JPG
Find where Photoshop saved a file

title: File too large to submit
steps: Keep the original layered PSD unchanged. In File Explorer right-click the file and choose Properties to read its size.
Compare with the teacher's instructions. If a smaller image is allowed, use File > Export > Export As and adjust the copy's size or JPG quality as appropriate.
Do not flatten or delete layers in the original to meet a size limit. Ask the teacher about an approved Drive submission if the PSD is required.
why: Reducing the original file may remove useful editing information.

title: Photoshop warns about saving format
steps: Read the warning in the save dialog; JPG and PNG cannot preserve editable Photoshop layers.
Cancel if needed, then choose File > Save As and Photoshop (PSD) to preserve your project.
Use File > Export > Export As for a separate PNG or JPG. Check both filenames before submitting.
why: Not all file types preserve editable layers.

title: Missing Properties panel
steps: Click Window on the top menu and choose Properties.
Look at the right side for the Properties panel or its icon. Click a shape with V to reveal its controls.
If nothing is selected, the panel shows document controls instead of object controls.
why: Properties changes with the selected object.

title: Missing Align panel
steps: Click Window > Align.
Look for icons resembling lined-up rectangles. Press V and Shift-click your shapes.
Choose Align To: Selection or Artboard as appropriate before clicking an alignment icon.
why: The available alignment controls depend on the selection.

title: Missing Pathfinder panel
steps: Click Window > Pathfinder.
Look for the Shape Modes row of four icons. Press V and Shift-click overlapping vector shapes.
Hover to find Unite, Minus Front, Intersect or Exclude; don't click until you know which result you need.
why: Pathfinder acts on selected vector artwork.

title: Missing Character panel
steps: Click Window > Type > Character.
Look for font family, size and spacing fields. Select the text object with V or highlight letters with T.
The fields should show the selected text's formatting.
why: Character controls apply to letters rather than the whole artboard.

title: Missing Stroke panel
steps: Click Window > Stroke.
Select a path with V and look for Weight near the top of Stroke.
If Cap or Corner controls are missing, open the panel menu and choose Show Options.
why: Stroke options control the edge of a path.

title: Missing Swatches panel
steps: Click Window > Swatches.
Select your shape with V; click the solid Fill or hollow Stroke square near the bottom of the toolbar.
Click a color tile in Swatches and check that the correct part changes.
why: Swatches apply to the active paint attribute.

title: Missing Gradient panel
steps: Click Window > Gradient.
Select a shape with V and bring Fill to the front using the solid color square.
The Gradient panel shows a color ramp; click it to apply a gradient if your shape has none.
why: The panel edits gradient colors and stops.

title: Canvas suddenly fills screen
steps: Press Esc to exit presentation or an active tool.
If the menu bar is still hidden, press F once at a time outside text editing.
Stop when the normal menu bar and window return.
why: Screen modes can hide the interface without losing artwork.

title: All panels vanished
steps: Press Esc to leave a text field or path, then press Tab once to show panels hidden by the Tab shortcut.
If they stay hidden, choose Window > Workspace > Essentials, then open Window > Workspace again and choose Reset Essentials (or the reset option for the selected workspace).
Look for the toolbar on the left and panels on the right. If one panel is still missing, use Window to open that panel.
If the workspace still looks different, ask your teacher. Do not reset the computer or the artwork.
why: Tab temporarily hides or shows many panels.

title: Only side panels vanished
steps: Press Esc so no text field is active, then press Shift+Tab once. The right-side panels may reappear.
If Layers or Properties is missing, open it from the Window menu.
If many panels remain missing, use Window > Workspace > Essentials, then Window > Workspace > Reset Essentials (or the reset option for your selected workspace).
why: Shift + Tab toggles panels other than the toolbar and control panel.

title: Zoom out to see all artboards
steps: Click View > Fit All in Window at the top.
All artboards should shrink into view together.
Click the board you need and use Ctrl+0 to fit that board later.
why: Fitting all artboards changes the view, not the design.

title: Fit one artboard in the window
steps: Click the intended artboard with V without moving artwork.
Press Ctrl+0 (zero), or choose View > Fit Artboard in Window.
The active white board should fill most of the workspace.
why: Fitting a board does not resize its contents.

title: Pan around artwork
steps: Press Esc if you are typing. Hold the spacebar; the cursor should become a hand.
Keep holding Space and drag the canvas to the desired area.
Release the mouse and Space; the artwork itself should not move.
why: Panning moves the view only.

title: View actual size
steps: Click View > Actual Size, or press Ctrl+1 outside text editing.
Look for about 100% in the zoom display at the bottom of the window.
Use Ctrl+0 to fit the board again if only part is visible.
why: Zoom changes only the on-screen view.

title: Perspective grid will not go away
steps: Click View > Perspective Grid > Hide Grid.
The colored perspective lines and plane selector should disappear.
Press V to return to editing. If a regular square grid remains, use View > Hide Grid instead.
why: The perspective grid is a view aid, not exported artwork.

title: Artboard edges disappeared
steps: Open View and look for Show Artboards; choose it if available.
The white board boundaries should appear again.
Press Ctrl+0 to fit the active board. If the artwork has no color, check Preview mode instead.
why: Artboard visibility affects the view only.

title: Everything else is dimmed
steps: Look just above the artwork for a breadcrumb bar naming a group or layer.
Press Esc once or click the left-pointing arrow in that bar until it disappears.
Other artwork should return to normal brightness.
why: Isolation mode limits editing to one group or object.

title: Bounding box not visible
steps: Press V and click your object.
Click View > Show Bounding Box if that command appears.
Look for a rectangle with small handles around the object; drag a corner only if you intend resizing.
why: The bounding box provides scale and rotation handles.

title: Anchor points not visible
steps: Open View > Show Edges if that command appears.
Press A for the white Direct Selection arrow and click the path edge.
Small square anchor points should appear; click one to select it.
why: Hidden edges can conceal selection points without changing paths.

title: Toolbar only has a few tools
steps: Look at the bottom of the left toolbar for the three-dot Edit Toolbar button, or hold a related tool icon.
For a fuller toolbar, click Window > Toolbars > Advanced if your teacher permits the workspace change.
Look again for the missing icon; no software installation is needed.
why: Many Illustrator tools share a toolbar slot.

title: Draw exact size rectangle
steps: Press M for Rectangle. Click once, without dragging, on the artboard.
In the Rectangle dialog, enter Width and Height with the units from your assignment.
Click OK; use Window > Transform with the shape selected to confirm its dimensions.
why: Clicking instead of dragging allows precise dimensions.

title: Draw an exact circle
steps: Press L for Ellipse.
Hold Shift while dragging diagonally on the artboard; release the mouse before Shift.
Select with V and compare W and H in Properties; they should match.
why: A modifier constrains the shape to equal width and height.

title: Round rectangle corners
steps: Press A and click the rectangle path.
Look just inside each corner for a small circular corner widget.
Drag a widget inward or enter a radius in the available Corners field. Stop when the rounding looks right.
why: Live corner controls round the existing vector geometry.

title: Make a polygon
steps: Hold the Rectangle tool in the left toolbar and choose Polygon (show Advanced toolbar if necessary).
Click once on the board. Enter Radius and Sides in the dialog.
Click OK and count the edges before styling the shape.
why: The side count determines the regular polygon geometry.

title: Make a star
steps: Hold the Rectangle tool and choose Star from the flyout.
Click once on the artboard. Set Radius 1, Radius 2 and Points in the dialog.
Click OK; inspect the point count and undo if you need a different shape.
why: The inner and outer radii determine how pointed a star looks.

title: Draw a straight line
steps: Find Line Segment in the left toolbar (backslash shortcut on standard Windows keyboards).
Drag from the starting point to the end. Hold Shift for a horizontal, vertical or 45-degree line.
Click the hollow Stroke square and choose a visible color and weight; a line with no stroke may be invisible.
why: An open line needs a stroke to be seen clearly.

title: Draw a grid of rectangles
steps: Hold Line Segment in the Advanced toolbar and choose Rectangular Grid.
Click once on the artboard. Set Width, Height, Horizontal Dividers and Vertical Dividers. Four dividers make five spaces in that direction.
Click OK, select with V and give the grid a visible Stroke. Use no Fill if the squares must remain empty.
If this is a project planning grid, keep it visible in your screenshots as directed. A real drawn grid is different from View > Show Grid.
why: Grid dividers produce multiple cells inside the selected area.

alternatives.label: Need a screenshot with the grid

title: Draw concentric circles
steps: Hold Line Segment and choose Polar Grid in the Advanced toolbar.
Click once on the board; set Width and Height and the concentric/radial divider counts. Set radial dividers to zero for rings only.
Click OK and set a visible Stroke; check the rings and spokes.
why: The polar grid makes rings and radial dividers.

title: Resize without stretching
steps: Press V and click the object. Look for a bounding-box corner handle.
Hold Shift while dragging a corner handle; release the mouse first.
Check the proportions. If handles are missing, choose View > Show Bounding Box.
why: Constrained scaling preserves the aspect ratio.

title: Resize precisely with Transform
steps: Press V, select your object and choose Window > Transform.
Find W and H; click the chain-link control to preserve proportions if required.
Enter the requested size and unit in W or H and press Enter. Check both values.
why: Transform values let you set measured dimensions.

title: Rotate to a specific angle
steps: Select the object using V, then click Object > Transform > Rotate.
Enter the angle in the dialog and check Preview.
Click OK if correct, or Copy if a second rotated object is needed.
why: A numeric rotation avoids imprecise dragging.

title: Flip an object horizontally
steps: Select with V and choose Object > Transform > Reflect.
Choose Vertical axis, which mirrors left to right, and check Preview.
Click OK or Copy. Verify that left and right exchanged places.
why: Reflection mirrors across the chosen axis.

title: Flip an object vertically
steps: Select with V and choose Object > Transform > Reflect.
Choose Horizontal axis, which mirrors top to bottom, and check Preview.
Click OK or Copy and verify the direction.
why: The axis is the mirror line, not the direction of movement.

title: Duplicate with Alt drag
steps: Press V and select an object you own.
Hold Alt and drag the object away from its starting position; release the mouse before Alt.
Look for two separate objects. Ctrl+Z reverses an unwanted copy.
why: Alt-drag duplicates instead of moving the original.

title: Repeat the last transform
steps: Select a shape and make a measured move or rotation using Object > Transform.
If you made a copy, keep the new copy selected and press Ctrl+D (Object > Transform > Transform Again).
Check that each repeated copy has the same offset or angle.
why: Illustrator remembers the most recent transform operation.

title: Move by an exact amount
steps: Select with V and choose Object > Transform > Move.
Enter Horizontal and Vertical distances. Check Preview to see the direction before committing.
Click OK to move or Copy to duplicate, then check the position.
why: Precise moves help keep layouts consistent.

title: Paste in front
steps: Select an object with V and press Ctrl+C.
Click Edit > Paste in Front (Ctrl+F). The duplicate sits directly over the original.
Move the selected copy slightly if needed to see both, or inspect Layers.
why: The copy starts at the same position, so it can look like nothing changed.

title: Paste behind
steps: Select the object with V and press Ctrl+C.
Click Edit > Paste in Back (Ctrl+B). The new copy is directly behind the source.
Inspect the expanded Layers panel to confirm the second object instead of assuming nothing happened.
why: Stack order determines what is visible.

title: Scale stroke separately from shape
steps: Select your stroked artwork with V and choose Object > Transform > Scale.
Enter the required percentage; locate Scale Strokes & Effects and check it to scale the outline too, or uncheck to preserve its weight.
Enable Preview and click OK only after comparing the stroke thickness.
why: Scaling geometry and scaling stroke weights are separate choices.

title: Object moves too far with arrow keys
steps: Choose V and select the object. Open Window > Transform.
Find X and Y and enter the exact target coordinate with units; press Enter.
Check the position. Do not change keyboard increment preferences on the school computer.
why: Document coordinates permit exact adjustments without system changes.

title: Black arrow versus white arrow
steps: Press V for the black arrow and click a shape: a box around the whole shape means whole-object selection.
Press A for the white arrow and click its edge: small square anchors appear.
Use V for moving the entire shape and A for changing only a selected point or segment.
why: The two tools select different levels of vector geometry.

title: Draw angular path with Pen
steps: Press P for Pen. Click once on the artboard for the first corner.
Click each next corner without dragging. Click the first anchor when a small circle appears by the Pen cursor to close the shape.
For an open path press Esc instead. Set a visible stroke if needed.
why: Individual clicks create corner anchors.

title: Draw curves with Pen
steps: Press P and click-drag the first point to create direction handles.
Click-drag another point and watch the curve form between anchors; the handle angle changes its direction.
Press Esc for an open path, then A to fine-tune the handles without adding more points.
why: Handles control the direction and curvature of adjoining segments.

title: Curvature tool basics
steps: Find Curvature in the left toolbar (use Advanced toolbar if hidden).
Click successive points along the curve; double-click when you want a sharp corner.
Press Esc to finish an open curve or click its starting point to close it. Inspect with V.
why: The tool calculates smooth curves between points.

title: Stop drawing with Pen
steps: While drawing with Pen, press Esc once to finish the open path.
The preview line should stop following your pointer.
Press V before clicking elsewhere to avoid starting another path.
why: Ending a path prevents the next click from extending it.

title: Close an open path
steps: Press A to identify the two ends of your own open path.
Press P and hover over one endpoint until the continue-path cursor appears; click it.
Click the other endpoint when the small close-path circle appears. Check the closed outline.
why: A closed path encloses an area for fill and shape operations.

title: Join two endpoints
steps: Press A and Shift-click the two endpoints you want to connect.
Choose Object > Path > Join (Ctrl+J).
A line should connect the selected endpoints; undo if the wrong ends were selected.
why: Joining connects the selected path ends.

title: Average two endpoints first
steps: Press A and Shift-click exactly two endpoints.
Choose Object > Path > Average; choose Both and click OK if you want them at the same position.
Use Object > Path > Join to connect them if required. Check for a single continuous path.
why: Averaging moves points to a shared position before joining.

title: Add an anchor point
steps: Select a path with A. Hold Pen in the toolbar and choose Add Anchor Point.
Click directly on the existing path segment, not the blank artboard.
Press A and click the new small square to confirm it can be moved.
why: Adding an anchor provides another location to control geometry.

title: Remove an extra anchor
steps: Select the path with A and hold Pen to choose Delete Anchor Point.
Click only the extra anchor on your own path.
Check that the path remains continuous; Ctrl+Z if its shape changes too much.
why: Removing an anchor with this tool preserves path continuity.

title: Convert corner to smooth
steps: Select the corner anchor with A.
Hold Pen and choose Anchor Point tool (Shift+C). Drag outward from the corner to pull handles.
Check that the corner becomes a rounded curve; adjust handles with A.
why: A smooth point has handles that shape curves on both sides.

title: Convert smooth point to corner
steps: Select the smooth anchor with A.
Choose Anchor Point tool (Shift+C), then click that anchor once to remove its direction handles.
The curve at that point becomes a corner. Undo if the wrong point changes.
why: Corner points allow abrupt direction changes.

title: Move one anchor point
steps: Press A and click the path edge, then click one small anchor square.
Only that point should show as selected; drag it slightly.
The neighboring segments should change while other points stay put. Ctrl+Z if the whole object moves.
why: Direct Selection changes the path without moving the whole object.

title: Cut a path at two points
steps: Select your path and hold Eraser to find Scissors (C).
Click two locations on the path itself to split it.
Press V or A to select the resulting segment separately; undo if you cut the wrong section.
why: Scissors splits paths rather than trimming by a filled area.

title: Slice a filled shape
steps: Save a copy of your shape if it must remain editable. Select it with V.
Hold Eraser to find Knife; drag across the selected filled shape from outside one edge to outside another.
Press V and move one piece slightly to confirm the split, then undo the move if desired.
why: Knife can divide a filled vector object into separate shapes.

title: Erase part of vector artwork
steps: Select only the vector artwork you intend to erase with V.
Press Shift+E for Eraser and drag across the unwanted part.
Inspect the new path edges. Undo if other objects were affected; do not erase teacher templates.
why: Selection restricts which editable objects are affected.

title: Smooth a rough path
steps: Select your own rough vector path. Locate Smooth under the Pencil/Shaper tool group in the Advanced toolbar.
Drag Smooth along a small rough section of the selected path.
Compare curves and undo if detail was lost; repeat gently rather than smoothing the entire drawing at once.
why: Smoothing reduces irregular path geometry.

title: Simplify dense vector points
steps: Duplicate the original path before simplifying it.
Select the duplicate with V and choose Object > Path > Simplify.
Compare the preview and point count; adjust the slider until the intended shape remains, then confirm.
why: Simplification reduces anchors and can change fine detail.

title: Find and remove stray points
steps: Save your file and click away from artwork.
Choose Select > Object > Stray Points. Inspect any selected isolated anchors before deleting.
Press Delete only if they are unwanted points in your own work; undo if anything useful disappears.
why: Unconnected points can be left behind by editing.

title: Offset a path
steps: Select your closed shape with V and choose Object > Path > Offset Path.
Enter a positive offset for a larger outline or negative for an inset; turn on Preview.
Click OK and inspect the additional path in Layers. Keep or style it as the assignment requires.
why: An offset creates a new contour at a measured distance.

title: Remove the fill only
steps: Select a shape with V. Click the solid Fill square at the bottom of the left toolbar.
Click the None swatch, the white square with a red diagonal slash.
The inside should become empty while the outline stays visible.
why: Removing fill makes the interior unpainted.

title: Remove the stroke only
steps: Select your shape with V and click the hollow Stroke square at the bottom of the toolbar.
Click None (red diagonal slash).
The outline disappears while the fill remains. If both are gone, use Ctrl+Z.
why: Fill and stroke can be edited independently.

title: Swap fill and stroke
steps: Select your shape with V. Find the overlapping Fill and Stroke squares at the bottom of the toolbar.
Click the small curved double arrow beside them or press Shift+X.
The inside color and outline color should exchange places.
why: The swap exchanges both paint attributes.

title: Reset default paint colors
steps: Select only the artwork you want to reset with V.
Press D outside text editing, or click the small black-and-white default swatch below Fill and Stroke.
The shape should have white fill and black stroke; undo if this was not intended.
why: D applies the standard paint attributes.

title: Outline has wrong thickness
steps: Select your path with V and open Window > Stroke.
Find Weight at the top and enter a larger or smaller value in pt.
Check the outline on the artboard; a 0 or None stroke may not be visible.
why: Weight sets the thickness of the path outline.

title: Make dashed lines
steps: Select a path with V, then open Window > Stroke and Show Options from the panel menu if needed.
Check Dashed Line. Enter a dash length and gap length.
Inspect the repeating spaces along the stroke; change the values to match the assignment.
why: Dash settings create repeated painted and unpainted segments.

title: Round line ends
steps: Select a stroked open line with V. Open Window > Stroke and expand options.
In Cap, click the middle Round Cap icon (hover to confirm).
The line ends should look semicircular rather than square.
why: Caps affect the endpoints of open strokes.

title: Round stroke corners
steps: Select a stroked path with corners and open Window > Stroke.
Under Corner, click Round Join, usually the middle icon.
Inspect the stroke at a corner; the original anchor location stays unchanged.
why: Joins determine how stroke edges meet at corners.

title: Align stroke inside shape
steps: Select a closed shape with V. Open Window > Stroke and show options.
Find Align Stroke and select Align Stroke to Inside.
Check that the outer boundary now follows the original path; open paths may not offer this option.
why: Stroke alignment positions the outline relative to the path.

title: Sample color from another object
steps: Select the object whose color should change using V.
Press I for Eyedropper and click the donor object's colored area.
Check the selected object's appearance. Eyedropper can copy other appearance attributes too; undo if undesired.
why: Eyedropper can sample appearance as well as color.

title: Enter a hex color
steps: Select your object and click the solid Fill or hollow Stroke square.
Double-click the chosen square to open Color Picker. Find the field marked # and enter the six-character hex value.
Click OK and verify the intended part of the object changed.
why: Numeric color values support consistent palettes.

title: Save reusable color swatch
steps: Choose the desired Fill color first. Open Window > Swatches.
Click New Swatch (plus icon or panel menu > New Swatch), enter a name and confirm.
Select a different object and click the new swatch to verify it is reusable.
why: Swatches let you reuse colors throughout the document.

title: Change one gradient stop
steps: Select your gradient-filled shape with V and open Window > Gradient.
Double-click the small color stop beneath the gradient ramp that you want to change.
Choose a new color in the pop-up; the other stop should remain unchanged.
why: Each stop controls color at a different gradient position.

title: Change gradient direction
steps: Select your gradient-filled shape and press G for Gradient.
Drag across the shape in the direction you want the colors to flow; start and end positions affect the transition.
Inspect the result, then press V to exit Gradient.
why: Gradient direction controls the transition across the shape.

title: Make a radial gradient
steps: Select your object and open Window > Gradient.
Click Radial Gradient in the type controls (circle icon, or Type menu).
Adjust the stops and use G to position the center; check that colors radiate outward.
why: A radial gradient spreads from a center point.

title: Add a gradient color stop
steps: Select the gradient object and open Window > Gradient.
Click just beneath the ramp between existing color stops to add a stop; double-click the new stop to set its color.
Move the stop along the ramp to position the transition.
why: Additional stops introduce intermediate colors.

title: Remove an unwanted gradient stop
steps: Select the gradient object and open Window > Gradient.
Click the unwanted color stop under the ramp, then click the Delete Stop/trash icon or drag it away from the ramp.
Verify that the remaining colors still blend; keep at least two stops.
why: Removing a stop simplifies the transition.

title: Set object opacity
steps: Select only the intended object with V. Open Window > Transparency.
Find Opacity and change the percentage, such as 50% for a semitransparent shape.
Objects underneath should become visible through it. Restore 100% for an opaque object.
why: Opacity changes how much underlying artwork shows through.

title: Make a variable-width stroke
steps: Select a path with a visible stroke and press Shift+W for Width tool.
Hover over the path until a width marker appears, then drag outward from the path.
The stroke widens locally; press V to inspect the tapered result.
why: Width points vary stroke thickness along a path.

title: Artwork color looks faded
steps: Select the faded object with V and open Window > Transparency; check Opacity and blending mode.
If the opacity is low, restore it to 100% if appropriate. In Window > Appearance, check if its fill itself has lower opacity.
Check whether Isolation mode is dimming other objects. Press Esc if a group breadcrumb appears above the artwork.
why: Opacity and appearance effects can alter visible color.

title: Add a drop shadow
steps: Select your artwork with V. Open Effect > Stylize > Drop Shadow (under Illustrator Effects).
Enable Preview; adjust Opacity, X Offset, Y Offset and Blur to create a readable shadow.
Click OK and check the shadow behind the artwork, not covering your text.
why: A live effect adds a shadow without changing the original path.

title: Edit a live effect
steps: Select the object with the effect. Open Window > Appearance.
Locate the named effect entry, such as Drop Shadow, and click its underlined name.
Adjust the effect dialog with Preview, then confirm; avoid adding a second copy of the same effect.
why: Live effects stay editable in Appearance.

title: Remove a live effect
steps: Select the object and open Window > Appearance.
Click the row for the unwanted effect only, then click the trash button at the bottom of the panel.
Verify that the object remains and just that effect disappears.
why: Removing the effect preserves the underlying geometry.

title: Add another stroke
steps: Select your object and open Window > Appearance.
Open the panel menu and choose Add New Stroke. Click its new Stroke row to set its color and weight.
Reorder the appearance rows if necessary so both outlines are visible.
why: Appearance can stack multiple strokes on one object.

title: Subtract with Shape Builder
steps: Press V and select both overlapping vector shapes with Shift-click.
Press Shift+M. Hold Alt and move over the unwanted region; the cursor should show a minus sign.
Click or drag across only that region, then release Alt and inspect the resulting shapes.
why: Alt switches the tool from combining to subtracting.

title: Shape Builder does nothing
steps: Press V and Shift-click each editable overlapping vector shape. Confirm both have selection edges.
Press Shift+M and hover over the overlap. If no region highlights, check for a placed raster image, locked shapes or lack of overlap.
Use actual vector paths and retry. If you only want a picture cropped, use Clipping Mask instead.
why: The tool needs eligible selected paths and usable regions.

title: Shape Builder leaves small gaps
steps: Zoom in with Z to see whether the paths really overlap or have a tiny gap.
Use A to adjust your own anchor points or V to overlap the two shapes slightly.
Select both with V, press Shift+M again and check that the intended region highlights before merging.
why: Visible outlines may appear connected while the underlying paths are separated.

title: Unite overlapping objects
steps: Select two overlapping shapes with V and Shift-click. Open Window > Pathfinder.
Under Shape Modes, hover over the first icon to confirm Unite and click it.
The internal dividing edge should disappear and one combined outline remain. Undo if the result is wrong.
why: Unite combines filled regions into a single resulting shape or compound path.

title: Cut front shape out of back
steps: Put the cutter shape above the base using Object > Arrange > Bring to Front if necessary.
With V, Shift-select the cutter and base. Open Window > Pathfinder and click Minus Front (second Shape Modes icon).
Check that the front shape has cut a hole or notch in the back shape. Undo if reversed.
why: Minus Front subtracts front shapes from the back shape.

title: Keep only overlap
steps: Select overlapping vector shapes with V and Shift-click. Open Window > Pathfinder.
Click Intersect, the third Shape Modes icon.
Only the overlapping region should remain; Ctrl+Z restores the originals if needed.
why: Intersect retains their common area.

title: Remove overlap but keep outer pieces
steps: Select two overlapping shapes using V and Shift-click. Open Window > Pathfinder.
Click Exclude, the fourth Shape Modes icon.
The overlap should become a cutout while the outer regions remain. Inspect the result before saving.
why: Exclude removes the shared region between two overlapping shapes.

title: Split every overlapping region
steps: Select the overlapping shapes with V and open Window > Pathfinder.
Click Divide in the lower Pathfinders row. Use Object > Ungroup if necessary.
Click away, then select an individual region with V to check that it is separate.
why: Divide separates artwork at intersections.

title: Pathfinder removes wrong shape
steps: Press Ctrl+Z to recover your original shapes.
Open Window > Layers and verify which object sits above the other; select only the two intended objects with V.
For Minus Front, bring the cutter above the base via Object > Arrange and apply again. For overlap-only, use Intersect.
why: Subtraction depends on which object is in front.

title: Make a hole inside a shape
steps: Draw a smaller closed path inside a larger closed path. Select both with V and Shift-click.
Choose Object > Compound Path > Make (Ctrl+8).
Check that the middle shows through. If not, inspect whether the inner shape is fully enclosed and the paths are closed.
why: Compound paths can define unpainted interiors.

title: Release a compound path
steps: Select your compound path with V and choose Object > Compound Path > Release.
Look at the artboard and Layers panel; the inner and outer paths become separate objects again.
Restore their fills or use Ctrl+Z if you wanted to preserve the hole.
why: Release returns constituent paths, which may have different visible appearance.

title: Crop artwork with a shape
steps: Place a closed vector shape above the artwork you want to crop. With V, Shift-select both.
Choose Object > Clipping Mask > Make (Ctrl+7).
Only artwork within the top shape should remain visible; the hidden part is not deleted.
why: The upper path defines what remains visible without deleting hidden areas.

title: Clipping mask is blank
steps: Press Ctrl+Z if the mask was just made. In Window > Layers, inspect the stacking order.
Ensure the top object is a closed vector path and overlaps the intended image; select both with V.
