Choose Object > Clipping Mask > Make again. If blank, check image position within the mask.
why: The topmost selected object becomes the clipping path.

title: Move image inside clipping mask
steps: Select the clipping group with V and double-click it to enter Isolation mode.
Use A or the Edit Contents control in Properties to select the image inside, not the outer path.
Drag the image inside the outline, then press Esc to exit. The clipping boundary should stay still.
why: Mask geometry and its contents remain separately editable.

title: Change clipping mask shape
steps: Select the clipping group with V. In Properties, choose Edit Clipping Path if shown, or use A to select its boundary.
Drag the mask's anchors or resize its path carefully, without moving the image.
Press Esc and verify that the newly visible crop matches the edited boundary.
why: A mask can be edited without replacing the image.

title: Uncrop a clipping mask
steps: Select your clipping group with V. Choose Object > Clipping Mask > Release.
The full original artwork should reappear; the former mask path may have no fill or stroke.
Inspect Layers before deleting or styling the now separate mask path.
why: Releasing makes the original artwork visible again.

title: Draw inside existing shape
steps: Select a filled shape with V. At the bottom of the toolbar click Draw Inside (or cycle drawing modes with Shift+D until Draw Inside is indicated).
A dashed corner outline should surround the selected shape. Draw or place your new artwork inside it.
Choose Draw Normal when finished; the new artwork should remain clipped to the shape.
why: Draw Inside clips new marks to the chosen shape.

title: Drawing goes behind everything
steps: Look under the Fill and Stroke squares at the drawing mode icons; Draw Behind may be active.
Click Draw Normal (first icon) before creating another shape.
Check new artwork appears in front of its current layer's objects. For existing art use Object > Arrange.
why: Draw Behind inserts artwork beneath the selected object or existing stack.

title: Live Paint Bucket basics
steps: Select overlapping vector paths with V. Choose Object > Live Paint > Make.
Press K for Live Paint Bucket, choose a swatch, then hover inside a region until it highlights.
Click to fill only that region. Repeat with other colors as needed.
why: Live Paint treats bounded regions as individually paintable areas.

title: Live Paint refuses to fill region
steps: Check whether the paths belong to a Live Paint group by selecting them; create one with Object > Live Paint > Make if necessary.
Press K and hover the area. If the boundary does not highlight, zoom in and inspect gaps between paths.
Close the gaps in your own paths or use Object > Live Paint > Gap Options with Preview if appropriate.
why: A gap can prevent a region from being recognized as closed.

title: Expand Live Paint artwork
steps: Save an editable copy of the Live Paint group first.
Select the group with V and choose Object > Live Paint > Expand.
Use A to inspect individual regions. They no longer behave as a live paint group.
why: Expansion converts live regions into ordinary editable vector objects.

title: Convert stroke to a filled shape
steps: Duplicate the stroked object first if you might need an editable stroke.
Select the copy with V and choose Object > Path > Outline Stroke.
Use A to inspect the new filled outline; Stroke Weight no longer controls its original width.
why: An outlined stroke becomes filled vector geometry rather than a stroke attribute.

title: Expand appearance safely
steps: Save the original artwork or duplicate it. Select the copy with V.
Choose Object > Expand Appearance when available; if not, the object may not have a live appearance to expand.
Open Window > Layers to inspect the new shapes. Undo if editability was needed.
why: Expansion may create more paths and remove live-effect editability.

title: Text cursor will not leave typing
steps: If a text caret is blinking, press Ctrl+Enter to finish editing and select the type object.
Press V for the black arrow, then click an empty area if you want to deselect.
When no caret is blinking, letter shortcuts should work instead of typing into the title.
why: Text editing and object selection are separate modes.

title: Change font family
steps: Select your type object with V or highlight specific letters with T.
Open Window > Type > Character. Click the Font Family field at the top and type an installed font name.
Choose the matching font and check the selected text; ask the teacher if the font is missing.
why: A selected font changes the appearance of your own words.

title: Change font size
steps: Select your type object with V or highlight part of it with T.
Open Window > Type > Character and find the Font Size field (pt). Enter the intended size.
Press Enter and check the text fits the design; undo if other letters changed unintentionally.
why: Font size controls letter scale without needing to drag the entire object.

title: Change text color
steps: Press T and highlight the letters to recolor, or use V for the whole type object.
Click the solid Fill square at the bottom of the left toolbar; double-click to open Color Picker.
Choose a color and click OK. If only an outline changes, select Fill instead of Stroke.
why: Type inherits fill and stroke like other vector artwork.

title: Bold or italic text
steps: Select the text with T or the entire object with V. Open Window > Type > Character.
Open the Font Style dropdown below or beside the family name. Choose Bold or Italic if that font provides it.
Check the result; use an approved alternative font if the style is not available.
why: Font styles depend on the installed font family.

title: Create a paragraph text box
steps: Press T and drag a rectangle on the artboard, rather than clicking once.
Type your own words into the text area; lines should wrap at the box edges.
With V, resize the box using its handles, and check that all text is visible.
why: Area type wraps text inside a defined boundary.

title: Text box has red plus
steps: Select the text box with V. Look for a small red plus near its lower-right output port, meaning text overflows.
Drag a box edge outward to enlarge the area, or highlight text with T and reduce the size via Character.
Check the red plus disappears and the last words are visible.
why: The plus indicates more text than fits inside the box.

title: Convert point type to area type
steps: Select your point text using V. Choose Type > Convert to Area Type when available (or double-click the conversion widget near its edge).
Use V to resize the new text box, watching lines wrap instead of stretching.
If the option is unavailable, create an area text box with T and copy your own text into it.
why: Area type flows within a defined boundary.

title: Point type stretched accidentally
steps: Press Ctrl+Z if you just stretched the letters. Select the text with V.
Open Window > Type > Character, show options and check Horizontal Scale and Vertical Scale; set to 100% if the assignment requires unstretched type.
Change Font Size instead for proportional sizing. If outlines were already made, return to the editable original.
why: Changing font size is different from distorting the object.

title: Adjust space between lines
steps: Highlight the lines using T, then open Window > Type > Character.
Find Leading (the stacked A symbols) and increase or decrease the pt value.
Inspect the gap between lines and make sure letters do not overlap.
why: Leading controls the distance between text baselines.

title: Change spacing across a word
steps: Highlight the word or range with T. Open Window > Type > Character.
Find Tracking (VA with a horizontal arrow) and slightly increase or decrease the value.
Check the overall spacing changes evenly across the selection.
why: Tracking adds or removes spacing across multiple selected characters.

title: Adjust spacing between two letters
steps: Press T and click between the two letters you want to adjust, without selecting the whole word.
Open Window > Type > Character and find Kerning (V/A spacing field). Enter a small positive or negative value.
Check only that letter pair changes spacing; leave others as they were.
why: Kerning controls spacing for an individual letter pair.

title: Align a paragraph
steps: Click inside your paragraph or select its text box. Open Window > Type > Paragraph.
Click Align Left, Center or Align Right; hover over the horizontal line icons to identify them.
Check how lines align within the text box, not the artboard itself.
why: Paragraph alignment positions lines within the text area or relative to its point.

title: Make superscript characters
steps: With T, highlight just the characters meant to sit above the baseline.
Open Window > Type > Character and choose Superscript from its panel menu.
The highlighted characters should get smaller and rise; undo if the entire title changed.
why: Superscript raises and typically reduces selected characters.

title: Make subscript characters
steps: With T, highlight just the characters meant to sit below the baseline.
Open Window > Type > Character and choose Subscript from the panel menu.
Check that the selected characters are smaller and lower than adjacent text.
why: Subscript positions characters below the main baseline.

title: Move selected letters up or down
steps: Highlight the relevant letters with T. Open Window > Type > Character and choose Show Options if needed.
Find Baseline Shift (A with an up/down arrow). Enter a small positive value to raise or negative to lower.
Check that only the selected letters move relative to the text line.
why: Baseline shift adjusts vertical placement without moving the entire text object.

title: Put text around a circle
steps: Draw a circle with L and Shift-drag; duplicate it first if you also need the visible circle.
Hold T in the left toolbar and choose Type on a Path Tool, then click the circle edge.
Type your own text. Use V to select the resulting text path and Character to change size. The original circle's fill/stroke may disappear when converted to type.
why: Type follows the selected path, whose original paint may be removed.

title: Text on path is upside down
steps: Select the curved text object with V. Open Type > Type on a Path > Type on a Path Options.
Check or uncheck Flip and enable Preview to see which side the letters sit on.
Click OK when the words face the correct direction; adjust spacing if needed.
why: The flip option changes which side of the path carries text.

title: Move text along a curve
steps: Select the text path with V or A. Look for the small start, center and end brackets near its baseline.
Drag the center bracket along the curve without pulling it across the path unless you want to flip it.
Check the text moves along the curve; keep the end brackets far enough apart to show all letters.
why: The brackets define the position of the type along its path.

title: Text on path disappears
steps: Select the type path with V. Look for a red plus at its end bracket, indicating overflow.
Reduce the font size in Window > Type > Character or move the end bracket farther along the path.
If text is still missing, check the Fill color and that the layer eye is visible.
why: Type requires enough usable path length for all characters.

title: Warp text with live effect
steps: Select your live text object with V; keep an editable copy.
Open Effect > Warp and choose the requested style, such as Arc. Check Preview and adjust Bend.
Confirm only once the text remains readable. Edit later through Window > Appearance.
why: A live warp changes appearance while preserving editable type.

title: Convert text to outlines
steps: Save the live-text AI file first. Duplicate the text on a separate layer if you need to preserve editability.
Select the duplicate with V and choose Type > Create Outlines (Ctrl+Shift+O).
Press A to see vector anchor points instead of a text caret; spelling cannot be edited in the outlined copy.
why: Outlined letters become vector paths and no longer edit as ordinary text.

title: Cannot type into outlined letters
steps: Select the letters with A and check for anchor points rather than a blinking caret.
If they were just outlined, press Ctrl+Z. Otherwise open the saved live-text version or use T to create a new editable text object.
Use Character to match the style; do not expect outlined paths to work like ordinary text.
why: Outlining removes live type information.

title: Missing font warning
steps: Read the missing-font name in the warning. Keep the original file unchanged.
Use Type > Find/Replace Font or select the text and choose an approved installed substitute via Character, only if the teacher permits.
Check line breaks and appearance after substitution. Do not install fonts or sign into extra services.
why: Font availability varies between computers.

title: Outline a title with a stroke
aliases: make text have a colored edge illustrator
steps: Select the live title with V and open Window > Appearance. Click the panel menu > Add New Stroke.
Click the new Stroke row; choose a contrasting color and enter a readable Weight. Keep its row below Characters so the outline doesn't cover letter interiors.
Check that the text is still editable and the stroke is clearly visible. Reduce Weight if the letters become hard to read.
why: A stroke below the fill keeps the letter interiors readable.

title: Insert a special character
steps: Press T and place the caret where your symbol belongs.
Open Window > Type > Glyphs. Choose the correct font if necessary and double-click the desired symbol cell.
The symbol should appear at the caret; if absent, use an approved font that includes it.
why: Glyphs are characters included in the selected font.

title: Text behind other artwork
steps: Open Window > Layers and expand the layer containing the type object. Select the text using the far-right selection column.
Choose Object > Arrange > Bring to Front, or move its selection square to a higher unlocked layer of your own.
Check the title appears above the covering artwork without deleting it.
why: Other objects can cover otherwise valid text.

title: Center object on artboard
steps: Select your intended object with V and open Window > Align.
Find Align To and choose Align to Artboard. Click Horizontal Align Center, then Vertical Align Center.
The object's center should match the active white board's center; verify the correct board was active.
why: The artboard becomes the alignment reference.

title: Align several objects to each other
steps: Press V and Shift-click each intended shape, then open Window > Align.
Set Align To: Selection. Hover over the icons to choose the correct edge or center.
Click once and inspect whether the shapes line up with each other, not the page.
why: The selected set provides the alignment boundary.

title: Align to a key object
steps: Select all intended objects with V and Shift-click. Click the reference object again without Shift; its outline should get thicker.
Open Window > Align and verify Align to Key Object is selected.
Apply the desired alignment. The key object should stay put while others move.
why: The key object stays fixed while others align to it.

title: Space objects evenly
steps: Select three or more objects using V and Shift-click. Open Window > Align; show options if needed.
Under Distribute Spacing choose horizontal or vertical spacing. To set a fixed gap, click one selected object again to make it key and enter the spacing value.
Click the distribution icon and inspect the gaps between object edges.
why: Equal gaps differ from equal center-to-center distances.

title: Show document grid
steps: Click View > Show Grid in the top menu (Ctrl+apostrophe in standard Windows Illustrator).
Look for a regular square guide grid across the document. Keep it visible when capturing required project progress screenshots.
If the assignment calls for actual grid lines in the exported design, use Rectangular Grid instead; view grids are not exported.
why: The document grid is a view aid and does not appear in exported artwork.

title: Objects keep snapping to grid
steps: Look at View > Snap to Grid in the top menu. A check mark means snapping is on.
If your teacher allows freely positioning this artwork, click the checked option to turn it off without changing other preferences.
Use V to drag the object again. If it still jumps, inspect Smart Guides or Snap to Point in View.
why: Snapping can constrain a drag to nearby grid positions.

title: Smart Guides missing
aliases: purple lines when moving shapes illustrator
steps: Click View > Smart Guides to enable it if no check mark appears (Ctrl+U).
Press V and drag your shape near another shape's edge or center.
Look for colored guide lines or labels such as intersect or center. Release when aligned.
why: Smart Guides provide temporary alignment hints while editing.

title: Show rulers
steps: Click View > Rulers > Show Rulers (Ctrl+R).
Horizontal and vertical scales should appear along the top and left of the workspace.
Use their markings to check positions. Do not change unit preferences unless instructed.
why: Rulers show document measurements without printing them.

title: Make a ruler guide
steps: Show rulers with View > Rulers > Show Rulers.
Drag from the top ruler down for a horizontal guide, or from the left ruler right for a vertical guide.
Release at the desired position. The guide is a reference line, not printable artwork.
why: Guides help position artwork and do not export as design objects.

title: Guide will not move
steps: Click View > Guides and inspect Lock Guides; if checked, your guides may be locked.
Only with permission and only for your own guides, click Lock Guides to toggle it off. Select the intended guide with V and move it.
Relock the guides afterward. Do not unlock teacher-protected template elements.
why: Guide locking prevents accidental layout changes.

title: Hide guide lines
steps: Click View > Guides > Hide Guides.
The guide lines should disappear without deleting them. To show them again, use View > Guides > Show Guides.
If the line stays visible it may be a real vector path or document grid; inspect before editing.
why: Guides are nonprinting layout aids; real paths remain visible.

title: Create an extra artboard
steps: Press Shift+O to activate Artboard tool.
Drag an empty workspace rectangle for a new board, away from existing artwork, or open Window > Artboards and click New Artboard.
Press Esc and check the new numbered board in Window > Artboards.
why: Multiple artboards allow separate designs in one document.

title: Rename an artboard
steps: Open Window > Artboards and locate the board number that contains your project.
Double-click its name or open Artboard Options using the panel controls, then enter the requested name.
Confirm and check the renamed entry; exports may use this name.
why: Names help identify boards and may become export filenames.

title: Reorder artboards
steps: Open Window > Artboards and select the board entry in the list.
Drag its row to a new order or use Move Up/Down buttons when shown.
Verify the board numbering in the panel; physical positions may not change.
why: Document order can differ from the physical layout on screen.

title: Move artboard with its artwork
steps: Press Shift+O and select the board. In Properties or the top controls, look for Move Artwork with Artboard.
Enable that option if you want the artwork to travel with the board, then drag the board boundary.
Inspect both board and artwork. Ctrl+Z if an unintended item moved, then Esc.
why: Artboard movement can optionally carry its artwork.

title: Resize artboard without changing artwork
steps: Press Shift+O and click the intended board.
Enter its new W and H in Properties or drag a boundary handle; do not use V to scale selected artwork.
Press Esc and verify the board size changed while artwork retained its original dimensions.
why: Artboards define output regions independently of object size.

title: Landscape versus portrait artboard
steps: Press Shift+O and select the active artboard. Find portrait and landscape icons in Properties or the top controls.
Choose the requested orientation or swap the W and H values.
Press Esc and inspect whether the design fits; artwork is not automatically rearranged.
why: Orientation changes the board boundary, not necessarily the artwork direction.

title: Remove an extra artboard safely
steps: Save a copy first. Open Window > Artboards and identify the extra board by its number or name.
Select only that board's row and click the trash/Delete Artboard control. Do not delete the last board.
Inspect remaining boards and artwork; deleting the board does not necessarily remove its objects.
why: Deleting an artboard does not automatically delete its artwork.

title: Preview just the artboard
steps: Click View > Trim View to hide artwork outside the boards temporarily.
Inspect the design at its board edges. Nothing should be deleted.
Click View > Trim View again to return to normal editing. Use Artboards when exporting for a true crop.
why: Trim View previews cropped artwork without deleting outside geometry.

title: Arrange repeated rows
steps: Select one object with V. Choose Object > Transform > Move, enter the desired horizontal spacing and click Copy.
Press Ctrl+D to repeat that move for the remaining row. Select the row and group it with Ctrl+G if helpful.
Use Move with vertical spacing and Copy to repeat rows. Verify count and spacing against the assignment grid.
why: Measured duplication and distribution produce consistent spacing.

title: Set up a bleed for print
steps: Ask the teacher for the exact bleed measurement before making changes.
Open File > Document Setup and locate the Bleed fields. Enter the assigned value only in your own document.
Check the red bleed boundary beyond the artboard and extend background objects to it only if required for print.
why: Bleed is a print allowance outside the trim boundary.

title: Make a new layer
steps: Open Window > Layers. Identify the layer above or below which your new work belongs.
Click Create New Layer at the bottom of the panel (plus icon), not New Sublayer unless required.
Double-click its name, rename it and select its row before drawing.
why: Independent layers organize objects and stacking.

title: Rename a layer
steps: Open Window > Layers and find your layer by its current name.
Double-click the layer name, or open Layer Options if the dialog appears, and enter a descriptive label.
Press Enter or OK and verify the row shows the new name.
why: Clear names make objects easier to locate.

title: Hide a layer temporarily
steps: Open Window > Layers. Find your layer and the eye icon at its far left.
Click its eye to hide the layer temporarily; click the empty eye column to show it again.
Verify required artwork is visible before saving, exporting or taking a progress screenshot.
why: Hiding a layer does not erase its contents.

title: Lock a background layer
steps: Open Window > Layers. Identify your own background layer.
Click the empty lock column between the eye column and layer name area; a padlock should appear.
Try selecting a foreground shape with V. Your background should no longer move accidentally.
why: Locking prevents accidental selection and edits.

title: Unlock your own object
steps: Open Window > Layers and expand your own layer using its triangle.
Look for a padlock beside the specific item. Click only the lock on your own accidentally locked artwork.
Try V again. Ask the teacher if the lock belongs to a template or you are unsure.
why: A lock blocks selection and editing until released.

title: Move artwork to another layer
steps: Select the object with V and open Window > Layers.
Find the small colored selection square at the far right of its current layer. Drag it onto the target unlocked layer row.
Expand that layer and verify the object moved there; check whether its front/back order changed.
why: Moving the selection indicator relocates the object without recreating it.

title: Group related objects
steps: Press V and Shift-click each related object until all have selection edges.
Choose Object > Group (Ctrl+G).
Click the group with V and check that one bounding box surrounds the set. Use A to edit parts.
why: Grouping allows multiple objects to move as one unit.

title: Ungroup artwork
steps: Select your own group using V. Click Object > Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G).
Click away, then select one former member with V.
If it still selects the whole set, it may contain nested groups; ungroup only as needed.
why: Ungroup removes one level of grouping at a time.

title: Edit inside a group
steps: Double-click the group with V. Look for a breadcrumb bar above the artboard and dimmed outside artwork.
Select and edit the desired member without moving the whole group.
Press Esc to exit Isolation mode; all artwork should return to normal brightness.
why: Isolation temporarily limits selections to the group.

title: Select hidden object in Layers
steps: Open Window > Layers and expand the relevant layer/group triangles.
If your object is hidden, click its empty eye column and ensure its parent layer is visible. If it's merely covered, leave visibility as is.
Click the far-right selection column of the intended item. Look for its colored selection edges before editing.
why: Layers can locate artwork that is difficult to click directly.

title: Send object behind others
steps: Select your object with V. Open Object > Arrange from the top menu.
Choose Send Backward to move one step, or Send to Back to go behind items in its layer.
Inspect the result. Move it to a lower layer if it must sit behind artwork on other layers.
why: Arrange affects relative stacking within the active hierarchy.

title: Place an image file
steps: Click File > Place. Navigate to the assigned folder and select the approved image, then click Place.
The cursor carries a small preview; click for original size or drag on your artboard for a chosen size.
Use V to position it and Shift-drag a corner if resizing proportionally.
why: Placed images can remain linked or be embedded in the document.

title: Missing linked image warning
steps: Open Window > Links and look for a missing-link warning beside the image filename.
Select that entry, click Relink (chain/link icon or panel menu), and navigate to the actual original image file.
Confirm the correct image reappears. If you cannot find the file, ask the teacher rather than substituting a random image.
why: Linked artwork depends on an accessible external file.

title: Embed a linked image
steps: Select the placed image with V and open Window > Links.
Select its link entry and choose Embed Image(s) from the panel menu, or click Embed in Properties if available.
Save and verify Links no longer reports a missing external file for that image; the AI size may increase.
why: Embedding stores image data with the AI document but can increase file size.

title: Image looks pixelated in Illustrator
steps: Press Ctrl+1 to view the image at actual size. Compare its detail with the intended output size.
If the source photo is blurry at normal size, use File > Place to insert a higher-resolution approved original rather than stretching it.
Remember that photos are pixels even inside a vector document; zooming far in can reveal pixels normally.
why: Raster photographs retain their pixel limits even in a vector document.

title: Image Trace basics
steps: Keep a copy of the original approved image. Select the placed image with V and open Window > Image Trace.
Choose an appropriate non-generative preset, enable Preview and compare the traced shapes with the source.
Click Expand only if the assignment requires editable vector paths, then inspect with A.
why: Image Trace approximates raster shapes with vector paths; it is not image generation.

title: Image Trace has too much detail
steps: Select the still-live traced image and open Window > Image Trace.
Choose a simpler preset or reduce Colors when the mode supports it. Use Preview to compare edge detail.
Keep the original photo and only expand after the preview meets the assignment.
why: Trace complexity affects detail and the number of paths.

title: Export only one artboard
steps: Save the AI with Ctrl+S. Open Window > Artboards to find the required board number.
Choose File > Export > Export As, select PNG/JPG and check Use Artboards. Select Range and enter that number.
Click Export, choose the required background and resolution, and inspect the new image in your destination folder.
why: A range limits export to specified artboards.

title: Export every artboard at once
steps: Save the AI, then click File > Export > Export for Screens.
Select the Artboards tab, check the boards required, choose the destination and add the requested format/scale.
Click Export Artboard and inspect every output filename and image. For an opaque PNG, use an actual background shape or Export As with White background.
why: Batch export creates separate outputs for multiple boards.

title: PNG has a white background
steps: Open View > Show Transparency Grid to see whether the white-looking area is transparent or an actual white rectangle.
If the assignment really needs transparency, hide only your own background shape, then save the AI.
Choose File > Export > Export As > PNG, check Use Artboards, and choose Transparent in PNG Background Color. For projects requiring opaque white, do not remove the background.
why: PNG can store transparent pixels, but actual white artwork remains white.

title: PNG should have a colored background
steps: Open the active board and use M to draw a rectangle covering it from corner to corner. Set its Fill to the required color and Stroke to None.
Choose Object > Arrange > Send to Back; if needed, place the rectangle on your own bottom background layer and lock it.
Save the AI, then File > Export > Export As > PNG with Use Artboards; choose White instead of Transparent if opaque white is required. Reopen the exported image to confirm coverage.
why: A solid object supplies a planned background color.

title: Exported image includes extra artwork
steps: Save the AI and choose File > Export > Export As.
Select the output format, check Use Artboards and choose the intended board range.
Export to a new filename, then open it to verify that off-board objects are cropped and the required board is intact.
why: Use Artboards restricts export to board boundaries.

title: Exported image looks blurry
steps: Open the original AI, not the small PNG. Check the size/resolution required by your teacher.
Choose File > Export > Export As > PNG and Use Artboards. Select the required Resolution in PNG Options (or Export for Screens with the required scale).
Open the new file at normal size. A low-resolution placed photo will still be blurry; replacing it with an approved higher-resolution original may be necessary.
why: Raster export quality depends on its pixel dimensions.

title: Export SVG for vector use
steps: Save your editable AI. Choose File > Export > Export As and select SVG in the format dropdown.
Check Use Artboards for the required boundary and choose the assigned output folder.
Click Export, confirm the requested SVG options, and inspect the result. Keep the original AI for further editing.
why: SVG represents scalable artwork but may handle effects and fonts differently.

title: Save PDF copy
steps: Press Ctrl+S to save the AI first. Click File > Save a Copy and choose Adobe PDF as the format.
Choose the assigned folder and filename, then click Save. Use the PDF preset your teacher requests.
Open the PDF and verify its pages. Return to editing the original AI, not the PDF copy.
why: PDF is useful for viewing and printing but should not replace the working AI.

title: Find exported files
steps: If you remember where you exported, press Windows+E and click that folder in File Explorer.
If not, open Illustrator File > Export > Export As to see the last destination, then cancel without overwriting. Navigate to that location in Explorer.
Sort by Date modified or search for the project name. Open the .png or .jpg to verify it is the correct image, not the .ai.
why: The export destination may differ from the working document folder.

title: Submit AI and PNG together
steps: In Illustrator press Ctrl+S to save the editable AI. Then File > Export > Export As > PNG, check Use Artboards and select the assigned opaque background.
Open File Explorer with Windows+E and verify both the .ai and .png in the assigned folder.
In Classroom click your class > Classwork > assignment title > View assignment. Under Your work choose + Add or create > File; upload both files, check the names, then Turn in and confirm.
If your assignment has a Slides template, insert the required PNG and progress screenshots there too, as your teacher directs.
why: The teacher may need both editable geometry and the finished image.

title: Keep an earlier version
steps: Open File > Save As and choose the assigned storage location.
Give the new AI a distinct version name such as project-v2.ai; do not overwrite your earlier version.
Click Save and check the document tab shows the new filename before continuing.
why: Versioned copies preserve earlier stages of a design.

title: AI file not opening from browser
steps: In Chrome press Ctrl+J and locate the downloaded AI file; use Show in folder if available.
Open Illustrator, click File > Open, navigate to the downloaded file and select it.
If it remains unreadable, tell your teacher the exact error. Do not install an unknown app or change file permissions.
why: Browser previews may not support native Illustrator artwork.

title: Export warning about missing fonts
steps: Read the warning and keep the live-text AI file saved.
Use Window > Type > Character or Type > Find/Replace Font to identify the missing font. Ask whether an installed substitute or an outlined copy is acceptable.
Make changes only in an approved copy and compare the export with the original layout.
why: Different machines and formats can render unavailable fonts differently.

title: Illustrator freezes during export
steps: Stop clicking Export repeatedly. Wait briefly and check whether the progress indicator advances.
If Illustrator responds, cancel once and save your AI before retrying to an approved folder.
If the entire program remains frozen, leave it open and ask the teacher; unsaved work may be lost if forced closed.
why: Forced closure can lose unsaved work.

title: Adobe file save fails
steps: Read the exact save error and keep the document open.
Choose File > Save As, select an approved writable school folder and enter a new simple filename ending in .ai.
If it still fails or requests administrator permission, stop and show the teacher the error. Do not close unsaved work.
why: Saving to an unavailable location can fail even when artwork is intact.

title: Screenshot Illustrator progress
steps: Fit the artwork with Ctrl+0 and show the required grid via View > Show Grid (or make the actual planning grid visible). Open the relevant panel via Window so your process is visible.
Press Windows+Shift+S, select Rectangular Snip and drag around your work, including the visible grid and required evidence.
Open your project Slides, select the correct progress slide and press Ctrl+V. Check the image is readable. Save the screenshot through the snipping notification if a file is required.
why: Progress screenshots document the tools and steps you used.
